# THE OCEAN OF THE KULA

<insert><unclear>26 VII</unclear></insert>
# TANTRA
<note>Tantra refers to a vast body of esoteric Indian scriptures focusing on ritual, meditation, and the expansion of consciousness.</note>

->**RAM KUMAR RAI**<-

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the Kularnava Tantra, a foundational text of the Kaula school of Tantra. It establishes the traditional setting of a divine dialogue between Shiva and Parvati.</meta>

# The Holy Kularnava Tantra

## First Chapter

---

> Seated upon the peak of Mount Kailasa, Parvati questioned the Supreme Lord, the God of Gods, the Teacher of the World, the Lord of Supreme Bliss. (1)

<note>Mount Kailasa is traditionally considered the earthly abode of Lord Shiva and a symbol of the highest state of consciousness.</note>

->The Holy Goddess said:<-

> O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Ordainer of the five sacred acts <note>The five acts (panchakritya) are creation, preservation, destruction, concealment, and grace.</note>, All-Knowing One, easily reached through devotion, Lover of those who seek refuge! (2)
>
> Lord of the Kula <term>Kula: the divine family or the path of Shakti</term>, Supreme Sovereign, Ocean of the nectar of compassion! In this essence-less, terrible cycle of worldly existence <term>Samsara: the continuous cycle of birth, death, and rebirth</term>, which is stained by every kind of misery, (3)
>
> Infinite multitudes of living beings, inhabiting various types of bodies, are born and die, yet no liberation is found for them. (4)
>
> Always afflicted by sorrow, O God, nowhere is happiness found. By what means, O Lord of Gods, can they be released? Tell me, my Lord. (5)

<summary>The text opens with Goddess Parvati asking Lord Shiva how living beings, trapped in the painful and repetitive cycle of birth and death, can find ultimate spiritual liberation.</summary>
<keywords>Kularnava Tantra, Shiva, Parvati, Kailasa, Samsara, Moksha, compassion, liberation, five sacred acts</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>On the previous page, Goddess Parvati expressed her compassion for living beings trapped in the cycle of birth and death (Samsara) and asked Lord Shiva for the means of their liberation. This page begins Shiva's response, establishing the metaphysical foundation of the soul's relationship to the Divine.</meta>

# In the Holy Kularnava Tantra

The Holy Lord said:

->Listen, O Goddess, I shall speak of that which you ask me;<-
->merely by hearing this, a person is liberated from the cycle of worldly existence. (6)<-

->O Goddess, there exists the Partless Shiva, whose nature is the Supreme Reality;<-
->He is all-knowing, the creator of all, the Lord of all, stainless, and one without a second. (7)<-
<note>original: "Parabrahma" — the absolute, ultimate reality in Hindu philosophy.</note>

->He is self-luminous, without beginning or end, changeless, and higher than the highest;<-
->He is without qualities, consisting of Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss. Portions of Him are called living beings. (8)<-
<note>original: "Saccidananda" — a compound describing the nature of the divine as Being (Sat), Consciousness (Cit), and Bliss (Ananda).</note>
->Covered by beginningless ignorance, they are like sparks from a fire.<-

### *Forms of Shiva, characteristics of Creatures and their conditions:*

Self-luminous, without a beginning or an end, devoid of all attributes, changeless, highest of the highest, devoid of qualities, He is Truth-Consciousness-Bliss. All the myriad living creatures <term>Jivas: individual souls or living beings</term> are just a portion of Him, but due to ageless ignorance, they have separated from Him like sparks; though emerging from a fire, they appear separate from it.

->Separated by the conditions of the womb and other limitations, they are bound by actions and instruments;<-
->all of these bring sorrow, as beings are controlled by their own merits and sins. (9-10)<-
->In every birth, these ignorant humans attain a body, a lifespan,<-
->and experiences produced by their past deeds, according to their respective species.<-
->The subtle body is indestructible, my dear, until the moment of final liberation. (11)<-
<term>Linga-sharira: the subtle or "sign" body that carries the soul's impressions (samskaras) from one life to the next.</term>

Due to bearing the label of being "born" and their beginningless actions, they remain separated from Shiva and are regulated by the happiness of their virtues and the pains of their sins. In accordance with their deeds, they obtain bodily forms, lifespans, and destinies according to their respective species. These ignorant creatures endlessly pass from birth to birth.

->Stationary objects, worms, water-born creatures, birds, animals, humans,<-
->the righteous, the gods, and likewise those seeking liberation, follow this order. (12)<-
->Taking up the four kinds of bodies thousands and thousands of times.<-

### *Four kinds of Creatures:*

Various kinds of living beings are born on this earth a thousand times in various gradations of life: for example, those born from the ground <note>original: "Udbhij" — such as plants or minerals</note>; those born from sweat <note>original: "Svedaja" — such as insects or lice</note>; such...

<summary>Lord Shiva describes the nature of the Supreme Reality (Shiva) as pure consciousness and explains how individual souls (Jivas) are like sparks of that divine fire, separated by ignorance and bound to the cycle of rebirth by their karma.</summary>
<keywords>Shiva, Parabrahma, Saccidananda, Jiva, Karma, Rebirth, Samsara, Subtle Body, Four types of birth</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse by Lord Shiva regarding the soul's journey through various incarnations, following the previous page's description of the soul being like a spark separated from the divine fire of Shiva (Saccidananda).</meta>

...as, insects etc.; <term>Andaja: those born from eggs</term>, such as birds, etc.; and <term>Jarayuja: those born from a womb</term>, such as animals, humans in different stages of development, Gods, and the Liberated Beings.

->By virtuous deeds one becomes human; if one becomes a knower, one attains liberation. (13)<-
->Among the eighty-four hundred thousand types of bodies for the embodied,<-
->the knowledge of Truth is not found anywhere except in the human state. (14)<-
->In this world, even after thousands upon thousands of births, O Parvati!<-
->a creature occasionally attains human birth through the accumulation of merit. (15)<-
<note>Pārvatī: The Goddess and consort of Shiva, who is receiving this teaching.</note>

### *Superiority of human body :*

Of the 8.4 million bodily forms, the human body is the most important, for it is this form in which one gets <note>original: "Tattvajnana" — the direct realization of the ultimate Essence or Truth.</note> knowledge of the Essence. This knowledge of Essence cannot be attained in any other form than human. Even in hundreds of thousands of births, O Pārvatī! when due to the accumulation of virtuous deeds, a human being with efforts obtains the knowledge of Essence, he becomes Liberated.

->Having attained the rare human form, which serves as a ladder to liberation,<-
->if one does not save one's self, then who in this world is a greater sinner? (16)<-

Endowed with the human form as a ladder for <term>Emancipation: Moksha, or the release from the cycle of rebirth</term>, if one does not liberate his <term>Atman: the individual soul or inner Self</term>, then who can be a greater sinner than him?

->Furthermore, having attained a superior birth and the full use of the senses,<-
->one who does not recognize what is good for the soul is a self-slayer. (17)<-

Obtaining a superior birth and bestowed with a beautiful set of motor and sensory organs, one who does not understand the best of his interests <note>The text suggests that "best interests" refers to spiritual welfare rather than material gain.</note> is like one who is a self-slayer.

->Without a body, the <term>Purusharthas: the four goals of human life</term> cannot be realized.<-
->Therefore, having gained the wealth of the body, one should perform virtuous deeds. (18)<-

No creature in any other form of body than human can pursue higher aims of life. Therefore, endowed with the precious wealth of a human body, one should indulge in virtuous deeds.

->One should protect the self with all one's soul, for the self is the vessel of all.<-
->One should strive in this protection as long as one does not yet see the Truth. (19)<-

### *Preservation of the body :*

With all effort, one should preserve his Self. The self is the efficient cause of everything. Therefore, with all care, one should preserve his Self.

<summary>This page emphasizes the extreme rarity and spiritual value of human birth, describing it as a unique "ladder" to liberation (Moksha) that is only achieved after millions of other incarnations. Lord Shiva warns that failing to seek spiritual truth while in human form is a form of self-destruction, as the human body is the necessary vessel for virtuous deeds and realization.</summary>

<keywords>human birth, reincarnation, 8.4 million bodies, Tattvajnana, Moksha, Atman, Purushartha, self-preservation, virtuous deeds, Kularnava Tantra</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse by Lord Shiva to Goddess Parvati, following the previous page's assertion that the human body is a rare "ladder to liberation." Here, Shiva emphasizes the extreme fragility of life and the urgency of spiritual practice before the body fails.</meta>

### In the Kularnava Tantra

->Villages, fields, wealth, and homes may be regained;<-
->even the fruits of good and bad deeds may come again, but the human body does not return again and again. (20)<-

Wealth, property, and social standing are temporary and can be recovered if lost. However, the unique opportunity of a human incarnation, once expired, is not easily reclaimed.

->People always make great efforts to preserve their bodies;<-
->they do not wish to give up the physical form even when suffering from terrible diseases like leprosy. (21)<-

Human beings possess an instinctual drive to survive. Even when the body is wracked with pain or <term>Leprosy: a chronic infectious disease used here as a metaphor for extreme physical suffering</term>, the will to live remains. This drive should be harnessed for spiritual goals rather than just physical survival.

->Therefore, the body should be diligently maintained for the sake of duty and knowledge.<-
->Knowledge leads to the practice of meditation and spiritual union, through which one is swiftly liberated. (22)<-

One should care for the body not out of vanity, but because it is the instrument for <term>Dharma: the path of righteousness and cosmic order</term>. This leads to <term>Dhyāna: deep meditation</term> and <note>original: "Yoga" — here meaning the disciplined path toward union with the Divine.</note> Yoga, which ultimately grants <term>Moksha: liberation from the cycle of suffering</term>.

->If a person does not protect their own soul from what is harmful,<-
->who else will act for their benefit? Who else will help the soul cross over to safety? (23)<-

Spiritual liberation is a personal responsibility. If an individual does not take the initiative to turn away from harmful distractions, no external force can save them.

->One who does not seek a cure for the "disease of hell" while still in this world—<-
->what will that diseased person do when they reach the "place without medicine"? (24)<-

<note>The "disease of hell" refers to the ignorance and attachments that lead to lower rebirths. The "place without medicine" is the state after death where the opportunity for conscious spiritual practice is lost.</note>

->What fool begins to dig a well only when his house is already engulfed in flames?<-
->As long as this body remains, one should practice the realization of the Ultimate Truth. (25)<-

It is foolish to wait for a crisis or the end of life to begin spiritual practice. One must seek the <note>original: "Tattva" — the essential Reality or Truth.</note> Ultimate Truth while the body is still healthy and the mind is clear.

->Old age crouches like a tigress; life ebbs away like water from a cracked jar.<-
->Diseases strike like enemies; therefore, one should practice what is spiritually beneficial. (26)<-

->Before suffering takes hold, before calamities arrive,<-
->and before the senses fail, one should practice that which leads to the highest good. (27)<-

The text uses vivid imagery to describe the passage of time: <term>Jarā: old age</term> is a predator waiting to pounce, and our lifespan is like water slowly leaking from a broken pot. One must act before <term>Indriya-vaikalya: the failure or impairment of the senses</term> makes meditation and study impossible.

<summary>This page warns of the fleeting nature of human life, using metaphors like a burning house and a leaking jar to urge the seeker to pursue spiritual liberation immediately before old age and disease take hold.</summary>
<keywords>human body, Dharma, Dhyana, Yoga, liberation, urgency of practice, Tattva, Kularnava Tantra</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse by Lord Shiva to Goddess Parvati, emphasizing the extreme fragility of life and the urgency of spiritual practice. Having established in the previous section that the human body is a rare gift, Shiva now warns how easily time is wasted and how death is often ignored until it is too late.</meta>

### The First Chapter

->Time passes unperceived amidst the many activities born of worldly existence.<-
->Attached to pleasures and pains, the living being does not know what is truly in his own best interest. (28)<-

> In the various worldly pursuits, time flies unnoticed. Involved in his pleasures and pains, the <term>Jīva: the individual soul or living spark</term> remains unaware of his true self-interests.

->Seeing those who are paralyzed, afflicted, dead, fallen into misfortune, and deeply suffering,<-
->the world—having drunk the wine of delusion—is never afraid. (29)<-
->Wealth is like a dream; youth is like a flower;<-
->and life is as flickering as lightning. Who, knowing this, can remain complacent? (30)<-

> Infatuated by the wine of ignorance, the human being does not fear even when he sees in the world those who are torpid, afflicted, dead, struck by calamity, and extremely miserable. He does not realize that prosperity is like a dream, youth is like a perishable blossom, and his life-span is as momentary as lightning; thus, he remains complacent.

->A lifespan of a hundred years is very brief; half of it is stolen away by sleep.<-
->The other half is made useless by the sufferings of childhood, illness, and old age. (31)<-

> Even a life of a hundred years is far too short, for half of it is spent in sleep, and the other half is made <note>original: "nisphalam" — fruit-less or unproductive</note> unproductive by the vulnerabilities of infancy, disease, misery, and the decline of old age.

->He is indifferent when he should be active; he sleeps when he should be awake;<-
->He trusts where there is cause for fear. Why would he not be struck down by the killers? (32)<-

> He lacks industry where he ought to be active; he sleeps where he should be spiritually awake; he remains assured in situations where he should be apprehensive—given this, why would death not eventually strike him down?

->The body is like a bubble of foam, and the soul resides within it like a bird.<-
->In this transient and unpleasant world, how can people remain without fear? (33)<-

> The body is short-lived, like a bubble on the water. With the <term>Jīva</term> residing in it temporarily, like a bird perched on a branch, how can a soul remain fearless in an unpleasant and perishable <term>Samsara: the cycle of worldly existence</term>?

->He thinks the harmful is beneficial; he thinks the unstable is permanent;<-
->He sees profit in what is useless, and he does not recognize his own approaching death. (34)<-

> The living being considers favorable that which is actually harmful; he considers permanent that which is transitory; he considers useful that which is of no use; and he remains blind to his own inevitable death.

<summary>Lord Shiva describes the tragedy of human ignorance, where individuals waste their brief lives on worldly distractions while remaining oblivious to the fleeting nature of youth, wealth, and life itself.</summary>
<keywords>transience of life, Jīva, delusion, Samsara, death, ignorance, spiritual urgency, Kularnava Tantra</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues Lord Shiva’s discourse to the Goddess on the vanity of worldly attachments. Following the previous page's warning about how humans ignore the signs of mortality, Shiva now describes how the power of illusion (Māyā) blinds even those who are educated, leading them to procrastinate their spiritual duties while death approaches like a predator.</meta>

### In the Kularnava Tantra

(35) O Goddess! Deluded by your <term>Māyā: the divine power of illusion that makes the temporary world seem real</term>, a person looks but does not see; they hear but do not understand; and they read but do not truly know.

(36) This world is sinking into the deep ocean of Time. The <term>Jīva: the individual soul or living being</term> does not perceive the crocodiles of death, disease, and old age lurking within those depths.

(37) It is not noticed that this body decays with every passing moment. Like an unbaked clay pot sitting in water, the body dissolves and is destroyed without one even realizing it.

(38) One might attempt to wrap up the wind, or divide the sky into pieces, or even try to thread the waves of the sea together; however, it is just as impossible to place any certain reliance or hope upon the duration of one's life.

(39) O Goddess! If the very earth is eventually scorched by fire, if even the great Mount <term>Meru: the sacred golden mountain at the center of the universe</term> crumbles, and the waters of the oceans dry up, then what can be said of the fragile human body? It must surely perish.

(40) "My children, my wife, my wealth, and my kin!"—while the mortal man prattles on in this way, the <note>original: "kāla-vṛkaḥ" — the wolf of Time</note> wolf of Time seizes him by force.

(41) "This I have finished, this is yet to be done, and this other task is half-completed"—while a person is thus occupied with their various strivings and desires, O Beloved, Death strikes.

(42) Therefore, what is to be done tomorrow should be done today; what is meant for the afternoon should be completed in the morning. For Death does not wait to see whether one’s work is finished or left undone.

<summary>Lord Shiva explains that humanity is blinded by illusion, ignoring the constant decay of the body and the certainty of death. He urges immediate spiritual action, warning that death (the "wolf of Time") strikes regardless of one's unfinished worldly plans.</summary>

<keywords>Maya, Jiva, mortality, Time, Mount Meru, Kularnava Tantra, urgency of practice, death</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse from the previous page where Lord Shiva warned that Death strikes while one is preoccupied with unfinished worldly tasks. It transitions from the inevitability of death to the specific behaviors and spiritual negligences that hasten one's demise.</meta>

# First Chapter

->Death is the enemy who approaches, with old age showing him the path and a host of terrible diseases as his army. O wise man, do you not see him coming? (43)<-

->Man is the banquet of Death: he is pierced through by the needle of desire, basted in the oil of sensory enjoyments, and cooked in the fire of likes and dislikes. (44)<-

->Death devours everyone—the unborn in the womb, the infant, the youth, and the elderly. Such is the way of this world. (45)<-

->*The perishability of the Gods, such as Brahmā and others:*<-

->Even the gods like <term>Brahmā: the creator god</term>, <term>Viṣṇu: the preserver god</term>, and <term>Maheśa: Shiva, the destroyer</term>, along with all types of living beings, are racing toward their own end. Therefore, one should perform deeds that lead to the highest good. (46)<-

->*Causes for the shortening of the human life span:*<-

->A man’s life is shortened by failing to follow the duties of his own <term>Varna: social class or occupation</term> and <term>Ashrama: the four stages of life</term>, by accepting improper gifts, and by greed for the wealth or the wife of another. (47)<-

->Neglecting the study of the <term>Vedas: the most ancient and sacred Hindu scriptures</term> and other holy texts, failing to honor the <term>Guru: a spiritual teacher and guide</term>, and failing to restrain the desires of the senses—all these cause a man's life to decay. (48)<-

->Whether by disease, mental suffering, poison, weapons, serpents, or wild animals, living beings must go by whatever means of death has been destined for them. (49)<-

<note>original vocabulary: जरा (old age), मृत्यु (death), व्याधि (disease), ब्रह्म (Brahmā), विष्णु (Viṣṇu), महेश (Maheśa), आयु:क्षय (decrease in life-span), गुर्वनर्चना (neglecting the Guru), पञ्चाग्नि (the fire of desire/austerity)</note>

<summary>Lord Shiva describes Death as an inescapable predator that consumes all living things, including the gods, and explains how immoral behavior and spiritual neglect shorten the human life span.</summary>
<keywords>Death, mortality, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, dharma, life span, Guru, Varna, Ashrama, desire</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of life and death. While the previous page focused on the inevitability and causes of a shortened lifespan, this page explains the mechanics of reincarnation (Samsara), the law of Karma, and the necessity of non-attachment for spiritual liberation.</meta>

### In the Kularnava Tantra

->Like a leech moving on grass, the <term>Jiva: the individual soul</term> travels from one body to another; only after grasping a new body does it abandon the previous one. (50)<-
<note>original: "जीवस्तृणजलौकेव" (Jivastrīnajalaukeva). The "grass-leech" is a classic Indian metaphor for the soul's transition, illustrating how it firmly grips its next destination before letting go of the old.</note>

->Just as within a single body the Jiva passes through infancy, youth, and old age, so too does it transition into another body, moving as if from one house to another. (51)<-

->*Fruits of actions of one life reaped in another:*<-

->In this world, people perform actions and experience their results as pleasure or pain. Those who lack spiritual knowledge, O Goddess, cycle through birth and death again and again. (52)<-

->The actions performed in this world are experienced in the next. Just as a tree watered at its roots eventually produces fruit on its branches, the deeds of the present bear fruit in the future. (53)<-

->*Sufferings due to one's own sins:*<-

->Poverty, sorrow, disease, imprisonment, and addictions—these are the fruits growing from the tree of a person's own transgressions. (54)<-
<note>original: "आत्मापराधवृक्षस्य" (atmaparadha-vrikshasya) literally means "the tree of one's own offenses."</note>

->*Non-attachment is Liberation:*<-

->Freedom from attachment is <term>Moksha: liberation from the cycle of rebirth</term>; all vices are born from attachment. Therefore, by abandoning attachment and remaining fixed in the Truth, one becomes happy. If even the wise can be swayed by attachment, how much more so those with little knowledge? (55)<-

->Attachment should be abandoned by every means. If it cannot be fully renounced, then one should seek the company of the virtuous, for the company of the holy acts as a medicine. (56)<-
<note>The text highlights <term>Sanga: attachment or association</term>. When directed toward worldly things, it is a bond; when directed toward the holy (Satsanga), it is a cure for the soul's ailments.</note>

<summary>This page describes the soul's journey between bodies using the metaphor of a leech and explains that current suffering is the direct result of past actions. It concludes that non-attachment is the only path to liberation, suggesting the company of the virtuous as a remedy for worldly attachment.</summary>

### First Illumination

->The company of holy people and <term>Viveka: spiritual discernment</term> are like two clear, stainless eyes. One who lacks them is blind; how could such a person not stray onto the wrong path? (57)<-
<note>original: "सत्सङ्गश्च विवेकश्च" (Satsangaśca vivekaśca). In Indian philosophy, "Viveka" is the essential ability to distinguish between the eternal soul and the temporary material world.</note>

->For every dear relationship a living being forms in their mind, that many spikes of sorrow pierce their heart. (58)<-

->O <term>Kuleshvari: Sovereign Goddess of the Kula lineage</term>! When this <term>Jiva: the individual soul</term> must eventually depart even from its own body, what is the point of clinging to relationships such as wife, mother, father, or son? (59)<-

->*The Evils of Mundane Existence:*<-

->This worldly existence is the root of all suffering; whoever dwells within it suffers. Therefore, only the one who has renounced it is truly happy—there is no other way, O Beloved! (60)<-
<note>original: "संसार" (Samsara). This refers to the cycle of aimless wandering through births and deaths.</note>

->The world is the source of all sorrows, the refuge of all calamities, and the dwelling place of all sins. Therefore, O Beloved, one should abandon attachment to this <term>Samsara: the cycle of worldly existence</term>. (61)<-

->For those whose minds are attached to the world, it is a terrible bondage even without ropes, a life mixed with potent poison, and a way of being cut to pieces without a weapon, O <term>Devi: Goddess</term>. (62)<-

->Since there is nothing but suffering in the beginning, the middle, and the end of this worldly life, one should renounce it and become fixed in the Truth to find true happiness. (63)<-

### In the Kularnava Tantra

->Even one who is bound tightly by chains made of iron or wood may eventually be set free; but the person shackled by attachment to partners and wealth is never liberated. (64)<-
<note>original: "लौहदारुमयैः पाशैः" (lauhadarumayaiḥ pāśaiḥ). The text contrasts physical imprisonment with the much more durable "fetters" of emotional and material desire.</note>

->For a person consumed by anxieties over family life, their virtues—such as sacred learning and good character—simply dissolve away, much like water held in an unbaked clay pot. (65)<-
<note>An "unbaked pot" (apackva-kumbha) is a common Indian metaphor for something fragile and unready that disintegrates when it comes into contact with the "water" of worldly experience.</note>

->Alas! This world is perpetually ruined by the "thieves" dwelling within the body—the senses. They steal away the focus of the heart while feeding on the objects of desire. (66)<-

->Just as a fish, greedy for a piece of meat, does not see the iron hook, so too does the embodied soul, greedy for worldly pleasure, fail to see the approaching torment of <term>Yama: the God of Death and Justice</term>. (67)<-

->O Beloved! Those who cannot distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful, who constantly stray onto the wrong path and care only for filling their stomachs—such ignorant ones are like residents of hell. (68)<-
<note>The address "Beloved" (Priya) indicates that this text is a dialogue where the God Shiva is teaching the Goddess Parvati.</note>

->Sleep, procreation, and eating are common to all living creatures. A human being is truly defined only by the possession of <term>Jnana: spiritual knowledge or wisdom</term>; one who lacks this knowledge is no better than a beast. (69)<-

->O Beloved! Humans are plagued by the demands of the body: by the need for elimination in the morning, by hunger and thirst when the sun is at its zenith, and by lust and sleep at night. (70)<-

->Devoted only to the needs of their own bodies and their families, all living beings are born and die—alas!—utterly deluded by ignorance. (71)<-
<note>original: "अज्ञानमोहिताः" (ajñānamohitāḥ). This refers to the state of being clouded or "fuddled" by a lack of spiritual awareness, which leads to the cycle of reincarnation.</note>

<summary>This page lists the various distractions—family, wealth, bodily functions, and the senses—that trap a soul in the cycle of suffering, emphasizing that spiritual knowledge (Jnana) is the only quality that distinguishes humans from animals.</summary>

### First Chapter: Page 11

->All human beings, fully absorbed in the traditional duties of their social class and stage of life,<-
->do not recognize the Supreme Truth. O Pārvatī! These fools are lost. (72)<-
<note>original: "स्वस्ववर्णाश्रमाचारनिरताः" (svasvavarṇāśramācāraniratāḥ). This refers to the strict social and religious codes known as *Varnashrama Dharma* which the text argues are insufficient for true enlightenment.</note>

Engaged ceaselessly in the performance of their respective class-duties and little else, men do not see the Supreme Truth; and, O <term>Pārvatī: the Goddess to whom Shiva is speaking</term>! the fools thus perish.

->Some are obsessed with the labor of rituals, devoted to performing ceremonies and sacrifices;<-
->but with their souls shrouded in ignorance, these deceivers wander aimlessly. (73)<-

Some are engrossed in rituals; some perform worship and sacrifices; but engrossed in utter ignorance such persons deceive themselves and others.

->Satisfied by mere labels, these men—intent only on the ritualistic path—<-
->are led astray by the chanting of <term>Mantras: sacred sounds</term>, <term>Homa: fire offerings</term>, and elaborate ceremonies. (74)<-

Content only with name, these men delighting in the rituals, are deluded by the repetition of prayers, fire-offerings, and elaborate sacrifices.

->Through practices like eating only once a day, fasting, and other rules that wither the body,<-
->these fools hope for the Unseen, for they are utterly deluded by your <term>Māyā: the power of illusion</term>. (75)<-

Deluded by your divine illusion, these fools hope to realize the highest by austerities and emaciation of their bodies.

->What liberation can there be for those without discernment through the mere punishment of the body?<-
->O Goddess! If one strikes an ant-hill, is the great serpent living within it actually killed? (76)<-
<note>This striking metaphor explains that the "serpent" of the ego or ignorance lives inside the "ant-hill" of the body. Attacking the body through fasting or pain does not harm the ignorance inside.</note>

If the ignorant could achieve freedom only by torturing their bodies, the serpent would lie dead, O Goddess, when the ant-hill is struck.

->Devoted only to amassing wealth and food, these hypocrites wear the robes of the devout.<-
->They wander the world as if they were wise men, yet they lead others into delusion. (77)<-

*Without the wisdom of discernment, there is no liberation even through the wasting away of the body:*

Beware of these pseudo-gurus, intent on amassing wealth, showily attired in disguise, who wander everywhere as <term>Jñānīs: those who possess spiritual knowledge</term> and throw others into delusion.

->One who is addicted to worldly pleasures yet claims, "I know the <term>Brahma: the Ultimate Reality</term>,"<-
->has failed in both religious duty and spiritual knowledge. One should shun such a person as if they were an outcast. (78)<-

Attached to pleasures of the world, they yet proclaim "I know the Supreme Reality." Fallen both from proper deeds and from true knowledge, such people are to be avoided.

# In the Kulārṇava Tantra
<note>original: "कुलार्णवतन्त्रे" (Kulārṇavatantre). This is one of the most important texts of the Kaula school of Tantra, presented as a dialogue between Lord Shiva and the Goddess.</note>

->Do asses and similar animals not wander about naked and without shame,<-
->treating the home and the forest as the same? Do they become Yogis because of this? (79)<-
<note>The text mocks the idea that merely being naked (a practice of some ascetics) or wandering aimlessly constitutes spiritual "renunciation."</note>

### The Fault of Ritualistic Practices Alone:

Are there no asses and the like to whom home and forest are alike and who wander about naked without shame? Do they all become <term>Yogis: those who have achieved spiritual union</term> thereby?

->O Goddess! If humans could be liberated by eating or smearing themselves with mud and ashes,<-
->would all the simple country folk who live amidst mud and ashes be liberated? (80)<-

If men could get liberated by smearing themselves with dust and ashes, are all the country folk, who live amidst dust and ashes, liberated?

->O Devi! The deer and other animals of the forest always<-
->subsist on grass, leaves, and water. Do they become Yogis because of that? (81)<-

Denizens of the forest like deer and other animals subsist on grass, leaves, and water. Then, O <term>Devi: the Goddess</term>! do they become Yogis thereby?

->From birth until death, frogs and fish remain in the waters of<-
->rivers like the Ganges; do they acquire special merit because of that? (82)<-

Frogs and fishes live all their lives in rivers like the Ganges; do they acquire special merit thereby?
<note>The Ganges is considered the holiest river in India; the author argues that physical proximity to a holy site is meaningless without internal transformation.</note>

->O Devi! Parrots and starlings recite words with delight before<-
->people; are they to be regarded as great scholars from such recitations? (83)<-

O Devi! Parrots and *mynās* <note>original: "शुकसारिकाः" (śuka-sārikāḥ) referring to parrots and the common hill myna, both known for mimicking human speech.</note> recite before people the sacred words with delight; are they to be regarded as great scholars from such recitations?

->O Supreme Goddess! Pigeons eat only stones, and the Cātaka birds<-
->do not drink water from the earth; are these too, Yogins? (84)<-

Pigeons eat nothing but stone; <term>Cātakas: the Pied Cuckoo (Cucculus Melanoleucus)</term>, which legend says drinks only raindrops and never water from the ground; are these too, Yogins?

->O Beloved! Animals like pigs endure the winter cold and summer heat,<-
->and for them, food—whether fit or unfit—is all the same; are they Yogins? (85)<-

Animals like pigs bear the winter cold and summer heat and for them food fit or unfit is alike; are they Yogins thereby?

->Therefore, O Queen of the Kula, such actions are merely for deceiving the world;<-
->the direct cause of Liberation is the Knowledge of Truth. (86)<-

Indeed, such privations and self-denials are, O <term>Kuleśvarī: Goddess of the Kula tradition</term>, only for deceiving the world while direct <term>Tattvajñāna: Knowledge of Truth or Reality</term> alone is the means for <term>Moksha: liberation from the cycle of rebirth</term>.

<summary>This page uses a series of satirical analogies involving animals to argue that external asceticism—such as nakedness, living in nature, or dietary restrictions—is spiritually useless without the internal "Knowledge of Truth."</summary>
<keywords>Kularnava Tantra, Yoga, Devi, Liberation, Moksha, Ritualism, Tattvajnana, Kulesvari, Cataka bird, Asceticism</keywords>

# First Chapter
<note>original: "प्रथम उल्लासः" (Prathama Ullāsaḥ)</note>

Those controlled by the bonds of their animal nature do not know the supreme truth. (87)
Tossed here and there in the terrifying ocean of the <term>Vedas: the oldest sacred Hindu scriptures</term> and <term>Shastras: technical or religious treatises</term>, those who use faulty logic remain trapped, swallowed by the crocodiles of the waves of time. (88)

->*No Liberation from the study of the Śāstras alone without Spiritual Knowledge:*<-

O My Beloved! People fallen into the deep well of the <term>Six Systems of Philosophy: the classical schools of Indian thought</term> but controlled by <term>animal-bondage: the "pasha" or ties that bind the soul to the material world</term> are unable to attain <term>Spiritual knowledge: "Paramārtha," the highest reality</term>. Struggling in the deep ocean of Vedas and Shastras, they are caught up by the terrible waves and crocodiles residing therein in the form of philosophical discussions and debates.

One who knows the Vedas, <term>Agamas: tantric scriptures</term>, and <term>Puranas: ancient mythological texts</term>, but does not know the supreme truth, is a mere pretender; everything such a person says is like the cawing of a crow. (89)
Preoccupied with worries like "This is knowledge" and "This is what must be known," they read day and night, O Goddess, yet they turn their backs on the highest reality. (90)
Distressed by their own anxieties and with their senses in a whirl, these fools remain caught in the construction of sentences and meters, adorned with the ornaments of poetry and rhetoric. (91)

They who have read the Vedas, Agamas and Puranas, and yet know not of the Highest Truth of the Divine—the true object of life—are a fraud, cawing like the crow. With their backs turned on the Real Truth to be known, they ponder over books ceaselessly, anxiously saying 'this is to be known', 'this is knowledge' and so on. Embellished with such knowledge of style, syntax, poetry and rhetorical ornaments of the sense and sound, these fools stand befuddled and apprehensive.

The supreme truth is one thing, but people exert themselves for something else; the true intent of the scriptures is one thing, but they provide a different explanation entirely. (92)

The real truth is one and what they understand is quite other; one is the purport of the Scriptures and the other is what they interpret.

They talk about the state of <term>Unmani: a state of "mindlessness" or pure consciousness beyond the intellect</term>, yet they do not experience it themselves. Some are destroyed by their own ego, while others are depri<unclear>v</unclear>ed of proper instruction. (93)
They read the Vedas and scriptures and argue with one another, but they do not know the supreme truth—just as a ladle does not know the taste of the soup it carries. (94)

They speak of egoless consciousness (<term>Unmanī-avasthā: the state of being beyond the mind</term>) but do not experience this state. Some are the victims of Egoism, and some remain deprived of instructions. They chant the Vedas and dispute among themselves but like the ladle that does not know the taste of the <note>original: "pākarasam" (the flavor of the cooked food)</note> treacle it holds, they know not the Truth.

<summary>This page argues that intellectual mastery of scriptures and philosophy is useless for liberation if it lacks direct spiritual experience. It famously compares a dry scholar to a ladle that carries delicious food but can never actually taste it.</summary>

<keywords>Paramartha, Veda, Shastra, Agama, Purana, Unmani-avastha, Intellectualism, Spiritual Experience, Egoism, Six Systems of Philosophy</keywords>

### In the Kularnava Tantra
<note>original: "कुलार्णवतन्त्रे" (Kulārṇavatantre)</note>

->The head carries the flowers, but it is the nose that knows their fragrance. Many recite the <term>Vedas: the oldest sacred scriptures of India</term> and the <term>Shastras: religious and legal treatises</term>, but rare is the one who understands their true inner spirit. (95)<-

*Truth inherent in the self:*

The head may bear the flowers, but it is the nose which gets their fragrance. So there may be persons who chant the Vedas and scriptures, but rare are they who become one with their spirit.

->Not realizing that the Divine Truth resides within themselves, the fool becomes lost in the scriptures; like a foolish shepherd who looks for a goat in a well when it is already right there in the flock. (96)<-
<note>Note: The Sanskrit *kakṣagatam* implies the goat is "under the arm" or "nearby," while the OCR English translation suggests it is "in the flock." Both emphasize that the object is already close at hand.</note>

Forgetting that the Divine Truth is within themselves, they look for it in the books, like the shepherd who searches for the goat in the well when it is already in the flock.

->Mere words are not enough to destroy the delusions of this worldly existence; just as darkness is never dispelled by simply talking about a lamp. (97)<-

->Study for a person without wisdom is like a blind man looking into a mirror. O <term>Devi: the Goddess</term>, it is only for the person of awakened wisdom that the scriptures serve as a means to reach spiritual knowledge. (98)<-

Verbal knowledge is of no avail for the destruction of the delusion of the world; just as darkness is not dispelled by mere talk of a lantern. The study of a person without wisdom is like a blind looking into a mirror. It is only the men of awakened wisdom that can benefit from the <term>Śāstras: technical or religious texts</term>.

->In front, behind, and on both sides, some people argue with one another, saying "The Truth is like this" or "It is like that." These men may be famous for qualities such as learning, philanthropy, and valor. (99)<-

->But if they do not have direct perception, how can they grasp the Truth through mere talk? Those who are thus deluded by the scriptures are undoubtedly far from the Truth. (100)<-

Men famous for the qualities like learning, philanthropy and valour keep on discussing forward, backward and sideways that the Divine Truth is of this kind or that; but if they do not apprehend that Truth directly what is the use of talking about it. Those who are foolishly thus involved in the Śāstras are undoubtedly far from the Truth.

->“This is knowledge, and this is what must be known”—one desires to hear this from every direction. But O Devi, even if one were to live for a thousand years, they would never reach the end of the scriptures. (101)<-

Everywhere they like to hear such things as 'this is knowledge and this should be acquired'; but O Devi ! one may spend a thousand years hearing the knowledge of Śāstras, yet he will never reach their end.

# Page 15
## First Chapter
<note>original: "प्रथम उल्लासः" (Prathama Ullāsaḥ)</note>

->The <term>Vedas: the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism</term> and the various <term>Shastras: formal treatises on law, ritual, and philosophy</term> are endless, but life is short and obstacles are millions. Therefore, one should grasp the essence, just as a swan extracts milk from water. (102)<-
<note>original: "वेदाश्च नैकशास्त्राणि... क्षीरं हंस इवाम्भसः" — The hamsa (swan) is a traditional Indian symbol for discernment, believed to be able to drink only the milk from a mixture of milk and water.</note>

The scriptures are vast and life is brief. Wisdom lies in going straight to the core of the teachings, much like a swan sips only the milk out of a bowl of water.

->After studying all the scriptures and realizing the essential Truth, the wise person should discard the books, just as someone seeking grain throws away the husk. (103)<-
<note>original: "पलालमिव धान्यार्थी" (like a grain-seeker with the husk)</note>

An intelligent person, having practiced the scriptures and found their inner Truth, should leave the books behind, just as one seeking grain discards the useless chaff.

->Just as one who is satisfied by <term>Amrita: the nectar of immortality</term> has no need for ordinary food, so too, O <term>Devi: the Goddess</term>, the one who has known the Essence of Truth has no further need for the scriptures. (104)<-

As one who is full from a drink of Nectar requires no other food, so, O Goddess, the person who has realized the ultimate Truth has no further use for the knowledge found in books.

->Liberation comes only through Real Knowledge:<-
->Liberation is not attained by chanting the Vedas nor by studying the Shastras. O <term>Viravandite: She who is worshipped by heroes</term>! <term>Jnana: direct spiritual wisdom</term> alone grants liberation, and nothing else. (105)<-

*Liberation only through Real Knowledge:*
Freedom is not found in reciting ancient hymns or reading technical treatises. O Goddess! Only direct, realized knowledge can bring liberation.

->The <term>Ashramas: the four stages of social and religious life</term> are not the cause of liberation, nor are the philosophical systems. Likewise, the scriptures themselves are not the cause; wisdom alone is the cause. (106)<-
->The single word of the <term>Guru: spiritual teacher</term> grants liberation; all other forms of learning are mere mockeries. Amidst the exhausting burden of "wood" (the weight of worldly study), this one living truth is supreme. (107)<-

*The Guru's Instruction alone gives Liberation:*
Neither your social station, nor your philosophy, nor your scientific study provides the means for freedom. Only the internalizing of wisdom—which is received through the living words of a teacher—can grant it. All other intellectual pursuits are deceptive and burdensome; this realization alone is life-giving.

->The supreme knowledge of <term>Advaita: non-duality, the oneness of the individual and the Divine</term> was declared by Lord <term>Shiva</term>. It is free from the exhaustion of rituals and is to be received from the lips of the Guru; it cannot be found even through millions of other <term>Agamas: traditional scriptures</term>. (108)<-

The highest knowledge of Oneness spoken by Lord Shiva is free from the toil of complicated rituals. It must be heard directly from a teacher’s mouth; it cannot be reached by reading millions of books.

## In the Kularnava Tantra
<note>original: "कुलार्णवतन्त्रे" (Kulārṇavatantra)</note>

->Knowledge is said to be of two kinds: that which arises from the scriptures and that which arises from discernment.<-
->The knowledge of scriptures is known as <term>Shabda-Brahma: the Divine as revealed through sound and word</term>, while the Supreme Truth born of discernment is <term>Para-Brahma: the Ultimate Reality beyond words</term>. (106)<-

*Two kinds of knowledge: Scriptural and Mental Reasoning:*
Knowledge is of two kinds: one derived from the Scriptures and the other born out of Mental Reasoning. Knowledge derived from Scriptures is in the form of Shabda-Brahma, and that born out of Mental Reasoning is in the form of Para-Brahma.

->Some prefer <term>Non-dualism: the belief that the soul and God are one</term>, and others prefer <term>Dualism: the belief that the soul and God are separate</term>.<-
->But they do not know My Truth, which is free from both dualism and non-dualism. (110)<-
<note>original: "द्वैताद्वैतविवर्जितम्" (dvaitādvaita-vivarjitam) — This suggests a state of "Non-duality" (Advaya) that transcends the philosophical categories of "one" or "two."</note>

Some prefer Non-dualism, and some others dualism; but neither of them know My Truth, which is above both dualism and non-dualism.

->Two words determine bondage and release: "mine" and "not mine."<-
->A creature is bound by the thought of "mine" and is liberated by the thought of "not mine." (111)<-

"Mine" and "not mine" convey bondage and release. "Mine" is the term that acts for bondage, and "not mine" spells Release.

->True action is that which does not lead to bondage; True knowledge is that which leads to liberation.<-
->Any other action is merely cause for exhaustion; any other knowledge is just a display of artistic skill. (112)<-

True action is that which binds not, True knowledge is that gives Release. Other actions are causes of pain; other knowledge makes only for artistry.

->As long as the fire of desire and other passions burn, as long as there is an attachment to worldly existence,<-
->and as long as the senses remain fickle, how can there be a discussion of the <term>Higher Purpose: the essential Truth or Tattva</term>? (113)<-

*No Spiritual knowledge without control of Senses and kindness of Guru:*
As long as there is sensual desire, as long as there is attachment to worldliness and as long as there is activity of the senses, so long how can there be a talk of Higher Purpose?

->As long as there is the frantic impulse of effort, as long as there is the building of mental constructs,<-
->and as long as the mind is not steady, how can there be a discussion of the Higher Purpose? (114)<-

So long as there is agitation of exertion, so long as there is activity of thought, so long as there is no steadiness of mind; how can there be a talk of Higher Purpose?

->As long as there is pride in the physical body and a sense of "me and mine,"<-
->and as long as there is no <term>Grace: the transformative kindness and power</term> of the Guru, how can there be a discussion of the Higher Purpose? (115)<-

As long as there is identification with body, as long as there is ego-identification and as long as there is no Grace of the Guru, so long how can there be a talk of Higher Purpose?

<vocab>Shabda-Brahma, Para-Brahma, Non-dualism, dualism, bondage, release, True action, True knowledge, Higher Purpose, Guru, Kularnava Tantra</vocab>

<summary>This page defines the difference between scriptural knowledge and experiential realization, asserting that the ultimate Truth transcends the philosophical debate between dualism and non-dualism. It lists the psychological barriers to spiritual insight, concluding that the Grace of the Guru is essential for realizing the Higher Purpose.</summary>

It sets the stage for the rest of the revelation by concluding the description of the human condition (Jiva-sthiti).</meta>

# Page 17
## First Chapter
<note>original: "प्रथम उल्लासः" (Prathama Ullāsaḥ)</note>

->Austerities, vows, pilgrimages, <term>Japa: meditative mantra repetition</term>, <term>Homa: fire offerings</term>, and ritual purifications;<-
->The study of the Vedas, the scriptures, and the sacred histories—all these are practiced only until the Ultimate Truth is found. (116)<-

Austerities, observances, pilgrimages, Japa, Homa, Worship, Vedas, <term>Agamas: traditional scriptures</term> and <term>Shastras: law books or treatises</term>—all these are resorted to only so long as the Supreme Truth is not attained.

->Therefore, O Goddess, with every effort, in every state, and at all times,<-
->one should be devoted to the Truth if they desire the liberation of the self. (117)<-

Therefore, O <term>Devi: Goddess</term>! If one desires his Liberation, he should be mindful of the Truth Divine, always, with all his efforts and in all conditions.

->Scorched by the agony of the threefold distress, one should seek the shade of the Tree of Liberation,<-
->where <term>Dharma: righteousness</term> and <term>Jnana: wisdom</term> are the beautiful flowers, and the fruit is the World of Heaven. (118)<-
<note>The "threefold distress" (tapatraya) refers to the traditional Indian classification of suffering: those caused by oneself (mental/physical), by other living beings, and by natural or supernatural forces.</note>

Afflicted as one is with threefold distress, he should take to the shade of the Tree of Liberation on whose branches flower Dharma and Jñāna and whose fruit is the World of Bliss.

->Why speak at length? Listen to the secret, O Parvati!<-
->Without <term>Kula-dharma: the specific path and duties of this Tantric lineage</term>, there is no liberation; this is the truth, without doubt. (119)<-

Why to talk much? In a word, O <term>Parvati: the Goddess as daughter of the mountain</term>! Listen to the secret. Indeed and without doubt it is the Kula-dharma that Liberates.

->Therefore, I give this Truth to you; once it is understood from the mouth of the <term>Guru: spiritual teacher</term>,<-
->O Goddess, one is easily released from the terrible bonds of worldly existence. (120)<-

Thus, O Devi! I have told you the Truth; which after knowing from the mouth of Guru, men effortlessly free themselves from the bondage of the world.

->I have thus described to you, My Beloved, the various states of living beings.<-
->In brief, O Queen of the Kula, what else do you wish to hear? (121)<-

O My Beloved! I have thus declared to you in brief the conditions of the <term>Jivas: individual souls</term>. Now, O <term>Kuleshvari: Sovereign Goddess of the Kula tradition</term>! what else you want to hear?

<meta>This page begins the Second Chapter (Ullāsa) of the Kularnava Tantra. While the previous page concluded the description of the suffering human condition and the search for liberation, this page shifts to a dialogue between the Goddess (Devi) and the Lord (Shiva). The Goddess requests a detailed explanation of the specific spiritual path known as Kuladharma, which was only briefly mentioned at the end of the first chapter.</meta>

# Second Chapter
<note>original: "द्वितीय उल्लास:" (Dvitīya Ullāsaḥ)</note>

<image-desc>A horizontal decorative divider consisting of three parallel lines with stylized floral flourishes at both ends.</image-desc>

->The Goddess said:<-

O <term>Kulesha: Lord of the Kula lineage</term>! O treasure-house of mercy for all <term>Jivas: individual living souls</term>! I wish to hear more. You have indicated the <term>Kuladharma: the sacred path of the Kula tradition</term>, but you have not yet fully revealed it. (1)

Tell me, O Lord, about the greatness of that path—the most excellent of all spiritual paths—and the significance of the <term>Urdhvamnaya: the 'Upper Tradition' or highest school of Tantric revelation</term>. Tell me its doctrines, O <term>Parameshana: Supreme Ruler</term>, if you have kindness for me. (2)

->The Lord said:<-

Listen, O Goddess! I shall speak of what you have asked. Simply by hearing this, one becomes beloved of the <term>Yoginis: semi-divine female spirits or practitioners of yoga</term>. (3)

In ages past, I did not reveal this even to <term>Brahma: the Creator</term>, <term>Vishnu: the Preserver</term>, or <term>Guha: another name for Kartikeya, the god of war</term>. Yet, out of love for you, I shall tell it; listen with a single-pointed mind. (4)

Handed down through the succession of tradition and residing within my five mouths <note>Shiva is often depicted with five faces representing different directions and categories of scripture</note>, this doctrine is inexpressible in its ultimate essence. Nevertheless, I shall tell it to you. (5)

<summary>The Goddess requests a full revelation of the Kuladharma and the Upper Tradition (Urdhvamnaya). Lord Shiva agrees to reveal these secrets, noting that they are so profound they were previously withheld from other major deities.</summary>
<keywords>Kuladharma, Urdhvamnaya, Shiva and Parvati, Tantric revelation, Kulesha, secret doctrine</keywords>

--- Page 28 ---
<meta>This page continues the Second Chapter (Ullāsa) of the Kularnava Tantra. It follows the Lord's (Shiva's) initial agreement to reveal the highest spiritual doctrine to the Goddess. This section focuses on the supreme status of the Kuladharma relative to all other religious paths and the necessity of keeping this knowledge secret from the uninitiated.</meta>

## Second Chapter 16
<note>original: "द्वितीय उल्लासः १६" (Dvitīya Ullāsaḥ 16)</note>

->You must also keep this secret; it is not to be given to just anyone.<-
->It should be given only to a devotee or a disciple; otherwise, a spiritual downfall may occur. (6)<-

*Superiority of the <term>Kuladharma: the sacred path of the Kula lineage</term>:*

<note>The following lines emphasize that this knowledge is not for general public consumption and requires a specific, sacred bond between teacher and student.</note>

You must keep this hidden and not communicate it to anyone else except a devotee and a disciple. If given to those who lack the proper disposition, it will lead to their spiritual ruin.

->The <term>Vedas: the foundational scriptures of ancient India</term> are superior to all; the <term>Vaishnava: the path centered on the worship of Vishnu</term> is higher than the Vedas.<-
->The <term>Shaiva: the path centered on the worship of Shiva</term> is higher than the Vaishnava; the <term>Dakshina: the "Right-hand" Tantric path</term> is higher than the Shaiva. (7)<-
->The <term>Vama: the "Left-hand" Tantric path</term> is higher than the Dakshina; the <term>Siddhanta: the "Established Doctrine" path</term> is higher than the Vama.<-
->The <term>Kaula: the path of the Kula tradition</term> is higher than the Siddhanta; and there is nothing higher than the Kaula. (8)<-

*Order of superiority:*

The Vedic tradition is the base; the path of devotion to Vishnu is superior; the path of devotion to Shiva is higher still; the "Right-hand" path is superior to those; the "Left-hand" path is superior to the Right; the "Established Doctrine" is superior to the Left; the Kula path is the highest of all, and no spiritual path exists beyond it.

->O Goddess! The Kula tradition is the most secret of all secrets, the essence of all essences, the highest of the high.<-
->O Goddess, it directly bestows the state of Shiva and is passed from ear to ear in a continuous tradition. (9)<-

O <term>Devi: the Goddess</term>! The Kula (or <term>Kulachara: the conduct of the Kula</term>) is the most secret of all secrets; the essence of all essences; the best among the best. It is handed down "from ear to ear" <note>original: "karṇākarṇigataṃ"</note>, meaning through the direct oral tradition from Guru to disciple, and it is the true revealer of the nature of Shiva himself.

->Having churned the great ocean of the Vedas and <term>Agamas: traditional Tantric scriptures</term> with the rod of <term>Jnana: spiritual knowledge</term>,<-
->I, the knower of the essence, have extracted this Kuladharma, O Goddess. (10)<-

From the vast ocean of the Vedas and the Agamas, using the churning rod of spiritual knowledge, I have extracted this essence of the Kula path, just as butter is extracted from milk.

->My beloved! If all other religions, sacrifices, pilgrimages, and vows were on one side,<-
->And the Kuladharma was on the other, the Kaula path would be greater. (11)<-

My Beloved! If on one side of a scale you were to place all other religions, sacred pilgrimage sites, and religious vows, and on the other side you placed the Kuladharma, the latter would prove heavier and more significant than all of them combined.

->Just as rivers, whether flowing straight or winding, ultimately enter the sea,<-
->So too do the various religions enter into the Kuladharma. (12)<-

As rivers flowing over long distances—some straight and some winding—ultimately merge into the sea, in the same way, all the various spiritual paths and religious duties find their final destination and fulfillment within the Kuladharma.

<summary>This page establishes a spiritual hierarchy, placing the Kaula tradition at the pinnacle of all religious and Tantric paths. Shiva explains to the Goddess that the Kuladharma is the secret essence of all scriptures and acts as the final ocean into which all other spiritual rivers flow.</summary>
<keywords>Kuladharma, Kaula, hierarchy of paths, secrecy, spiritual knowledge (Jnana), Shiva, Devi, oral tradition, Vedas, Agamas</keywords>

# Page 20

## In the Kularnava Tantra

<note>original: "यथा हस्तिपदे लीनं सर्वप्राणीपदं भवेत् । दर्शनानि च सर्वाणि कुल एव तथा प्रिये ।। १३ ।।"</note>
Just as the footprints of all living creatures are lost within the footprint of an elephant, so too, My Beloved, are all <term>philosophical systems: known as darshanas</term> absorbed into the doctrine of Kula. (13)

<note>original: "यदा जाम्बुनदानाञ्च सदृशं लौहमस्ति चेत् । तदा च कुलधर्मेण समयोऽन्यः समो भवेत् ।। १४ ।।"</note>
If iron were ever equal to gold, then another doctrine might be equal to the <term>Kula-dharma: the sacred way of the Kula lineage</term>. (14)

<note>original: "यथामरतरङ्गिण्या न समाः सकलापगाः । तथैव समयाः सर्वे कुलधर्मेण नो समाः ।। १५ ।।"</note>
Just as all other rivers are not equal to the <term>Ganges: literally 'the river of the immortals'</term>, so all other traditions are not equal to the Kula-dharma. (15)

<note>original: "मेरुसर्षपयोर्यद्वत् सूर्यखद्योतयोर्यथा । तथान्यसमयस्यापि कुलस्य महदन्तरम् ।। १६ ।।"</note>
Just as there is a vast difference between <term>Mount Sumeru: the great golden mountain at the center of the universe</term> and a mustard seed, or between the sun and a firefly, so is there a great distance between other doctrines and the Kula. (16)

<note>original: "अस्ति चेत्त्वत्समा नारी मत्समः पुरुषोऽस्ति चेत् । कुलेन समधर्मस्तु तथापि न कदाचन ।। १७ ।।"</note>
Even if there were a woman equal to You, or a man equal to Me, there could still never be a spiritual path equal to the Kula-dharma. (17)

<note>original: "कुलधर्मं हि मोहेन योऽन्यधर्मेण दुर्मतिः । बद्धः संसारपाशेन सोऽन्त्यजानां प्रियो भवेत् ।। १८ ।।"</note>
The fool who, out of delusion, considers other paths equal to Kula-dharma remains bound by the snares of worldly existence; he is fit only for the company of <term>outcasts: literally 'those born last,' referring to those outside the sacred social order</term>. (18)

<note>original: "यो वा कुलाधिकं धर्ममज्ञानाद्वदति प्रिये । ब्रह्महत्याधिकं पापं स प्राप्नोति न संशयः ।। १९ ।।"</note>
My Beloved! One who ignorantly speaks of another path as superior to the Kula undoubtedly commits a sin greater than <term>Brahmanicide: the grave sin of killing a priest or one who possesses sacred knowledge</term>. (19)

<note>original: "कुलधर्मप्रवहणं समारुह्य नरोत्तमः । स्वर्गादि द्वीपान्तरं गत्वा मोक्षरत्नं समश्नुते ।। २० ।।"</note>
Boarding the vessel of Kula-dharma, the best of men crosses beyond the islands of heaven to attain the jewel of <term>Moksha: the ultimate liberation from the cycle of birth and death</term>. (20)

<summary>This page uses several poetic analogies—such as the elephant's footprint, gold versus iron, and the sun versus a firefly—to emphasize that the Kula path is the supreme and all-encompassing spiritual doctrine. It warns that equating other paths to the Kula results in spiritual bondage and grave karmic consequences.</summary>

# Page 21

## Second Chapter

->In all other systems of philosophy, humans achieve liberation only after long and repeated practice; but in the path of Kula, they are liberated immediately—there is no doubt about it. (21)<-
<note>original: "दर्शनेषु च सर्वेषु चिराभ्यासेन मानवाः। मोक्षं लभन्ते कौले तु सद्य एव न संशयः।।"</note>

->Listen, My Beloved, the very breath of My life, O <term>Kula-nayika: the Mistress of the Kula lineage</term>! Why speak at such length? I swear by You that there is no spiritual path equal to the <term>Kula-dharma: the sacred law of the Kula</term>. (22)<-
<note>original: "बहुनात्र किमुक्तेन शृणु मत्प्राणवल्लभे। न कौलसमधर्मोऽस्ति त्वां शपे कुलनायिके।।"</note>

**The practitioner of Kaula enjoys both worldly fulfillment and spiritual union:**

->My Beloved! In this path, the practitioner of <term>Yoga: spiritual union</term> may also be one who enjoys the world, and the one who enjoys the world may also be a master of Yoga. Because the <term>Kaula: the doctrine of the Kula</term> consists of both <term>Bhoga: worldly enjoyment</term> and Yoga, it is the most excellent of all. (23)<-
<note>original: "योगी चैवेव भोगी स्याद्भोगी चैवेव योगवित्। भोगयोगात्मकं कौलं तस्मात् सर्वाधिकं प्रिये।।"</note>
<note>In many traditional Indian paths, one must choose between being a renunciant (Yogi) or a householder (Bhogi). Tantra argues that one can be both, using worldly experiences as a bridge to the Divine.</note>

->O <term>Kuleshvari: Sovereign Goddess of the Kula</term>! Within the Kula-dharma, enjoyment itself acts directly as a path to Yoga; what appears to be a sin in other systems is here transformed into a meritorious act; and <term>Samsara: the cycle of worldly existence</term> itself becomes the means for <term>Moksha: ultimate liberation</term>. (24)<-
<note>original: "भोगो योगायते साक्षात् पातकं सुकृतायते। मोक्षायते च संसारः कुलधर्मे कुलेश्वरि।।"</note>

**The Gods also adhere to the Kula-dharma:**

->Even the gods like <term>Brahma: the Creator</term>, <term>Indra: King of the Gods</term>, <term>Achyuta: Vishnu the Preserver</term>, and <term>Rudra: Shiva the Destroyer</term>, along with the most eminent of sages, are devoted to the Kula-dharma. O Goddess! If this is true for them, what then is there to say of mere mortals? (25)<-
<note>original: "ब्रह्मेन्द्राच्युतरुद्रादिदेवतामुनिपुङ्गवाः। कुलधर्मपरा देवि मानुषेषु च का कथा।।"</note>

->Therefore, if one desires the fulfillment of the Self, one should abandon all other religious duties and the various opinions of different gurus, and realize the Kula alone. (26)<-
<note>original: "विहाय सर्वधर्माश्च नानागुरुमतानि च। कुलमेव विजानीयाद्यदीच्छेत् सिद्धिमात्मनः।।"</note>

**Discipline undergone in previous lives provides the knowledge of Kula-dharma:**

->Through the spiritual practice performed in previous lives, the knowledge of Kula dawns upon a person spontaneously—like the sudden realization upon waking from a dream—without the need for external instruction. (27)<-
<note>original: "पूर्वजन्मकृताभ्यासात् कुलज्ञानं प्रकाशते। स्वप्नोत्थित प्रत्ययवदुपदेशादिकं विना।।"</note>

<summary>This page argues that the Kula path is the swiftest route to liberation because it uniquely integrates worldly enjoyment (Bhoga) with spiritual discipline (Yoga). It asserts that even the highest Hindu deities follow this path and suggests that true understanding of Kula is a result of spiritual merit accumulated across many lifetimes.</summary>

<keywords>Kula-dharma, Bhoga and Yoga, Kaula, Moksha, Samsara, Kuleshvari, Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma, Indra, spontaneous realization</keywords>

While the previous page discussed how the Kula path uniquely blends worldly enjoyment with spiritual liberation, this section explains the internal requirements for receiving this knowledge. It emphasizes that "Kula-jñāna" (wisdom of the Kula) is not merely taught, but is a result of spiritual merit accumulated over many lifetimes.</meta>

# Page 22

## Kularnava Tantra

Just as from the experiences of a dream arises knowledge without instructions, so out of the studies and disciplines of <term>Sādhanā: dedicated spiritual practice</term> of previous lives dawns the Knowledge of <term>Kuladharma: the sacred law of the Kula lineage</term>.

->The wisdom that is ingrained in humans over thousands of past lives—that is what a living being attains; external instruction alone is useless. (28)<-
<note>original: "जन्मान्तरसहस्रेषु या बुद्धिर्विहिता नृणाम्। तामेव लभते जन्तुरुपदेशो निरर्थकः।। २८।।"</note>

The maturation and development of the mind, which takes place during a thousand previous lives, is what yields knowledge even without direct instruction.

->For one whose heart is purified by the <term>Mantras: sacred sound formulas</term> originating from the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or Saura traditions, the knowledge of the Kula is revealed. (29)<-
<note>original: "शैववैष्णवदौर्गाकगाणपत्यार्क सम्भवैः। मन्त्रैर्विशुद्धचित्तस्य कुलज्ञानं प्रकाशते।। २९।।"</note>
<note>The text is inclusive here, suggesting that devotion to any of the major Hindu deities—Shiva, Vishnu, Durga, Ganesha, or the Sun—prepares the seeker for the higher Kula teachings.</note>

### *Knowledge of Kuladharma dawns upon a mind purified by Mantra and Japa:*

Knowledge of Kula-dharma dawns upon a mind purified by Mantras and <term>Japa: the meditative repetition of a divine name</term> of any origin, be it Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, or Saura.

->O Queen of the Gods, Knower of all Laws! It is remembered that followers of other paths are destined to return to the cycle of rebirth, but all those who stand firm in the Kula-dharma never return. (30)<-
<note>original: "सर्वधर्मज्ञ देवेशि पुनरावर्तकाः स्मृताः। कुलधर्मस्थिता ये च ते सर्वेऽप्यनिवर्तकाः।। ३०।।"</note>

*O Goddess!* followers of other paths return to the world again, but an adherent of Kula-dharma becomes free from all this.

->O Goddess, through the austerities, charity, sacrifices, pilgrimages, prayers, and vows performed in previous lives, the sins of men are washed away, and the knowledge of the Kula shines forth. (31)<-
<note>original: "पुराकृततपोदानयज्ञतीर्थजपव्रतैः। क्षीणांहसां नृणां देवि कुलज्ञानं प्रकाशते।। ३१।।"</note>

### *Eligibility for Knowledge:*

<term>Kulajñāna: Kula-knowledge</term> dawns upon a person whose body and mind are freed from the deforming elements of ignorance and ego as a result of austerity, charity, sacrifices, pilgrimages, Japa, and sacred observances undergone in the past.

->O Auspicious Goddess, Benefactress of all! This Kula-knowledge reveals itself to that person with whom both You and I are satisfied, and who possesses faith in the Deity and the Guru. (32)<-
<note>original: "त्वमहं देवि कल्याणि यस्य तुष्टावुभावपि। देवतागुरुभक्त्या च कुलज्ञानं प्रकाशते।। ३२।।"</note>

*O Goddess, Benefactress of all!* The Kula-jñāna dawns upon a person with whom both you and I are satisfied and who has faith in the <term>Devatā: the presiding deity</term> and the <term>Guru: the spiritual preceptor</term>.

->Kula-knowledge shines forth in one who is pure of heart, peaceful, diligent in performing duties, a servant of their Guru, intensely devoted to the Lord, and a secret practitioner. (33)<-
<note>original: "शुद्धचित्तस्य शान्तस्य कर्मिणो गुरुसेविनः। अतिभक्तस्य गुह्यस्य कुलज्ञानं प्रकाशते।। ३३।।"</note>

Kula-jñāna dawns in a person who is pure in mind, calm, diligent, a server of his Guru, intensely devoted to the Lord, and a secret <term>Sādhaka: a spiritual practitioner</term>.

<summary>This page outlines the spiritual prerequisites for Kula-knowledge, asserting that true understanding is the fruit of many lifetimes of diverse religious practice. It emphasizes that while other paths lead to rebirth, the Kula path leads to final liberation for those with a purified mind and devotion to their Guru.</summary>

<keywords>reincarnation, spiritual merit, purification, Guru-devotion, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, Saura, liberation, Kula-jñāna</keywords>

--- Page 32 ---
<meta>This page continues the Second Chapter of the Kularnava Tantra. Previously, it was established that Kula wisdom is a result of spiritual merit accumulated over thousands of lifetimes. This section details the specific qualities a student must possess and warns against sharing these secret teachings with those who are not yet ready.</meta>

# Page 23

## Second Chapter

->O <term>Kulāśraye: Refuge of the Kula tradition</term>! The wisdom of the Kula dawns upon a person who is firmly devoted to the Guru, the sacred Kula scriptures, and the practitioners of the Kula path. (34)<-
<note>original: "श्रीगुरौ कुलशास्त्रेषु कौलिकेषु कुलाश्रये। यस्य भक्तिर्दृढा तस्य कुलज्ञानं प्रकाशते।। ३४।।"</note>

The wisdom of the Kula tradition illuminates the heart of one who possesses unwavering devotion toward their spiritual teacher, the ancestral scriptures, and those who walk the Kaulika path.

->The knowledge of Kula is attained through faith, humility, and joy, combined with good conduct, steadfast vows, and obedience to the commands of the Guru. (35)<-

The wisdom of the Kula is obtained by a seeker who is faithful, submissive, and cheerful, dedicated to a life of disciplined observances and upright behavior, and who remains obedient to the instructions of their Guru.

->Knowledge of the Kula never remains with those who are unworthy. Therefore, as I have said, this wisdom should only be shared after testing the seeker’s suitability. (36)<-

### *The consequences of sharing the Kula path with the undeserving:*

The wisdom of the Kula is not obtained by those who are unfit, nor does it stay with them if given. Therefore, this secret knowledge that I have revealed must only be communicated after a thorough examination of the candidate's eligibility.

->One should not speak of the Kula path or its teachings to an unfit person. Whoever breaks this command shall incur the curse of the deity. (37)<-

The sacred law of the Kula and its governing scriptures should never be revealed to an undeserving person. Anyone who defies this divine order will face the spiritual weight of a divine curse.

->If a practitioner of the <term>Samayācāra: the internal, orthodox path of worship</term> reveals the Kula wisdom improperly, then both that teacher and that student will become as "cattle" before the <term>Yoginīs: powerful semi-divine female spirits</term>. (38)<-
<note>The term "cattle" (paśu) refers to a soul bound by worldly delusions and animalistic instincts, lacking the "heroic" insight of a Tantric initiate. The Yoginīs are the guardians of this secret knowledge.</note>

### *The Glory of the Kula Path:*

->When the Guru first awakens the student and then reveals the Kula wisdom, they both attain the direct companionship of the Yoginīs and the <term>Vīras: spiritual "heroes" or perfected practitioners</term>. (39)<-

->Through this effort, one easily crosses the ocean of worldly existence. By knowing this sacred law of the Kula, one is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (40)<-

If the Guru first awakens the consciousness of the student and then reveals this high knowledge of the Kula, then both the teacher and the recipient enjoy the direct company of the Yoginīs and the Vīras—the divine feminine and masculine powers of the universe. In this way, the seeker effortlessly traverses the turbulent sea of rebirth and finds ultimate liberation.

---

<note>Bhāskararāya, in his famous commentary *Saubhāgyabhāskara*, identifies three distinct schools of worshippers of <term>Śrīvidyā: the "Beautiful Wisdom" of the Goddess</term>. These are the Samaya-mata (the internal, more orthodox path), the Kaula-mata (the path of the Kula lineage), and the Miśra-mata (a mixed path). The conduct followed by the Samaya sect is known as Samayācāra. For further technical distinctions, scholars refer to Lakṣmīdhara's commentary on the 31st verse of the *Saundarya-Laharī* ("The Wave of Beauty").</note>

It warns that revealing these secrets to the unworthy results in spiritual downfall, whereas proper initiation leads to liberation and communion with divine forces.</summary>

(Invoking Lord Śiva) and even cross this worldly ocean effortlessly. Those who know the Kula tradition (Kuladharma) in this way are undoubtedly liberated.

->Those who travel the great highway of the Kula path shall reach the city of Liberation.<-
->Without a doubt, O Lord, one should therefore take refuge in the Kaula way. (41)<-
<note>original: "कुलधर्ममहामार्गगन्ता मुक्तिपुरीं व्रजेत्। अचिरान्नाथ सन्देहस्तस्मात् कौलं समाश्रयेत्।। ४१।।"</note>

Treading on the highway of the Kula path, they proceed to the eternal abode of Emancipation. Therefore, take shelter in the Kula tradition.

->Neglecting the Kula scriptures to practice the scriptures of the uninitiated,<-
->is like abandoning rice pudding in one's own home to wander for alms, O Pārvatī. (42)<-
<note>original: "कुलशास्त्रमनादृत्य पशुशास्त्राणि योऽभ्यसेत्। स्वगृहे पायसं त्यक्त्वा भिक्षामटति पार्वती।। ४२।।"</note>

O <term>Pārvatī: The Divine Mother and consort of Śiva</term>! One who ignores the <term>Kulaśāstra: The sacred Kula scriptures</term> to practice the <term>Paśuśāstra: Scriptures for those still bound by worldly limitations</term> is like a person who leaves the sweet rice and milk in their own house to beg for food elsewhere.

->Abandoning the Kula path to follow another spiritual law,<-
->is like throwing away a jewel in one's hand to seek a distant piece of glass. (43)<-
<note>original: "विहाय कुलधर्मं यः परधर्मपरो भवेत्। करस्थं रत्नमुत्सृज्य दूरस्थं काचमीहते।। ४३।।"</note>

One who leaves the Kula path to become an adherent of another tradition is like a person who discards a precious gem held in their own hand to chase after a distant shard of glass.

->Casting aside Kula mantras to chant the mantras of the uninitiated,<-
->is like discarding a heap of grain to gather a pile of dust. (44)<-
<note>original: "संत्त्यज्य कुलमन्त्राणि पशुमन्त्राणि यो जपेत्। स धान्यराशिमुत्सृज्य पांशुराशिं जिघृक्षति।। ४४।।"</note>

One who abandons the powerful <term>Kula-mantras</term> to perform <term>Japa: Meditative chanting</term> of <term>Paśu-mantras: Lower-tier or common spiritual formulas</term> is like a person who leaves behind a harvest of grain to collect a heap of chaff or dust.

->Leaving the Kula lineage to seek out another family,<-
->is like a thirsty man running from a lake toward a desert mirage. (45)<-
<note>original: "कुलान्वयं समुत्सृज्य योऽन्यमन्वयमीक्षते। तडागादिव तृष्णार्त्तो मृगतृष्णां प्रधावति।। ४५।।"</note>

One who leaves the spiritual family of the Kula to seek another lineage is like a person who, though dying of thirst, leaves a pool of clean water to run after a mirage in the desert.

->Just as a magical illusion provides only a moment of pleasure,<-
->so too are all paths other than the Kula, O Queen of the Kula. (46)<-
<note>original: "यथेन्द्रजालजा माया क्षणमेव सुखावहा। श्रीकौलादन्यसमयास्तादृशाः कुलनायिके।। ४६।।"</note>

Just as a trick of magic provides only a momentary delight, so O <term>Kulanāyike: Noble Lady of the Kula</term>, all spiritual paths other than the Kula provide only a fleeting sense of peace.

## Second Chapter

One who desires liberation from the cycle of worldly existence without knowing the <term>Kuladharma: The sacred path of the Kula tradition</term> is like a person who attempts to cross the vast, shoreless ocean using only their hands. (47)
<note>original: "कुलधर्ममजानन् यः संसारान्मोक्षमिच्छति। पारावारमपारं स पाणिभ्यां तर्तुमिच्छति।। ४७।।"</note>

->*Worship of Kula ( <term>Śaktidevī: The Divine Mother/Goddess</term> ) provides the Blissful State :*<-

<note>original: "यो वान्यदर्शनेभ्यश्च भुक्तिं मुक्तिञ्च काङ्क्षति। स्वप्नलब्धधनेनैव धनावन् स भवेत्तदा।। ४८।।"</note>

<note>original: "शुक्तौ रजतविभ्रान्तिर्यथा जायेत पार्वति। तथान्यसमयेभ्यश्च भुक्तिमुक्तिः प्रकाशते।। ४९।।"</note>

<note>original: "सर्वकर्म विहीनोऽपि वर्णाश्रमविवर्जितः। कुलनिष्ठः कुलेशानि भुक्तिमुक्त्योः स भाजनम्।। ५०।।"</note>

> O Kuleśāni! alone by itself, unaccompanied by rituals and observances of <term>Āśramas: The four stages of human life (student, householder, retiree, and renunciant)</term> the Kuladharma is capable of leading to the final Release.

<note>original: "कुलज्ञानविहीनोऽपि कुलभक्त्याश्रयो भवेत्। सोऽपि सद्गतिमाप्नोति किमुतस्य परायणः।। ५१।।"</note>

> Even if one lacks full knowledge of this doctrine of Kula, his mere faith and dedication to it are enough to deliver him; then what to speak of its adherents?

<note>original: "कुलधर्मो हतो हन्ति रक्षितो रक्षति प्रिये। पूजितः पूजयत्याशु तस्मात्तं न परित्यजेत्।। ५२।।"</note>

> O My Beloved! Break the Kuladharma and it will break you; guard it and it will guard you; adore it, revere it and it will immediately show you the same consideration.

The right attitude for the seeker of Truth of this lofty faith is: "Let my people look askance; let my wife and children forsake me; let
