# The Ninth Exultation
<note>original: "Navama Ullāsaḥ"</note>

---

->The Goddess said:<-

->O Lord of Kula <note>original: "Kuleśa"; Shiva as the head of the Kula lineage or tradition</note>, I wish to hear about Yoga, the characteristics of a master of Yoga, and the reward for worshipping those devoted to the Kula tradition. Tell me this, O Ocean of Mercy! || 1 ||<-

->The Lord said:<-

->Listen, O Goddess, and I shall explain what you ask. By merely hearing this, Yoga reveals itself directly. || 2 ||<-

->Meditation is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as "Gross" and "Subtle." Meditation upon a specific form is called Gross <note>original: "sthūla"; the physical or manifest form of a deity</note>, while meditation without a form is called Subtle <note>original: "sūkṣma"; the unmanifest or abstract essence</note>. || 3 ||<-

->Some recommend Gross meditation for the purpose of steadying the mind. Through the Gross, the mind becomes still, and it becomes still through the Subtle as well; both kinds of meditation promote the same objective: the steadiness of the mind. || 4 ||<-

->One should meditate upon the Supreme Lord <note>term: "Parameśvara" (The ultimate deity, Shiva)</note> as being without hands, feet, belly, or face. He is composed of all light, is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss <note>term: "Saccidānanda" (The Vedantic definition of the ultimate reality: Sat (existence), Cit (consciousness), and Ananda (bliss))</note>, and is partless <note>original: "niṣkala"; without divisions, limbs, or physical components</note>. || 5 ||<-

->He neither rises nor sets; He neither grows nor decays. He shines by Himself and illumines all other things without any external means. || 6 ||<-

<summary>The Goddess asks Shiva about the nature of Yoga and its practitioners, leading to an explanation of meditation (Dhyāna) in its Gross and Subtle forms. Shiva describes the Supreme Lord as an eternal, self-luminous essence of pure consciousness beyond physical form.</summary>

<keywords>Yoga, Dhyana, Meditation, Parameshwara, Saccidananda, Gross and Subtle meditation, Kula tradition, Shiva and Shakti</keywords>

--- Page 145 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the Ninth Exultation of the Kularnava Tantra. Following the description of the Supreme Lord as formless and all-pervading in the previous verses, the text now defines the internal states of realization, including the nature of spiritual knowledge, the signs of a true Yogi, and the characteristics of deep meditative absorption (Samādhi) and liberation while living (Jīvanamukti).</meta>

# In the Kularnava Tantra
<note>original: "Kulārṇavatantre"</note>

->That infinite light which has no form, which is pure existence and beyond the reach of the senses, perceived only by the mind—that knowledge is called the Knowledge of the Absolute. || 7 ||<-
<note>original: "Brahmajñāna"</note>

**Knowledge of the Absolute (Brahma-jñāna):**
That Infinite, Conditionless Form, not perceptible <note>original: "agocaram"; literally "beyond the range of the senses"</note>, yet simply existent, when experienced mentally, then that Knowledge is called <term>Brahmajñāna</term> (Knowledge of the Absolute).

->One who has arrested the movement of the life-breath, who is as motionless as a stone, and who knows the dwelling place of the Supreme Soul—that yogi is called a master of Yoga. || 8 ||<-

**Marks of a Yogi:**
Arresting the life-breath <note>original: "prāṇāyāma" or the cessation of breath</note>, becoming stable like a stone and knowing only the Supreme Self and its Abode is called a <term>Yogī</term> who knows Yoga.

->That state where there is no perception of "this" or "not this," remaining still like a calm ocean, and devoid of individual form—that meditation is designated as Absorption. || 9 ||<-
<note>original: "Samādhi"</note>

**Characteristics of Absorption (Samādhi):**
That condition of Meditation <note>term: "Dhyāna" (sustained concentration)</note> where there is no awareness of external objects, which is like a calm sea, and where there is an absence of individual Form—that <term>Dhyāna</term> is called <term>Samādhi</term> (Absorption).

->By thinking of nothing at all, Reality reveals itself of its own accord. When that Reality is self-revealed, one should instantly become absorbed in it. || 10 ||<-

**Characteristics of Release while Living:**
When the Reality <note>original: "Tattva"; the fundamental truth or essence</note> shines forth by itself and not by any effort of mental thinking; and when such a Reality shines forth on its own, one should immediately become engrossed in it.

->One who remains as if asleep even while in the states of dreaming or waking, and who is without the movement of inhalation or exhalation—he is certainly liberated. || 11 ||<-

One who appears as if asleep whether in the dreaming or the waking states, who neither inhales nor exhales and becomes immobile, he is truly Freed.

->With the collection of senses unmoving and the mind and breath dissolved in the Self, he who sits like one dead is called "Liberated while Living." || 12 ||<-
<note>original: "Jīvanamukta"</note>

Keeping his sense organs inactive <note>original: "niṣpanda-karaṇa-grāmaḥ"</note>, one merging his mind into his Self appears as if dead, and is called a veritable <term>Jīvanamukta</term> (one who is liberated while still in the body).

->He hears not, nor does he smell; he touches not, nor does he see. He knows neither pleasure nor pain, nor does his mind form intentions. || 13 ||<-

->He knows nothing at all, and perceives nothing, like a piece of wood. One whose soul is thus dissolved in Shiva is said to be established in Absorption. || 14 ||<-
<note>original: "Samādhistha"; one who stands or stays in Samādhi</note>

<summary>This page defines the highest states of Yoga, describing Samādhi as a state of deep stillness comparable to a calm ocean or a piece of wood, where the practitioner is "liberated while living" (Jīvanamukta) and entirely absorbed in the divine reality of Shiva.</summary>

<keywords>Brahmajñāna, Yogi, Samādhi, Jīvanamukta, Dhyāna, Kularnava Tantra, liberation, breath control, Shiva</keywords>

--- Page 146 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page continues the Ninth Exultation (Ullāsa) of the Kularnava Tantra. While the previous page defined the initial stages of meditative absorption (Samādhi), this section expands on the total non-duality between the individual soul and the Divine, using various physical metaphors to describe the state of a liberated Yogi.</meta>

# Ninth Exultation: Page 137
<note>original: "Navama Ullāsaḥ 137"</note>

### *Characteristics of a person in Samādhi:*

He neither hears, nor smells, nor touches, nor sees; he knows not the pleasures and pains and does not even exercise the mind. Like a log of wood, he neither cognizes anything nor is aware of anything. One who is thus absorbed in <term>Śiva</term> (the Supreme Consciousness) alone is said to be in <term>Samādhi</term> (complete meditative absorption).

->As water is poured into water, milk into milk, or clarified butter into clarified butter,<-
<note>original: "yathā jale jalaṃ kṣiptaṃ kṣīre kṣīraṃ ghṛte ghṛtam"</note>
->so the individual soul and the Supreme Soul become indistinguishable. || 15 ||<-
<note>original: "aviśeṣo bhavet-tadvaj-jīvātma-paramātmanoḥ"</note>

### *No difference between Jīvātmā and Paramātmā:*

Just as no differences exist when water is thrown into water, milk into milk, or Ghee <note>clarified butter</note> into Ghee; similarly, there remains no difference between the <term>Jīvātmā</term> (the individual soul) and <term>Paramātmā</term> (the Supreme Self).

->Just as by the power of concentration even an insect becomes a bee,<-
<note>original: "yathā dhyānasya sāmarthyāt kīṭo'pi bhramarāyate"</note>
->so by the power of absorption a man becomes the Absolute. || 16 ||<-
<note>original: "tathā samādhi-sāmarthyād-brahmabhūto bhaven-naraḥ"</note>

Even just as an insect becomes a bee <note>This refers to the 'Bhramara-Kīṭa' metaphor, where a caterpillar is said to transform into a wasp or bee by constantly meditating on it through fear or focus</note> by force of concentration, so a man becomes <term>Brahma</term> (the Absolute Reality) by dint of <term>Samādhi</term>.

->Just as Ghee extracted from milk, when thrown back into it, is not as it was before,<-
<note>original: "kṣīroddhṛtaṃ ghṛtaṃ yadvat tatra kṣiptaṃ na pūrvavat"</note>
->so the Self, once separated from the qualities of nature, is said to be liberated here. || 17 ||<-
<note>original: "pṛthakkṛto guṇebhyaḥ syādātmā tadvadihocyate"</note>

Just as Ghee extracted from milk does not mix with the same milk again in its original form <note>meaning it remains Ghee and does not turn back into milk</note>, similarly once the Self is separated from the <term>Gunas</term> (the three fundamental qualities of nature: harmony, passion, and inertia), it is never the same again.

->Just as one standing in thick darkness sees nothing here,<-
<note>original: "yathā gāḍhāndhakārastho na kiñcidiha paśyati"</note>
->so the Yogi, being focused on the invisible, does not see the worldly expansion. || 18 ||<-
<note>original: "alakṣyaśca tathā yogī prapañcaṃ naiva paśyati"</note>

Just as one in heavy darkness sees nothing, so indeed a <term>Yogī</term> sees nothing of the worldly object <note>original: "prapañca"; the manifest world of diversity</note>, which does not hold his attention.

->Just as at the time of closing the eyes one does not see the world,<-
<note>original: "yathā nimīlane kāle prapañcaṃ naiva paśyati"</note>
->so it should be even when the eyes are open; this is the mark of true meditation. || 19 ||<-
<note>original: "tathaivonmīlane'pi syād-etad-dhyānasya lakṣaṇam"</note>

### *Characteristics of Dhyāna:*

One does not see the world of objects when his eyes are closed. However, not seeing the world even when the eyes are open <note>attaining a state where the internal spiritual focus is not broken by external sight</note>, is the true characteristic of <term>Dhyāna</term> (sustained meditation).

->Just as a person knows the itching of their own body,<-
<note>original: "janaḥ svadeha-kaṇḍūtiṃ vijānāti yathā tathā"</note>
->one who has the nature of the Supreme Absolute knows the movements of the universe. || 20 ||<-
<note>original: "paraṃ brahmasvarūpī ca vetti viśva-viceṣṭitam"</note>

### *Fruit of the Knowledge of Supreme Reality:*

Just as men experience even the itches of their body, in the same manner a <term>Sādhaka</term> (spiritual practitioner) who has achieved the <term>Param Brahma</term> (Supreme Absolute) knows the activities of the objective world <note>The sense here is that the liberated soul perceives the universe as intimately as their own body, yet remains detached</note>.

<vocab>Samādhi (complete meditative absorption), Śiva (Supreme Consciousness), Jīvātmā (individual soul), Paramātmā (Supreme Soul), Brahma (the Absolute), Gunas (qualities of nature), Yogi (practitioner of Yoga), Dhyāna (meditation), Sādhaka (spiritual aspirant), Param Brahma (Highest Reality)</vocab>

<summary>This page describes the state of Samādhi as a total merging of the individual soul with the Supreme, using metaphors like milk mixing with milk and the transformation of an insect into a bee. It emphasizes that a true master perceives the spiritual reality even with eyes open, seeing the world's movements as intimately as a sensation on their own skin.</summary>

# In the Kulārṇava Tantra
<page-num>138</page-num>

->When the Supreme Reality is known—that which is beyond all letters and is unchanging—<-
<note>original: "vidite parame tattve varṇātīte hyavikriye"</note>
->then all sacred <term>Mantras</term> (incantations), along with the deities who preside over them, become like servants. || 21 ||<-
<note>original: "kiṅkaratvaṃ hi gacchanti mantrā mantrādhipaiḥ saha"</note>

All the <term>Mantras</term> <note>sacred sounds or syllables used in prayer</note> along with their Presiding Deities become servitors of a <term>Sādhaka</term> <note>a spiritual practitioner or seeker</note> who knows the Supreme Reality that exists beyond the physical letters of the alphabet.

->For one who is established in the singular consciousness of the Self, every movement is an act of worship;<-
<note>original: "ātmaikabhāvaniṣṭhasya yā yā ceṣṭā tadarcanam"</note>
->every word spoken is a true <term>Mantra</term>, and every gaze is a form of meditation. || 22 ||<-
<note>original: "yo yo jalpaḥ sa sanmantrastaddhyānaṃ yannirīkṣaṇam"</note>

For the person who is founded in the sole consciousness of the Self, every physical movement becomes an act of ritual worship, each casual utterance is equivalent to a sacred <term>Mantra</term>, and every sight or gaze is a state of deep meditation.

->When the identification with the body has dissolved and the Supreme Soul is realized,<-
<note>original: "dehābhimāne galite vijñāte paramātmani"</note>
->wherever the mind may wander, it finds a state of <term>Samādhi</term> (meditative absorption) there. || 23 ||<-
<note>original: "yatra yatra mano yāti tatra tatra samādhayaḥ"</note>
->The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed,<-
<note>original: "bhidyate hṛdayagranthiśchidyante sarvasaṃśayāḥ"</note>
->and one’s <term>Karma</term> (accumulated actions) withers away upon seeing that Supreme Self. || 24 ||<-
<note>original: "kṣīyante cāsya karmāṇi tasmin dṛṣṭe parātmani"</note>

When the <term>Paramātmā</term> <note>the Supreme Soul or Universal Self</note> is known, the ego-driven consciousness of the body ends entirely; and wherever such a <term>Sādhaka</term> goes, he obtains <term>Samādhi</term> <note>a state of intense concentration and union with the Divine</note> right there. The complex knot of his heart is cut asunder and all his doubts are removed. Because he has seen the Supreme Self, the weight of all his past actions dwindles away.

->When the great Yogi has attained the stainless and Supreme State,<-
<note>original: "yogīndreṇa yadā prāptaṃ nirmalaṃ paramaṃ padam"</note>
->even the high statuses of the Gods and Demons are no longer desired. || 25 ||<-
<note>original: "devāsurapadaṃ yattattrāsaścāpi na gṛhyate"</note>

In comparison to the pure and Supreme State obtained by the Master-yogī, even the celestial ranks of the <term>Devas</term> <note>Gods or benevolent celestial beings</note> and <term>Asuras</term> <note>demons or titans</note> are not considered worth accepting.

->One who sees the all-pervading, peaceful, blissful, and imperishable Reality,<-
<note>original: "yaḥ paśyet sarvagaṃ śāntamānandātmaka mavyayam"</note>
->for them, nothing remains to be attained, and no knowledge remains to be sought. || 26 ||<-
<note>original: "tasya kiñcidalabhyaṃ jñātavyaṃ nāvaśiṣyate"</note>

One who has seen the All-pervading, Peaceful, Blissful, and the Imperishable Reality finds that there is nothing left for him to achieve or to know.

->When knowledge and direct realization are achieved, and the Object of Knowledge is firmly seated in the heart,<-
<note>original: "samprāpte jñānavijñāne jñeye ca hṛdi saṃsthite"</note>
->and when the state of Peace is attained, O Goddess, there is no more need for Yoga or disciplined concentration. || 27 ||<-
<note>original: "labdhe śāntipade devi na yogo naiva dhāraṇā"</note>

When both theoretical knowledge and direct spiritual experience are attained, and when that which is to be known is alive within the heart, the state of total Peace is reached. At that point, O Goddess, neither formal <term>Yoga</term> nor <term>Dhāraṇā</term> <note>the sixth limb of yoga, meaning fixed concentration</note> is necessary anymore.

<summary>This page describes the "Jivanmukta" or the liberated soul, explaining that once a practitioner realizes the Supreme Reality, their every action becomes a form of worship and formal religious practices like Mantras or Yoga become unnecessary. The realization of the Self effectively severs the ties of ego and karma, rendering even the status of gods insignificant in comparison.</summary>

# Ninth Exultation
<page-num>136</page-num>

->When the Supreme Reality is known, all rules and regulations are no longer needed.<-
<note>original: "pare brahmaṇi viజ్ఞāte samastairniyamairalam"</note>
->What is the use of a palm-leaf fan once the cool southern breeze has been reached? || 28 ||<-
<note>original: "tālavṛntena kiṃ kāryaṃ labdhe malayamārute"</note>
<note>The "Malaya breeze" refers to the sandalwood-scented winds from the Malaya mountains, a traditional poetic symbol for ultimate comfort that makes artificial cooling—like a fan—unnecessary.</note>

For the one who sees themselves as the sacred syllable <term>Aum</term> <note>the primordial sound of the universe</note> or as the True Self, there is no longer a need for restrictive postures or the binding of the breath. There are no external restraints or obligatory observances. || 29 ||
<note>original: "āsikābandhanaṃ nāsti nāsikābandhanaṃ na hi | na yamo niyamo nāsti svayamomiti paśyatām"</note>

Yoga is not achieved merely through the "Lotus Position," nor is it found simply by staring at the tip of one’s nose. || 30a ||
<note>original: "na padmāsanato yogaṃ na nāsāgranirīkṣaṇam"</note>

**Characteristics of Yoga:**

The experts in Yoga declare that true Yoga is the union of the <term>Jīvātman</term> <note>the individual soul</note> and the <term>Ātman</term> <note>the universal or supreme soul</note>. || 30b ||
<note>original: "aikyaṃ jīvātmano... āhuḥ yogaṃ yogaviśāradāḥ"</note>

When a seeker meditates upon this Supreme Reality even for a single moment with faith, the immense spiritual merit that follows is so great it cannot be measured. || 31 ||
<note>original: "dhyāyatāṃ kṣaṇamātraṃ hi śraddhayā paramanviha | yad bhavet sumahat puṇyaṃ tasyānto naiva gaṇyate"</note>

->If one reflects for even a moment on the truth "I am the Absolute,"<-
<note>original: "kṣaṇaṃ brahmāhamasmīti yaḥ kuryādātmacintanam"</note>
->it destroys all sins, just as the rising sun dispels the deep darkness. || 32 ||<-
<note>original: "sa sarvapātakaṃ hanyāttamaḥ sūryodayo yathā"</note>

The knower of Truth attains ten million times the reward that is promised by religious vows, sacrifices, austerities, pilgrimages, charity, and the ritual worship of gods. || 33 ||
<note>original: "vratakratutapastīrthadānadevarcanādiṣu | yat phalaṃ koṭiguṇitaṃ tadavāpnoti tattvavit"</note>

**Four States of a Seeker:**

The "Natural State" of constant awareness is the highest; meditation and concentration are the middle state; the recitation of prayers and hymns is lower; and external fire sacrifices and ritual worship are the lowest of all. || 34 ||
<note>original: "uttamā sahajāvasthā madhyamā dhyānadhāraṇā | japastutiḥ syādadhamā homapūjā'dhamādhamā"</note>

Contemplating the Absolute Truth is the best path; preoccupation with <term>Japa</term> <note>repetitive chanting</note> is the middle path; the mere study of the <term>Śāstras</term> <note>sacred scriptures</note> is a low path; and being consumed by worldly affairs is the lowest path of all. || 35 ||
<note>original: "uttamā tattvacintā syājjapacintā tu madhyamā | śāstracintā'dhamā jñeyā lokacintā'dhamādhamā"</note>

<summary>This page defines true Yoga as the union of the individual and universal soul, arguing that direct realization of the Absolute (Brahman) renders external rituals, physical postures, and scriptural study secondary.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the Ninth Exultation of the Kulārṇava Tantra. # In the Kulārṇava Tantra
<page-num>140</page-num>

->A billion ritual worships are equal to a single hymn of praise; a billion hymns of praise are equal to a single recitation of a mantra.<-
->A billion recitations are equal to a single meditation; a billion meditations are equal to a single state of total absorption. || 36 ||<-
<note>original: "pūjākoṭisamaṃ stotraṃ stotrakoṭisamo japaḥ | japakoṭisamaṃ dhyānaṃ dhyānakoṭisamo layaḥ"</note>
<note>The term <term>Laya</term> refers to a state of spiritual dissolution where the individual mind merges completely into the Divine consciousness.</note>

->No sacred sound is higher than meditation; no deity is higher than the True Self.<-
->No worship is higher than inner contemplation; no spiritual fruit is higher than contentment. || 37 ||<-
<note>original: "na hi dhyānāt paro mantro na devasvātmanaḥ paraḥ | nānuisandhāt parā pūjā na hi tṛpteḥ paraṃ phalam"</note>

->The highest worship is being free from ritual action; the highest recitation is silence.<-
->The highest meditation is the absence of thought; the highest fruit is the absence of desire. || 38 ||<-
<note>original: "akriyaiva parā pūjā maunameva paro japaḥ | acintaiva paraṃ dhyānamanicchaiva paraṃ phalam"</note>

### *The Method of Worship for the Knower of Truth:*

->A practitioner of Yoga should always perform the twilight prayers without water or mantras, penance without ritual or fire-offerings, and worship without physical ceremonies. || 39 ||<-
<note>original: "mantrodakairvinā sandhyā pūjāhomairvinā tapaḥ | upacārairvinā pūjāṃ yogī nityaṃ samācaret"</note>
<note>This verse advocates for "internalized ritual," where the physical elements like <term>Sandhyā</term> (water offerings) and <term>Homa</term> (sacrificial fire) are replaced by mental focus and spiritual awareness.</note>

->Free from attachment, solitary, having crossed beyond the subconscious imprints and all limiting conditions, the Yogī—absorbed in his own true nature—knows the Supreme Truth. || 40 ||<-
<note>original: "niḥsaṅgaśca visaṅgaśca nistīrṇopādhivāsanāḥ | nijasvarūpanimagnaḥ sa yogī परतत्त्ववित् (paratattvavit)"</note>
<note><term>Vāsanā</term> refers to the latent tendencies or "karmic smells" left in the mind by past actions, which the advanced Yogī has successfully transcended.</note>

### *The Form of the Individual Soul and the Supreme Soul:*

->The body itself is the temple, O Goddess; the individual soul is the eternal God, the Ever-Auspicious One.<-
->Discard the faded floral offerings of ignorance and worship with the consciousness of "I am He." || 41 ||<-
<note>original: "deho devālayo devi jīvo devaḥ sadāśivaḥ | tyajedajñānanirmālyaṃ so’hambhāvena pūjayet"</note>
<note><term>So'ham</term> ("He am I") is a foundational mantra expressing the identity of the seeker with the Absolute. <term>Nirmālya</term> refers to flowers left over from a previous day's ritual; here, ignorance is poetically compared to stale, discarded offerings.</note>

->The individual soul is Shiva, and Shiva is the individual soul; the soul is indeed Shiva alone.<-
->When bound by ties, it is called the soul; when freed from those ties, it is known as the Ever-Auspicious One. || 42 ||<-
<note>original: "jīvaḥ śivaḥ śivo jīvaḥ sa jīvaḥ kevalaḥ śivaḥ | pāśabaddhaḥ smṛto jīvaḥ pāśamuktaḥ sadāśivaḥ"</note>
<note>The "ties" or <term>Pāśa</term> refer to the bonds of attachment, delusion, and karma that prevent the soul from recognizing its inherently divine nature as <term>Sadāśiva</term>.</note>

<summary>This page describes a spiritual hierarchy where internal absorption (Laya) and silent meditation far surpass external rituals. It concludes with the radical tantric teaching that the human body is a temple and the individual soul is essentially identical to the Divine (Shiva), separated only by the "bonds" of ignorance.</summary>

->As long as it is enclosed in the husk, it is called paddy; once freed from the husk, it is called rice.<-

->The Divine resides in the fire for the priests; in the heart for the contemplative;<-

### *Characteristics of a Yogi who knows the Supreme Truth:*

->He who remains equal in the face of both criticism and praise, in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and among friends and enemies, is a master of <term>Yoga</term>, free from both excitement and resentment. || 45 ||<-

<note>This "wayfarer" metaphor suggests that the Yogi inhabits the physical form without becoming attached to it, knowing their true home is in the spirit.</note>

->He is a Yogi who knows the Supreme Truth, free from worldly intentions, free from doubt, and untainted by the impressions of the past. He is forever immersed in the reality of his own true nature. || 47 ||<-

->O <term>Kuleśāni</term><note>A title for the Goddess, meaning "Mistress of the Divine Lineage."</note>! The Yogi who has realized the Truth lives in the world appearing as if he were lame, blind, deaf, impotent, intoxicated, or simple-minded. || 48 ||<-
<note>original: "paṅgvandhabadhiraklībonmattajaḍādayaḥ"</note>
<note>This verse describes the "holy fool" or "hidden saint" archetype; the Yogi hides their spiritual attainments by appearing insignificant or incapacitated to worldly eyes.</note>

->Filled with the Supreme Bliss that arises from the secret worship of the <term>Five Mudrās</term><note>Refers to the <italic>Pañcamakāra</italic>, the five ritual elements: Wine, Meat, Fish, Parched Grain, and Sexual Union. In this context, they are understood as internal spiritual states rather than just physical acts.</note>, that master Yogi beholds the Divine Self within his own self. || 49 ||<-

# In the Kulārṇava Tantra: 142
<page-num>142</page-num>

->O My Beloved! The pleasure derived from wine, meat, and sexual union<-
->is liberation for those who know the Truth, but it is sin for the ignorant. || 50 ||<-
<note>original: "alimāṃsāṅganāsaṅge yat sukhaṃ jāyate priye | tadeva mokṣo viduṣāmabudhānāntu pātakam"</note>

->One who always delights in the ecstasy of wine and meat, who is always contemplating the Divine Footprints,<-
->and is always free from doubt—such a person is called a <term>Kula Yogi</term>. || 51 ||<-
<note>A Kula Yogi is an advanced practitioner of the "Kula" tradition, which seeks to find the divine within the material world rather than by shunning it.</note>

### *Characteristics of Kula Yogis:*

->Drinking wine, eating meat, and following the path of his own will,<-
->he should live happily and contented, contemplating the unity of the "I" and "That." || 52 ||<-
<note>This "unity" refers to the non-dual realization that there is no fundamental difference between the individual seeker, the world, and the Divine.</note>

->Whose mouth is devoid of the scent of wine and meat<-
->must perform penance; he is to be avoided and is surely nothing but a <term>Paśu</term>. || 53 ||<-
<term>Paśu</term><note>Literally "beast" or "animal." In this tradition, it refers to the "bound" soul who is still trapped by social conventions, fear, and limited morality, unable to see the divine in all things.</note>

->As long as there is the scent of wine, the "beast" becomes the <term>Paśupati</term> himself;<-
->without the scent of wine and meat, even the "Lord of Beasts" is but a beast. || 54 ||<-
<note>original: "yāvadāsavagandhaḥ syāt paśuḥ paśupatiḥ svayam | vinālimāṃsagandhena sākṣāt paśupatiḥ paśuḥ"</note>
<term>Paśupati</term><note>The "Lord of Beasts," a name for the god Shiva. The text suggests that the ritual consumption of these substances acts as a catalyst, transforming a bound human into a god-like state.</note>

->What is considered low in the world is high here, and what is high in the world is low here;<-
->this Kula path was declared by the great-souled Lord <term>Bhairava</term>. || 55 ||<-
<note>Bhairava is the fierce manifestation of Shiva. The "Kula path" often involves "inverting" social norms to prove that the practitioner is no longer affected by worldly concepts of "pure" or "impure."</note>

### *No procedural restrictions for a Kaulika:*

->Improper conduct is proper conduct; what should not be done is the highest duty.<-
->Even what is false becomes truth for the <term>Kaulikas</term>, O <term>Kuleśvarī</term>! || 56 ||<-
<term>Kaulika</term><note>A follower of the Kula path.</note>
<term>Kuleśvarī</term><note>The "Goddess of the Kula," the feminine aspect of the divine to whom Lord Bhairava is speaking.</note>

<summary>This page describes the transgressive practices of the Kula path, where ritual consumption of wine and meat is used to transform the "bound soul" (Paśu) into a liberated being (Paśupati). It emphasizes that for the enlightened Yogi, worldly social morality and restrictions no longer apply.</summary>

<summary>This page describes the "Kaulika" (Tantric practitioner) as a being who has transcended all social and religious dualities, turning what is normally sinful or harmful into a path for liberation and worldly success.</summary>

# In the Kulārṇava Tantra
<page-num>144</page-num>

->In whatever disguise he may appear, and by whomever he remains unnoticed;<-
->in whatever <term>stage of life</term> he may stay, he is a Kula Yogi, O <term>Mistress of the Kula</term>! || 65 ||<-
<note>original: "yeun keunāpi veśena yeun keunāpyalakṣitaḥ | yatra kutrāśrame tiṣṭhet kulayogī kuleśvari"</note>
<term>stage of life</term><note>Āśrama: The traditional four stages of life (student, householder, retiree, ascetic). The text implies the Yogi's internal state transcends these external social categories.</note>
<term>Mistress of the Kula</term><note>Kuleśvari: An address to the Goddess as the supreme power of the Tantric lineage.</note>

*The Behaviour of a Kula Yogī:*

->Yogis, appearing in diverse guises for the welfare of humanity,<-
->wander upon this earth with their true nature unrecognized by others. || 66 ||<-
<note>original: "yogino vividhairvaiśairnarāṇāṃ hitakāriṇaḥ | bhramanti pṛthivīmetāmavijñātasvarūpiṇaḥ"</note>

->They never display their self-knowledge all at once, O Mistress of the Kula;<-
->in the midst of people, they live as if they were intoxicated, mute, or fools. || 67 ||<-
<note>original: "sakṛnnauvātmavijñānaṃ kṣapayanti kuleśvari | unmattamūkajaḍavannivse llo kamadhyataḥ"</note>
<note>This "mad-mute-idiot" behavior (unmatta-mūka-jaḍa) is a recognized spiritual discipline in many Indian traditions, used to protect the practitioner's inner peace from the distractions of fame or social expectation.</note>

->Just as the stars and the planets in the sky are not easily seen in the presence of the Sun and Moon,<-
->so too the conduct of the Yogis is imperceptible in the world. || 68 ||<-
<note>original: "alakṣyo hi yathā loke vyomni candrārkayogataḥ | nakṣatrāṇāṃ grahāṇāśca tathā vṛttantu yoginām"</note>

->As the path of birds in the sky or fish in the water cannot be seen, O Goddess,<-
->likewise the conduct of the Yogis is hidden from view. || 69 ||<-
<note>original: "ākāśe pakṣiṇāṃ devi jale'pi jalacāriṇām | yathā gatirna dṛśyeta tathā vṛttaṃ hi yoginām"</note>

->Those who are experts in Kula Yoga speak in the manner of the uncivil, O Beloved;<-
->they behave as if they were ignorant and appear like the lowly. || 70 ||<-
<note>original: "asanta iva bhāṣante carantyajñā iva priye | pāmarā iva dṛśyante kulayoga viśāradāḥ"</note>

->They behave in such a way that people might ignore them and not seek their company;<-
->the Yogi conducts himself by speaking nothing at all. || 71 ||<-
<note>original: "janā yathāvamanyante gaccheyurnaiva saṅgatim | na किञ्चिदपि bhāṣante tathā yogī pravarttate"</note>

->Though liberated, the Lord of the Kula may sport like a child and act like a dullard;<-
->the wise Kula Yogi speaks like a madman, O <term>Great Goddess</term>! || 72 ||<-
<note>original: "mukto'pi bālavat krīḍet kuleśo jaḍavaccaret | vadedunmattavadvidvān kulayogī maheśvari"</note>
<term>Great Goddess</term><note>Maheśvari: A title for the Goddess as the supreme sovereign (feminine form of Maheshvara/Shiva).</note>

<summary>This page describes the "hidden path" of the Kula Yogi, who deliberately disguises their high spiritual state by appearing as a fool, a madman, or a person of low status to avoid the distractions of society. The text uses metaphors of birds in flight and fish in water to illustrate the trackless and imperceptible nature of a liberated being's life.</summary>
<keywords>Kula Yogi, Kulesvari, secrecy, madness (unmatta), spiritual disguise, liberation (mukti), Maheśvari, Kularnava Tantra</keywords>

Following the description of the Yogi’s internal state of "secret conduct," these verses describe how the advanced practitioner transcends social conventions of purity and pollution, acting in ways that might appear erratic or lowly to the uninitiated while remaining internally immaculate.</meta>

# Ninth Exultation
<page-num>145</page-num>

->The Yogi conducts himself in such a way that the people of this world might laugh at him, feel disgusted by him, or revile him; seeing him from afar, they avoid him and pass him by. || 73 ||<-
<note>original: "yathā hasati loko'yaṃ jugupsati ca kutsati | vilokya dūrato yāti tathā yogī pravarttate"</note>
<note>By appearing "repulsive" or "mad," the Yogi protects his spiritual practice from the interference and expectations of society.</note>

->Sometimes appearing as a person of high status, sometimes as one who has fallen, and sometimes appearing like a ghost or a demon, the Yogi wanders the surface of the earth wearing various guises. || 74 ||<-
<note>original: "kvacicchiṣṭaḥ kvacidbhraṣṭaḥ kvacid bhūtapishācavat | nānāveśadharo yogī vicarejjagatītale"</note>
<note>The comparison to a ghost or demon (<term>Bhūta</term> or <term>Pishāca</term>) refers to the "Aghori" style of practice where a Yogi might stay in cremation grounds to conquer fear and social conditioning.</note>

->A Yogi enjoys the pleasures of life only for the benefit of the world and never out of his own personal craving. Bestowing grace upon all beings, he plays upon the earth. || 75 ||<-
<note>original: "yogī lokaupakārāya bhogān bhuṅkte na kāṅkṣayā | anugṛhṇan janān sarvān krīḍecca pṛthivītale"</note>

->Just as the **Sun** dries up everything, and as **Fire** consumes everything, the Yogi experiences all pleasures yet is never tainted by any sin. || 76 ||<-
<note>original: "sarvaśoṣī yathā sūryaḥ sarvabhogī yathā'nalaḥ | yogī bhuktvākhilān bhogān tathā pāpairna lipyate"</note>
<note>This is a famous metaphor in Tantric philosophy: the Sun draws moisture from both sewage and perfume without becoming "dirty," and Fire burns trash and incense alike, remaining pure. The Yogi’s consciousness is similarly "heat-tempered."</note>

->Like the **Wind** that touches everything, like the **Sky** that pervades everywhere, and like those who have bathed in sacred rivers, the Yogi is eternally pure. || 77 ||<-
<note>original: "sarvasparśī yathā vāyuryathākāśashca sarvagaḥ | sarve yathā nadīsnātāstathā yogī sadā śuciḥ"</note>

->Just as common village water becomes pure when it reaches a great river, so too do food and items from the house of an <term>outcaste</term> become pure when placed in the hands of a Yogi. || 78 ||<-
<note>original: "yathā grāmagataṃ toyaṃ nadīyuktaṃ bhavecchuci | tathā mlecchagṛhānnādi yogihastāpitaṃ śuci"</note>
<term>outcaste</term><note>Mlechchha: Historically used to describe those outside the traditional Vedic social order. The text argues that the Yogi's spiritual "fire" purifies any social or ritual pollution.</note>

->O **Goddess**! To the wise who seek their own spiritual welfare, the ways of those who are experts in **Kaula Knowledge** are indeed the most honored. || 79 ||<-
<note>original: "yathā''caranti deveśi kulajñānavishāradāḥ | tadeva viduṣāṃ mānyamātmano hitakāṅkṣiṇām"</note>
<note>Devi: The text is a dialogue where Lord Shiva instructs the Goddess (Devi/Deveshi).</note>

->The path upon which the Lords of Yoga travel is considered the Supreme Path; just as wherever the Sun rises is defined as the East. || 80 ||<-
<note>original: "yasmiṃshcaranti yogīśāḥ sa mārgaḥ paramo mataḥ | yasyāmudeti sūryo hi pūrvāśā sā nigadyate"</note>
<note>This verse asserts that the Yogi defines the path, rather than following a path defined by others. His actions create the "direction" of righteousness.</note>

**Vocabulary Notes:**
*   **Yogi:** A practitioner of Yoga who has achieved union with the divine.
*   **Agni (Anala):** The sacred fire, used here as a symbol of absolute purification.
*   **Kaula Knowledge:** The specific wisdom of the "Kula" tradition, which integrates worldly enjoyment with spiritual liberation.
*   **Devi:** The Goddess, addressed here as the student of this secret wisdom.

<summary>This page describes the "transcendent" behavior of a Kula Yogi, who may appear as a madman or an outcaste to the public while remaining internally pure. It uses metaphors of the Sun, Fire, and Wind to explain how an enlightened being remains untainted by the material world or social taboos.</summary>
<keywords>Kula Yogi, non-attachment, purity and pollution, Kaula Knowledge, Tantric metaphors, Aghora conduct, spiritual freedom</keywords>

# In the Kularnava Tantra
<page-num>146</page-num>

->Just as wherever an elephant walks, that becomes a path;<-
->so too, O Kuleshvari, wherever a Kula Yogi treads, that is the path. || 81 ||<-
<note>original: "yatra yatragajo yāti tatra mārgo yathā bhavet | kulayogī cared yatra sa sa mārgaḥ kuleśvari"</note>
<note><term>Kuleshvari</term> refers to the "Lady of the Kula," the Goddess to whom this teaching is addressed. This verse suggests that a master Yogi does not need to follow established social or religious roads; their very presence creates a legitimate spiritual way.</note>

->Who is able to make a winding river straight or to arrest its flood?<-
->Similarly, who is capable of deterring one who roams in peace, sporting as they will? || 82 ||<-
<note>original: "nadīṃ vakrāmr̥juṃ kartuṃ niroddhuṃ tatpravāhakam | svecchāvihāriṇaṃ śāntaṃ ko vā vārayituṃ kṣamaḥ"</note>

->Just as one fortified by the power of sacred sounds is not bitten by the snakes they play with,<-
->so the man of wisdom is not harmed by the "snakes" of the senses even while playing with them. || 83 ||<-
<note>original: "yadvanmantrabalopetaḥ krīḍanīyairna daṃśyate | tadvanna daṃśyate jñānī krīḍannindriyapannagaiḥ"</note>
<note>In Indian tradition, a snake charmer uses <term>Mantras</term> (sacred chants) to protect themselves. Here, the senses (sight, taste, etc.) are compared to dangerous serpents that "bite" ordinary people with desire, but the wise man (<term>Jnani</term>) interacts with the world without being poisoned by attachment.</note>

->Those who have turned away from misery, are contented, free from the "pairs of opposites," devoid of jealousy,<-
->devoted to the wisdom of the Kula, and are peaceful—they are Your devotees and are known as the Kaulikas. || 84 ||<-
<note>The <term>pairs of opposites</term> (dvandva) refer to dualities like heat and cold, pleasure and pain, or praise and blame that usually disturb the human mind.</note>

### Characteristics of a Superior Kulika :

->Without arrogance, anger, hypocrisy, longing, or ego; speakers of truth;<-
->the masters of the Kula are not fickle, for they are not enslaved by their senses. || 85 ||<-
<note>original: "amadakrodhadambhāśāhaṅkārāḥ satyavādinaḥ | kaulikendrā hyacapalā ye nendriyavaśānugāḥ"</note>

->When the Kula is being praised, those whose hair stands on end, whose voices falter with emotion,<-
->and whose tears of joy fall, O Goddess—they are declared the best of the Kaulikas. || 86 ||<-
<note>The physical signs described—horripilation (hair standing up) and trembling voice—are traditional Indian markers of intense spiritual devotion (<term>bhakti</term>).</note>

->The Kula-dharma, revealed by the Lord Shiva, is superior to all other religions in the world;<-
->those who possess this firm conviction are declared the best of the Kaulikas. || 87 ||<-
<note><term>Kula-dharma</term> refers to the specific "law" or "way of life" belonging to the Kula tradition, which often integrates worldly enjoyment with spiritual liberation.</note>

->He who knows the essential truth of the Kula, who is an expert in the Kula scriptures,<-
->and is devoted to Kula worship—he indeed is a Kaulika, and no other, my dear. || 88 ||<-
<note>original: "yo bhavet kulatattvajñaḥ kulaśāstraviśāradaḥ | kulārcanarataḥ sa syāt kauliko nāparaḥ priye"</note>

<summary>This page defines the "Kaulika" (a practitioner of the Kula path) not by outward status, but by internal qualities such as emotional devotion, self-control, and the ability to interact with the world's temptations without being harmed. It emphasizes that the Yogi is a law unto themselves, creating their own path much like an elephant in the wild.</summary>
<keywords>Kula-dharma, Kaulika, Yogi, Shiva, Kuleshvari, senses, devotion, spiritual mastery</keywords>

### Ninth Exultation
<page-num>147</page-num>

->He who is filled with joy upon seeing devotees of the Kula,<-
->those who know the Kula, and those who keep its traditions and vows,<-
->that Kaulika is dear to Me. || 59 ||<-
<note>original: "kulabhaktān kulajñānān kulācārakulavratān | prīto bhavati yo dr̥ṣṭvā kaulikaḥ sa ca me priyaḥ"</note>
<note>A <term>Kaulika</term> is a practitioner of the <term>Kula</term> tradition, a path that emphasizes the non-dual nature of reality and the presence of the Divine in all things.</note>

->Through initiation, one becomes a Kaulika—a knower of the three Principles,<-
->the Holy Feet, and the hidden meaning of the Root Mantra,<-
->devoted to the Deity and the Guru. || 60 ||<-
<note>original: "tattvatrayaśrīcaraṇamūlamantrārthatattvavit | devatāgurubhaktaśca kaulikaḥ syācca dīkṣayā"</note>
<note>The <term>Three Principles</term> (Tattvas) typically refer to the Self, Knowledge, and the Divine (Shiva). The <term>Root Mantra</term> (Mula Mantra) is the primary sacred chant given by a teacher during initiation.</note>

->O My Beloved! The sight of a Teacher of the Kula-dharma is rare in this world.<-
->He is found only through the happy ripening of previous merits, and not otherwise. || 61 ||<-
<note>original: "durlabhaṃ sarvalokeṣu kulācāryasya darśanam | supākenaiva puṇyānāṃ labhyate nānyathā priye"</note>

->Whether remembered, praised, seen, bowed to, or even spoken with,<-
->even an "outcaste" who is firmly established in the Kula-dharma<-
->spontaneously purifies others. || 62 ||<-
<note>original: "saṃsmr̥taḥ kīrtito dr̥ṣṭo vandino bhāṣito'pi vā | punāti kuladharmmiṣṭhāṃścāṇḍālo'pi yadrcchayā"</note>
<note>A <term>Chandala</term> traditionally refers to someone outside the social caste system, often considered "untouchable" in historical social hierarchies. Here, the text subverts this by stating that spiritual mastery in the Kula path overrides all social status; such a person becomes a source of purity regardless of their birth.</note>

**The Glory of a Kaulika:**

->Whether he is all-knowing or a fool, high-born or low-born,<-
->wherever there is a knower of the Kula, O Goddess,<-
->there I am, along with You. || 63 ||<-
<note>original: "sarvajño vāpi mūrkho vāpyuttamo vā'dhamo'pi vā | yatra devi kulajñānī tatrāhañca tvayā saha"</note>

->I do not dwell on Mount Kailasa, nor on Meru, nor on Mandara;<-
->I dwell, O Noble One, where the knowers of the Kula stay. || 64 ||<-
<note>original: "nāhaṃ vasāmi kailāse na merau na ca mandare | kulajñā yatra tiṣṭhanti tatra tiṣṭhāmi bhāvini"</note>
<note>Kailasa, Meru, and Mandara are sacred mountains in Hindu mythology, traditionally thought of as the homes of the gods. Shiva is saying that He is more present in the living practitioner than in geographical holy sites.</note>

->One should travel even a great distance to where the people of the Lord are.<-
->They must be sought out with effort, for I am truly present there. || 65 ||<-
<note>original: "sudūramapi gantavyaṃ yatra māheśvaro janaḥ | draṣṭavyaśca prayatnena tatra sannihito hyaham"</note>

->The Teacher of the Kula must be sought out even if he is very far away,<-
->but a "beast" should not be seen, O Beloved, even if he is standing nearby. || 66 ||<-
<note>original: "atidūrasthito vāpi draṣṭavyaḥ kuladeśikaḥ | samīpe varttamāno'pi na draṣṭavyaḥ paśuḥ priye"</note>
<note>The term <term>Pashu</term> (literally "beast" or "tethered one") refers to an uninitiated person who is still bound by social conventions, doubts, and worldly attachments, lacking the spiritual insight of the Kula path.</note>

<summary>This page emphasizes that the Divine (Shiva) resides within the community of Kula practitioners rather than in distant mountains or social hierarchies. It highlights the supreme importance of the Kula Guru and the company of fellow initiates over uninitiated "beasts."</summary>
<keywords>Kaulika, Kula-dharma, Shiva, Devi, Initiation, Guru, Chandala, Pashu, Tattva, Kailasa</keywords>

# Kularnava Tantra
<page-num>148</page-num>

->The land where a Knower of the Kula <note>original: "kulajñānī"</note> lives becomes filled with merit.<-
->Through the mere sight of him and through his worship, twenty-one generations of his family are liberated. || 67 ||<-
<note>The phrase "thrice seven" (tri-sapta) refers to the traditional Indian concept of liberating seven generations of ancestors, the current generation, and seven generations of descendants.</note>

->Upon seeing a Knower of Kula-wisdom <note>original: "kulajñāninam"</note> residing in their lineage,<-
->the ancestors rejoice, saying: "We shall surely reach the highest state." || 68 ||<-

->The ancestors take heart, just as farmers do when seeing a heavy rain,<-
->hoping that in their family line—whether as a son or a grandson—a practitioner of the Kula path <note>original: "kaulika"</note> might be born. || 69 ||<-

->That person is truly blessed in this world and freed from all sin,<-
->whom the Masters of the Kula approach with joy, O Beloved. || 100 ||<-
<note>The text jumps from verse 69 to verse 100, a common occurrence in manuscript transcriptions where sections may be grouped by theme rather than strict numerical sequence.</note>

->When a Great Lord of the Kaulikas arrives at the home of another practitioner,<-
->the perfected spirits, both male and female <note>original: "yoginyaḥ" and "yogibhiḥ"</note>, gather there with great joy, O Goddess. || 101 ||<-
<note>A <term>Yogini</term> is a female practitioner or a semi-divine female spirit who embodies the creative and transformative power of the Goddess.</note>

->Entering into the Great Lord of Kula-Yoga, the very ancestors themselves receive honor;<-
->therefore, one should worship those dedicated to Kula-knowledge with great devotion. || 102 ||<-
<note>This suggests that the practitioner becomes a living vessel for the divine and for the lineage's spirits.</note>

->**The Fruit of Worshipping a Practitioner of the Kula Path:**<-

->O Goddess, those who worship You but fail to honor Your devotees<-
->are sinners; they do not qualify to receive Your Grace. || 103 ||<-

->O Lotus-eyed One! When offerings are placed before You, You accept them with Your sight alone,<-
->while I, the Lord, taste their essence through the tongue of the devotee. || 104 ||<-
<note>In this tantric dialogue, the God (Shiva/Bhairava) explains that while the Goddess (Shakti) accepts the spiritual essence of an offering through her gaze, he physically experiences the offering through the senses of the living devotee.</note>

<summary>This page describes the spiritual rewards of honoring Kula practitioners, explaining that their presence sanctifies the land and liberates generations of ancestors. It concludes by emphasizing that the Divine experiences the world and accepts offerings specifically through the person of the dedicated devotee.</summary>

<keywords>liberation of ancestors, Kula-Jnani, Kaulika, sacred lineage, offerings, Divine Grace, Yoginis, worship of devotees</keywords>

# Ninth Exultation
<page-num>146</page-num>

->O Goddess <note>original: "devi"</note>, by worshipping your devotees, I am worshipped; there is no doubt of this.<-
->Therefore, he who wishes to please me should worship your devotees alone. || 105 ||<-

->What is done for those dedicated to the Kula path <note>original: "kulaniṣṭhānāṃ"</note> is truly done for the gods.<-
->All the gods <note>original: "surāḥ"</note> are lovers of the Kula tradition; therefore, one should worship the <term>Kaulika</term> <note>A practitioner of the Kula path.</note>. || 106 ||<-

->O Pārvati! I am not so pleased by worship anywhere else, even when performed with great devotion,<-
->as I am when the masters of the Kula are worshipped properly. || 107 ||<-

->The merit <note>original: "phalam," literally "fruit"</note> that is obtained by worshipping a master of the Kaulika path, O Beloved,<-
->cannot be attained through pilgrimages, <term>Tapas</term> <note>spiritual austerities or "heat-generating" penance</note>, charity, sacrifices, or religious vows. || 108 ||<-

->O Ambike <note>A title for the Mother Goddess</note>! If one disrespects a Knower of the Kula,<-
->whatever one gives, offers, or sacrifices into the fire, and whatever penance, worship, or <term>Japa</term> <note>meditative repetition of a mantra</note> one performs, it all becomes useless. || 109 ||<-

->O Goddess, if one enters the Kula religion <note>original: "kuladharma"</note> and yet remains ignorant of its conduct <note>original: "kulācāra"</note>,<-
->his home is no better than a cemetery, and he is a sinner lower than an outcast <note>original: "śvapaca," literally a "dog-cooker"</note>. || 110 ||<-

->Ignoring those devoted to the Kula to give charity to others is a fruitless act,<-
->and the giver goes to a hellish state. || 111 ||<-
->Such a gift is like water in a broken jar, seeds sown upon a rock,<-
->or a sacred offering poured into cold ashes rather than a living fire. || 112 ||<-

<summary>This page emphasizes that the worship of Kula devotees is equivalent to worshipping the Divine itself, warning that spiritual practices and charity are rendered useless if one disrespects or ignores the masters of the Kula path.</summary>
<keywords>Kula, Kaulika, Kuladharma, devotion, spiritual merit, Pārvati, Ambike, Tapas, Japa, ritual offerings</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the Ninth Exultation of the Kulārṇava Tantra, moving from the general necessity of respecting Kula masters to the specific merits and rituals involved in serving them. It focuses on the transformative power of the "Vīra" (Hero) and the "Kaulikendra" (Lord of the Kaulas) to sanctify both the offerings and the land they inhabit.</meta>

# In the Kulārṇava Tantra
<page-num>150</page-num>

->Whatever little someone may give to a Kula-Yogī <note>A practitioner who has mastered the "Kula" or "family" path of Tantra.</note> according to their capacity,<-
->especially on significant lunar dates <note>original: "viśeṣatithiṣu"</note> and with love, the merit of that cannot be described. || 113 ||<-

*Procedure for offering to a Kula-Yogī:*

Whatever is given according to one's capacity to the Kula-Yogīs with love on special days is superbly fruitful.

->O Goddess <note>original: "devi"</note>! When those wise in the Kula are personally invited on an auspicious day,<-
->and worshipped with the mindset that they are the Deity <note>original: "devatā-buddhyā"</note>, using perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings,<-
->satisfying them with the five sacred mudrās <note>original: "pañcamudrābhiḥ"; in this context, the "Five Ms" or transformative substances of the Tantric feast</note> and with true devotion—<-
->when they are satisfied, I am satisfied, and all the gods are satisfied. || 114–115 ||<-

->O Ruler of the Gods <note>original: "deveśi"</note>! Whoever offers a sister, a daughter, or a wife to a Kula-Yogī<-
->who is intoxicated by the divine nectar <note>original: "madhumattāya"; refers both to ritual wine and the resulting state of spiritual bliss</note>, his merit cannot be measured. || 116 ||<-

->The nectar <note>original: "madhu"</note> offered in the Circle of Heroes <note>original: "vīracakre," a ritual gathering of advanced practitioners</note>, though not buried in the ground and grown without labor,<-
->becomes the spiritual provision for the journey to the world beyond. || 117 ||<-

->That which is associated with sinful conduct and rejected by the whole world<-
->becomes a sacred Kula-substance <note>original: "kula-dravyam"</note> when it is offered to the great masters of the Kula-Yogīs. || 118 ||<-

->In whatever land a Hero <note>original: "vīraḥ," a practitioner who has overcome human limitations</note> resides who is devoted to Kula worship, O Beloved,<-
->that land itself becomes purified; how much more so those who dwell within that city! || 119 ||<-

->When a Lord of the Kaulas <note>original: "kaulikendre," a supreme practitioner of the path</note> eats but once, the merit becomes ten million times greater;<-
->how much more so when many of them have eaten—that merit simply cannot be counted. || 120 ||<-

<summary>This page details the immense spiritual merit gained by inviting, worshipping, and providing offerings to Kula practitioners, explaining that their presence and satisfaction can purify entire regions and transform worldly substances into sacred ones.</summary>
<keywords>Kula-Yogi, Vira Chakra, Madhu, Kula-dravya, Kaulikendra, merit, Tantric worship, purification</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the Ninth Exultation of the Kulārṇava Tantra. While the previous page focused on the merit gained from serving Kula-Yogīs and making ritual offerings, this section shifts toward the philosophical necessity of performing one's duties (Karma) and maintaining the Kula-tradition (Kuladharma) even while seeking liberation.</meta>

<page-num>151</page-num>
<header>Ninth Exultation, 151</header>

->Therefore, with all effort, in all conditions, and at all times,<-
->one should be devoted to the Kula-tradition <note>original: "kuladharma"</note> and worship the one who knows the Kula. || 121 ||<-

> Therefore, with all efforts, in all conditions, always be devoted to the <term>Kuladharma</term> <note>The specific religious and social duties belonging to the "Kula" or Tantric family tradition.</note> and worship those who are knowers of Kula.

->Whether one is a knower or ignorant, as long as the body is maintained,<-
->the conduct of one's class and stage of life <note>original: "varṇāśramācāra"</note> must be performed for the release from action. || 122 ||<-
->When ignorance is uprooted by action, one attains the state of Shiva through knowledge.<-
->In Shiva, liberation occurs through that very knowledge; therefore, one should perform action. || 123 ||<-

### *Following the practices of the Varṇāśrama*
### *and the aim of Karma:*

> Whether you are learned or not-learned, as long as you hold the body, the way laid down for your station in life <term>Varṇāśrama</term> <note>The traditional Indian system of four social classes (Varnas) and four stages of life (Ashramas).</note> shall be worked out for release from <term>Karma</term> <note>The cycle of cause and effect generated by actions.</note>. When ignorance is thus destroyed by prescribed action, you attain through knowledge to the state of <term>Śiva</term> <note>The Ultimate Reality or Pure Consciousness in this tradition.</note> and in Śiva you get the <term>Mukti</term> <note>Final liberation or release from the cycle of rebirth.</note>. Therefore, resort to the prescribed actions.

->One should perform blameless actions or carry out daily rituals.<-
->Released from action and desiring happiness, one devoted to action attains bliss. || 124 ||<-

> Do actions which are free from blemishes; do works that are enjoined for daily performances. Released by such actions, aspiring for happiness, devoted to work, live happily.

->It is not possible for a living being to abandon all actions.<-
->He who abandons the fruit of action is called a true renouncer. || 125 ||<-

### *Eligibility for Karma-Yoga:*

> It is not possible for one who bears the body to give up all the activities. Therefore, who abandons the fruit of actions <note>original: "karmaphalam"</note> he is called a true recluse <note>This echoes the teaching of the Bhagavad Gita, where true renunciation is defined as giving up the attachment to results rather than the actions themselves.</note>.

->One should reflect: "The senses engage in their own functions."<-
->He who acts after casting aside the sense of "I" <note>original: "ahambhāvam"</note> is not tainted. || 126 ||<-

> Bodily organs engage themselves in their functions; understanding this leave aside the ego-feeling. Actions so done do not taint.

->Actions performed after the attainment of knowledge<-
->do not touch the knower of Truth <note>original: "tattvajña"</note>, just as water does not stick to a lotus leaf. || 127 ||<-

> Actions done after attainment of Knowledge do not touch the performer of actions as water keeps away from the leaves of a lotus <note>A classic metaphor in Indian philosophy: just as a lotus leaf stays dry even while floating in water, the enlightened soul remains untainted by the world.</note>.

<summary>This page explains that as long as a person possesses a physical body, they must perform their social and religious duties (Karma) with detachment to reach liberation. It emphasizes that true renunciation is the abandonment of the "ego-feeling" and the fruits of one's labor, rather than the abandonment of action itself.</summary>
<keywords>Kuladharma, Varnashrama, Karma-Yoga, Shiva, Mukti, Tattvajña, detachment, lotus leaf analogy</keywords>

### For one settled in that Knowledge, actions—whether meritorious or sinful—dwindle away. They do not cling, even those performed again. || 128 ||

### O My Beloved! A natural joy <term>Sahajānanda</term> <note>The innate, spontaneous bliss that arises naturally from realizing one's true nature without external effort.</note> is attained by one engrossed in the pursuit of the Knowledge of Truth. Such a wise person leaves behind all mental intentions and all ritual actions. || 129 ||

### *Renouncing actions without being spiritually ready is forbidden:*
### The fools who discard the path of ritual action <term>Karmakāṇḍa</term> <note>The portion of the Vedas or scriptures dealing with ceremonial acts and sacrificial rites.</note> without purpose are but imposters who think themselves wise; they go to hell, My Dear. || 130 ||

### *Only a Knower of the Absolute and the Truth is free from the cycle of action:*
### Just as a tree indifferently drops its blossoms once it has attained the fruit, so the practitioner <term>Yogi</term> <note>One who seeks union with the divine through disciplined practice.</note> should let go of the burden of ritual works upon reaching the Truth. || 131 ||

### For those in whose heart the Absolute <term>Brahman</term> <note>The ultimate, infinite reality or world-soul in Hindu philosophy.</note> resides, they are not bound by the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices <term>Aśvamedha</term> <note>An ancient and highly prestigious Vedic ritual performed by kings to assert their sovereignty.</note>, nor are they tainted by the sin of ten thousand killings of a priest <note>original: "brahmahatyā"; traditionally considered one of the gravest sins.</note>. || 132 ||

### Whatever actions exist on this earth for the sake of the tongue or the reproductive organs—what business does one who has renounced the cravings of the tongue and the organs have with such actions? || 133 ||

### Thus I have described to you briefly some of the characteristics of Yoga and the masters of Yoga. O Mistress of the Kula <term>Kuleśāni</term> <note>An epithet for the Goddess as the sovereign of the Tantric "Kula" or spiritual family.</note>! What else do you wish to hear? || 134 ||

->Thus, in the Illustrious <term>Kulārṇava</term> <note>The "Ocean of the Kula Tradition," a foundational text of the Kaula school of Tantra.</note>,<-
->the door to liberation and final peace, the great mystery,<-
->the supreme among all scriptures, in the section of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses,<-
->in the fifth division, in the Tantra of the Upper Tradition <note>original: "ūrdhvāmnāya"</note>,<-
->ends the Ninth Exultation <note>original: "ullāsa"</note>,<-
->named the Discourse on the Establishment of Yoga.<-

<summary>This page concludes the discourse on Yoga, explaining that while ritual duties are necessary for the uninitiated, the true Knower of Brahman transcends the moral and ritual consequences of all actions. The Ninth Exultation ends by defining the liberated state as one of natural bliss (Sahajananda) where external rites are naturally shed like blossoms from a fruiting tree.</summary>

# Tenth Exultation

<image-desc>ornamental divider with a central floral motif and horizontal scrolls</image-desc>

->The Auspicious Goddess said:<-

> O Lord of the spiritual lineage <term>Kuleśa</term> <note>original: "Kuleśa"; referring to Shiva as the head of the Kula, or the divine family/tradition.</note>! I desire to hear about the worship performed on special days. O Supreme Lord <term>Parameśvara</term>, tell me also of the fruits gained from such worship. || 1 ||

->The Lord said:<-

> Listen, O Goddess, and I shall explain what you have asked. By the mere hearing of this, one is liberated from all sins. || 2 ||

> Daily worship is best; worship on festival days <term>Parva</term> <note>Significant days in the lunar calendar, such as the full or new moon.</note> is middling; and monthly worship is the lowest, O Goddess. Beyond a month without worship, one becomes a bound soul <term>Paśu</term> <note>original: "Paśu"; literally meaning "beast" or "cattle," it refers to a person bound by worldly fetters and ignorance who has lost their spiritual momentum.</note>. || 3 ||

### *Three kinds of Worship:*
Daily worship is best; worship on special occasions is middle and monthly worship is lowest. If a practitioner <term>Sādhaka</term> <note>One who follows a "Sadhana" or disciplined spiritual practice.</note> spends more than a month without worship he becomes a bound soul.

> If a bound soul <term>Paśu</term> desires to re-enter the practice after a lapse of more than a month <note>original: "māsādūrdhvaṃ"</note>, performing worship with the prescribed substances beginning with the letter "M," he must be initiated again. || 4 ||

> Wine, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union—these are the Five "M"s <term>Makāras</term>, O Goddess, which bring delight to the deity. || 5 ||

<note>The "Five Ms" (Madya, Māṃsa, Matsya, Mudrā, and Maithuna) are ritual elements in certain Tantric traditions used to transform worldly desires into spiritual liberation.</note>

> O Sovereign Goddess, the wise should resort to these five substances beginning with "M" <note>original: "mādipañcakam"</note> for the pleasure of the deity according to the sacred rules. If one resorts to them out of mere personal craving, he is a sinner. || 6 ||

### *Resorting to the Five M's out of personal desire is sin:*
One should resort to the Five M's in the prescribed manner for the pleasure of the Deity. If one resorts to them out of personal desire he commits a sin.

<summary>This page introduces the Tenth Exultation, detailing the hierarchy of worship frequency and introducing the Five Makāras (Five M's) as ritual tools, emphasizing that they must be used for divine pleasure rather than personal indulgence.</summary>
<keywords>Kulesa, Paramesvara, Pasu, Five Makaras, worship hierarchy, initiation, ritual purity, Tantric practice</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous discussion on the frequency of ritual (daily, festival, or monthly), Shiva continues to explain to the Goddess the specific lunar days and life events that demand special worship. <page-num>154</page-num>

# In the Kularnava Tantra

> The eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the dark fortnight, the full-moon day, and the days when the sun enters a new zodiac sign <term>Saṃkrānti</term> <note>original: "saṃkrānti"; these solar transitions are considered highly auspicious moments for spiritual alignment.</note>—these are the five sacred festival days. || 7 ||

### *Occasions for Worship:*

The 8th, 14th, and 15th days of the dark moon, the full-moon day, and the solar transitions <term>Saṃkrāntīs</term> are the five auspicious occasions for worship.

> When the birthday of the Guru arrives, or the birthday of the Grand-Guru <note>The teacher's teacher.</note> or the Great-Grand-Guru, or the birthdays of the human lineage of masters <term>Mānavaugha</term> <note>original: "mānavaugha"; the succession of human teachers who have preserved the tradition over generations.</note>, as well as on one's own birthday. || 8 ||

The birthdays of the Guru, the Supreme Guru <term>Parama Guru</term>, the Beyond-Supreme Guru <term>Parāpara Guru</term>, the human lineage <term>Mānavaugha</term>, and one's own birthday are auspicious days for worship.

> On the acquisition of wealth or upon a successful gain; during celebrations of austerities <term>Tapas</term>, initiation <term>Dīkṣā</term>, and sacred vows <term>Vrata</term>; when visiting a sacred power center <term>Pīṭha</term>, or the "Hero’s Seat" <term>Vīrapīṭha</term> <note>A specialized ritual location reserved for advanced practitioners or "heroes" (vīras) of the tantric path.</note>; upon meeting with one's own kin; || 9 ||
> On the arrival of a spiritual guide <term>Deśika</term>, and upon seeing a holy pilgrimage site or a deity—on these and other such special days, O Goddess of the Gods <term>Deveśi</term>, one should perform worship. || 10 ||

On the receipt of property or gain, in celebrations of spiritual discipline, initiation, and other observances, when visiting a sacred site <term>Pīṭha</term> or a <term>Vīrapīṭha</term>, on meeting dear relations, on the arrival of a teacher <term>Deśika</term>, or on seeing a sacred place or deity—these are special occasions when, O Goddess, one should offer worship.

> One should perform worship according to one's financial means, one’s faith, the materials <term>Dravya</term> <note>original: "dravya"; the physical items used in ritual, such as incense, flowers, or offerings.</note> available, and as is appropriate for the time and place. || 11 ||

On such occasions, one should worship according to their monetary resources, their faith, the quality of materials available, and the propriety of the specific time and location.

> One should have the worship of the sacred circle <term>Cakra</term> performed by an expert master <term>Ācārya</term> according to the rules; or, O Goddess, one may perform the worship oneself, beginning with the worship of the sacred drop <term>Bindu</term> <note>original: "bindu-pūjā"; this refers to the worship of the central point of a mandala or the consecration of ritual fluids.</note>. || 12 ||
> Such a person reaches the world of Truth, never to return to the cycle of rebirth. But a practitioner of the Kula path <term>Kaulika</term> who, out of delusion, fails to perform this worship, shall incur the curse of the deities. || 13 ||

### *Cakra Worship by the Practitioner or Teacher:*

The worship of the sacred circle <term>Cakra</term> should be performed in the prescribed manner by the Master <term>Ācārya</term>; alternatively, one focused on the "point-worship" <term>Bindu-worship</term> may perform it themselves. One who does so attains a divine state and is freed from the cycle of reincarnation. A member of this tradition <term>Kaulika</term> who neglects this worship through ignorance or confusion will be cursed by the gods.

<summary>This page lists the specific lunar, solar, and personal milestones—such as birthdays of the Guru lineage and the acquisition of wealth—that require special ritual worship. It emphasizes that worship must be scaled to one's means and warns that neglecting these duties leads to spiritual stagnation and divine displeasure.</summary>

# Tenth Chapter

> Whether every month, every three months, every six months, or even once a year, one should worship the Holy Guru with devotion. If the Guru is not available, one should worship his wife, sons, and family. || 14 ||
>
> If these are also unavailable, one should satisfy a knower of the tradition <term>Kulajña</term> <note>original: "kulajña"; one who understands the secrets and practices of the Kula path.</note>, a fellow disciple, or another practitioner <term>Yogi</term> with the sacred substances <term>Kuladravyas</term>, after first performing the traditional Kula-worship. || 15 ||

### *Worship of the Yoginīs for the pacification of diseases, etc.:*

> For the pacification of diseases, during calamities, in times of moral failings, when kept in bad company, or when faced with ill omens, one should worship the assembly of Yoginis <note>original: "yoginīvṛnda"; a group of female practitioners or semi-divine beings who embody the energy of the Goddess.</note>, O Goddess, to quiet those faults. || 16 ||

### *Characteristics of the Living Sacred Circle:*

> O Queen of the Kula, wherever there is a Master of the tradition <term>Kulācārya</term> who knows the truth of the sacred lineages <term>Āmnāyas</term>, along with three, four, or five male practitioners <term>Kaulikas</term> and female powers <term>Shaktis</term>, O Beloved— || 17 ||
>
> There, O Goddess, one should worship them either individually or in pairs <note>original: "mithunākārato"; representing the union of masculine and feminine principles.</note>. They should be beautifully adorned with perfumes, flowers, and sacred grains <term>Akṣata</term> <note>original: "akṣata"; literally "unbroken," these are usually whole grains of rice used in ritual.</note>, O Queen of the Gods, and satisfied with meat and other foods that possess the six flavors. || 18 ||
>
> If they dwell there together in a state of "Great Joy" <term>Prauḍhollāsa</term> <note>original: "prauḍhollāsa"; a high state of ritual intoxication or spiritual exultation described in Tantric texts.</note>, then that assembly is called a Sacred Circle <term>Śrī Cakra</term> <note>original: "śrīcakra"; while often a geometric diagram, here the term refers to the living "circle" of practitioners.</note>, and it is also known as a Gathering <term>Vṛnda</term>. || 19 ||

### *Worship of Nine Virgins and its fruits:*

> In the month of Ashvina <note>original: "āśvina"; the seventh month of the lunar calendar, usually occurring in September–October, coinciding with the great festival of the Goddess.</note>, one should perform the worship of nine young virgins <term>Kumārīs</term>. The practitioner <term>Sādhaka</term>, with a pure mind, should invite them with devotion in the morning. || 20 ||

It also introduces the ritual worship of nine young girls during the autumnal season.</summary>

->On the first day of the fortnight, after bathing a beautiful one-year-old girl who possesses auspicious physical marks,<-
->the practitioner <term>Sadhaka</term> <note>original: "mantrī"; one who is initiated into the use of sacred sounds.</note>, having purified his soul, should perform the ritual worship in due order, O Goddess. || 21 ||<-

->Once she has been anointed with oils and cleansed, he should bring her into the house of worship.<-
->Seating the girl in the presence of the Deity, he should worship her— || 22 ||<-
->with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps of the tradition <term>Kula-dipakas</term>;<-
->with various foods, snacks, and drinks, as well as milk, clarified butter <term>Ghee</term>, honey, and meat;<-
->and with fruits such as bananas and coconuts, he should ensure she is fully satisfied. || 23 ||<-

->Accompanied by his female partner <term>Shakti</term>, O Goddess, and filled with the exuberant joy of the ritual's peak <term>Praudhantollasa</term> <note>original: "prauḍhāntollāsa"; a technical term for the high state of spiritual intoxication or "exultation" reached during the later stages of a ritual.</note>,<-
->he should recite his sacred prayer <term>Mantra</term> according to his capacity, or increasing the count by one each time. || 24 ||<-
->While beholding the adorned girl, he should meditate upon his own Chosen Deity <term>Ista Devata</term>.<-
->Then, viewing the girl with the awareness that she is the Deity herself, he should bow to her and bid her farewell. || 25 ||<-

->On the second day, he should worship a two-year-old girl as well as the one-year-old girl.<-
->In this manner, on each lunar day <term>Tithi</term>, he should worship the young girls, including those worshipped on the preceding days. || 26 ||<-

->On the ninth day, he should worship girls ranging from one year old up to nine years of age.<-
->The nine names of these girls are declared to be:<-
->The Child <term>Bala</term>, the Pure One <term>Shuddha</term>, the Playful One <term>Lalita</term>, the Garlanded One <term>Malini</term>, and the Earth-Bearer <term>Vasundhara</term>;<-
->the Goddess of Wisdom <term>Sarasvati</term>, the Goddess of Fortune <term>Rama</term>, the Golden One <term>Gauri</term>, and the Inaccessible One <term>Durga</term>. || 27 ||<-

<meta>Continuity: Following the instructions from page 156 regarding the worship of young girls (Kumari Puja) on the first and second days of the lunar fortnight, Lord Shiva now explains the specific sacred sounds (Mantras) to be used for each of the nine girls and the inclusion of young boys representing Batuka and Ganesha in the ritual.</meta>

### Tenth Chapter: 157

->With the three-syllable 'Om' <note>The sacred syllable ॐ</note> at the beginning and 'Salutation' at the end, followed by the word for Deity,<-
->using the names in the fourth case <term>Dative case</term> <note>original: "caturthyantaih"; the grammatical form used to indicate "to" or "for" someone.</note>, one should worship them individually. || 28 ||<-

The sacred sounds <term>Mantras</term> for the worship of these nine girls should be formed by putting three *Aums* <note>The vowel sounds that make up the syllable Om</note> in the beginning, "Salutations" <note>original: "Namah"</note> at the end and in-between the name of the respective Goddess <term>Devi</term> and the word "Deity" <term>Devata</term> in the dative forms. Thus the nine Mantras for the nine Goddesses would be as follows:

1. **Om Om Om** to the Child Goddess <note>original: "Bālāyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
2. **Om Om Om** to the Pure Goddess <note>original: "Śuddhāyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
3. **Om Om Om** to the Playful Goddess <note>original: "Lalitāyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
4. **Om Om Om** to the Flower-Garlanded Goddess <note>original: "Mālinyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
5. **Om Om Om** to the Earth-Bearing Goddess <note>original: "Vasundharāyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
6. **Om Om Om** to the Goddess of Speech <note>original: "Sarasvatyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
7. **Om Om Om** to the Goddess of Fortune <note>original: "Ramāyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
8. **Om Om Om** to the Fair Goddess <note>original: "Gauryai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.
9. **Om Om Om** to the Impassable Goddess <note>original: "Durgāyai"</note> the Deity, Salutations.

The Nine should be worshipped separately with their respective Mantras.

->Also worship a boy <term>Batuka</term> <note>A young male initiate or a form of Bhairava.</note> of five years and a Lord of Hosts <term>Ganeshvara</term> of nine years,<-
->with fragrance, flowers, clothing, and ornaments, according to the extent of one's wealth. || 29 ||<-

Along with these girls, a five-year-old boy in the form of *Batuka* and another nine-year-old in the form of the elephant-headed Lord <term>Ganeshvara</term> should also be worshipped properly according to one's financial capacity, with fragrance, flowers and clothings.

->Viewing all these as the Divine, one should satisfy them with various offerings;<-
->to ensure the success of one's own goals, one must avoid being stingy with wealth. || 30 ||<-

Considering all these children as living Deities and without being thrifty, the practitioner <term>Sadhaka</term> should, for the fulfillment of his own desires, worship and satisfy them with various materials.

->During the Nine Nights <term>Navaratra</term> <note>A major festival dedicated to the Divine Mother.</note>, one should perform recitation <term>Japa</term>, increasing the number by one each day;<-
->O Goddess, one should then offer the entire merit of the Nine Nights' worship to the Great Goddess. || 31 ||<-

Thus in the *Navaratra* (the nine sacred days for the worship of the Goddess falling in the bright fortnight of the first and the seventh months of the Hindu Calendar), one should perform meditative recitation and increase the number of girls worshipped by one each day. Then, O Devi, offer the entire fruit of the *Navaratra* worship back to the Goddess.

->After offering betel leaves and a ritual gift <term>Dakshina</term>, one should bid farewell to those girls.<-
->Whoever performs this worship of the nine Virgins every year— || 32 ||<-
->that virtuous soul shall obtain the love of the Deity,<-
->and having fulfilled his heart's desire, shall dwell in Your presence. || 33 ||<-

Offering betel-leaves and ritual gifts, one should bid farewell to the young girls. One who performs this worship of nine Virgins every year, that virtuous practitioner obtains the blessing of the Deity and, fulfilling his heart's desire, attains a state of eternal residence in Your divine proximity.
