> Through the lack of <term>Saṁskāras</term> <note>Purificatory rites or sacraments that refine the soul.</note>, the violation of the Guru’s instructions, and the abandonment of proper conduct, O Goddess, a practitioner of the <term>Kula</term> path <note>original: "Kaulika"</note> falls from grace. || 101 ||

The lack of sacred sacraments, disregarding what the teacher has spoken, and the disgrace of traditional practices lead to the spiritual downfall of a seeker.

> The omission of daily and occasional rituals, ritual substances <note>original: "Dravyas"</note>, sacred chants <note>original: "Mantra"</note>, and meditative diagrams <note>original: "Yantra"</note>; the company of unfit "animals" <note>original: "Paśus"; a term for the uninitiated who live by instinct rather than spiritual discipline</note>; the intermixing of distinct chants; || 102 ||
> And the disclosure of secrets, whether done publicly or in private, whether done knowingly or in ignorance—these, My Beloved, are the faults; the weight of the sin depends on the gravity of the offense. || 103 ||

### *Penance for the guilty seeker:*
<note>original: "Sādhaka"</note>

> Having carefully considered the location, the time, the age, and the financial capacity of the person, the Guru should prescribes the proper penance <note>original: "Prāyaścitta"</note> for the purification of all sins. || 104 ||

The teacher acts as a spiritual physician, tailoring the "medicine" of penance to the specific circumstances of the student to ensure they are truly cleansed.

> The disciple must perform the penance exactly as commanded by the Guru. Alternatively, the meditative repetition <note>original: "Japa"</note> of the Guru’s name is traditionally held to be a penance for all sins. || 105 ||

The bond between teacher and student is so sacred that simply focusing on the teacher's name can serve as a powerful tool for spiritual realignment.

> Just as gold <note>original: "Jāmbūnada"</note> is cleansed of its impurities by fire, so should the stain of improper conduct be burned away in the fire of penance. || 106 ||

> Why say more on this? Listen to the secret, O <term>Pārvati</term> <note>The Goddess to whom the Shiva is speaking.</note>: for all stages and stations of life <note>original: "Varṇāśrama"</note>, proper conduct alone is what grants the highest destination. || 107 ||

### *Conduct to be instructed thrice by the Guru:*

> O <term>Kuleśvari</term> <note>“Mistress of the Kula”; a title for the Goddess.</note>! The Guru should explain the rules of conduct three times. If the disciple still does not adopt them, then the Guru bears no sin for the student's failure. || 108 ||

The responsibility of the teacher is to provide the map; if the traveler refuses to walk the path after three warnings, the teacher is no longer responsible for the traveler's safety.

It emphasizes that proper conduct (Achara) is the ultimate secret to spiritual success across all walks of life.</summary>

# Chapter Twelve

---

## The Great Goddess said:

->O Lord of the Kula <note>original: "Kulesha"</note>! I wish to hear the characteristics of devotion to the Sacred Sandals <term>Paduka</term> <note>Literally "sandals"; in this context, they represent the spiritual power of the Guru's feet and the lineage of teachers.</note>.<-
->O Lord of the Gods, O Ocean of Compassion, tell me also of the proper conduct <term>Achara</term> <note>The established rules of behavior and ritual practice in the Tantric tradition.</note> associated with them. || 1 ||<-

## The Lord said:

->Listen, O Goddess! I shall tell You what You have asked of Me.<-
->By merely hearing this, devotion springs forth immediately. || 2 ||<-

->Just as the primordial syllables of speech <note>original: "Vagbhava"</note> and the energetic threads <note>original: "Sutra"</note> are contained within the root-center <term>Muladhara</term> <note>The base chakra or energy center at the base of the spine, considered the seat of latent spiritual power.</note>,<-
->so too is all knowledge within the "Ocean of the Kula" <note>original: "Kularnava"</note> established upon the Sacred Sandals. || 3 ||<-

***The Glory of the Sacred Sandals:***

->The remembrance of the glorious Sacred Sandals is superior to<-
->billions upon billions of great acts of charity, billions of great vows, and billions of great fire-sacrifices. || 4 ||<-

->O Goddess! The remembrance of the glorious Sacred Sandals is superior to<-
->the repetition of billions of mantras <term>Japa</term> <note>The meditative practice of repeating a sacred name or syllable.</note>, bathing in billions of holy pilgrimage sites, and the worship of billions of deities. || 5 ||<-

->When remembered, the Sacred Sandals provide protection against<-
->great diseases, great upheavals, great faults, great fears, great calamities, and great sins. || 6 ||<-

<summary>This page marks the beginning of Chapter Twelve, introducing the "Sacred Sandals" (Paduka) as the foundational element of spiritual knowledge and devotion within the Kula tradition. Shiva explains to the Goddess that devotion to the Paduka outweighs the merit of all traditional rituals, charities, and pilgrimages combined.</summary>

<keywords>Paduka, Kulesha, Kularnava, Achara, Muladhara, Mantra-Japa, Devi, Ishvara, Kula, Devotion, Sacred Sandals</keywords>

# From the Kularnava Tantra

The remembrance of the Sacred Sandals <term>Paduka</term> <note>Literally "sandals," these symbolize the spiritual presence and authority of the Guru.</note> protects one from bad conduct, foul speech, evil company, and the improper acceptance of gifts. It likewise guards against wicked habits and a perverted intellect. || 7 ||

For the person who always holds the memory of the glorious Sacred Sandals on the tip of their tongue, everything—studying, remembering, knowing, sacrificing, giving, and worshipping—is perfected. || 8 ||

O Goddess! Whoever repeats the name of the glorious Sacred Sandals even once with devotion is freed from all sins and attains the supreme goal. || 9 ||

Whether one is ritually pure or impure, if they remember the Sacred Sandals with devotion, they effortlessly obtain the four goals of life: righteousness <term>Dharma</term>, worldly prosperity <term>Artha</term>, pleasure <term>Kama</term>, and spiritual liberation <term>Moksha</term>. || 10 ||

***The Identity of the Guru and the Divine Lord:***

In whichever direction the lotus feet of the venerable Master <note>original: "Shrinatha"</note> reside, one should bow in that direction with devotion every day, O Beloved. || 11 ||

There is no sacred chant <term>Mantra</term> higher than the Sacred Sandals; there is no deity higher than the venerable Guru. There is no initiation higher than the Shakta <term>Shakta</term> <note>Relating to the path of Shakti, the Divine Power.</note> initiation, and no spiritual merit greater than the worship of the Kula <term>Kula</term> <note>The spiritual "family" or lineage of the Tantric tradition.</note>. || 12 ||

The root of meditation <term>Dhyana</term> is the form of the Guru; the root of worship <term>Puja</term> is the feet of the Guru; the root of the mantra is the word of the Guru; and the root of liberation is the Guru's grace. || 13 ||

O Queen of the Kula <note>original: "Kulanayike"</note>! All sacred actions in this world are rooted in the Guru. Therefore, for the sake of attaining all spiritual perfections <term>Siddhis</term>, one should serve the Guru constantly with a heart full of devotion. || 14 ||

<summary>This page defines the Guru as the absolute foundation of all spiritual practice, asserting that devotion to the Guru's feet (Paduka) provides protection from sin and is the essential key to achieving liberation and worldly goals.</summary>
<keywords>Guru, Paduka, Kularnava Tantra, liberation, devotion, Shakta, Kula worship, meditation, grace</keywords>

# Twelfth Chapter

->Distress, fear, grief, greed, delusion, and confusion remain only<-
->until one takes refuge in the holy Master, who is full of love for his devotees. || 15 ||<-

*The condemnation of one who lacks devotion to the Master:*

> All fears of distress, grief, greed, delusion, and bewilderment exist only as long as one does not obtain the shelter of the Master <term>Guru</term> <note>The spiritual teacher who leads the seeker from the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge.</note>.

->Souls wander through this world stained by every kind of sorrow<-
->only as long as they lack devotion to a true Master, O Goddess. || 16 ||<-

> O Goddess <note>original: "Deveśī"</note>! All wanderings in this world fraught with grief and impurity last as long as one has no devotion to a holy Master.

->The beautiful sacred chant, which brings the fruit of all spiritual attainments, is purified here;<-
->the great path to the Supreme Truth is rooted in the Master's grace. || 17 ||<-

> The beautiful sacred chant <term>Mantra</term> <note>A sacred sound, syllable, or phrase used in ritual and meditation.</note> loaded with all spiritual attainments <term>Siddhis</term> <note>Supernatural powers or spiritual perfections attained through practice.</note> which purifies and leads to the Supreme Truth is rooted in the Grace of the Master.

->Just as the satisfied and gracious Master bestows the sacred chant,<-
->so too should one strive to please the Master with devotion, wealth, and one’s own life. || 18 ||<-

*The fruit of devotion to the Master:*

> When satisfied and pleased, the Master gives the sacred chant; therefore, one should try to please him with devotion, wealth, and even with his very life.

->When the best of teachers gives his very self to his disciple,<-
->then the disciple becomes liberated, and there is no more rebirth. || 19 ||<-

> Indeed, it is only when a great Master gives his own self to his disciple that the disciple becomes liberated and free from the cycle of rebirth.

->A disciple should worship as long as it takes for the Master to be pleased;<-
->when the Master is pleased, the disciple’s sins are immediately destroyed. || 20 ||<-

> The disciple should worship the Master until he is pleased; for once the Master is pleased, all the sins of the disciple are immediately destroyed.

->Even those desires which followers do not even dare to wish for in their hearts,<-
->the Masters, who love their devotees, fulfill them all. || 21 ||<-

> The rewards which people may not have even dared to hope for in their hearts are all fulfilled by the Grace of a kind Lord.

->The Creator, the Sustainer, the Destroyer, and other gods, sages, and practitioners,<-
->undoubtedly bestow their favor once the Master is satisfied. || 22 ||<-

> When the Master is satisfied, then the Gods—such as the Creator <term>Brahmā</term>, the Sustainer <term>Viṣṇu</term>, and the Destroyer <term>Maheśa</term>—along with sages and practitioners <term>Yogīs</term> <note>Those who practice the discipline of Yoga to achieve union with the Divine.</note>, indubitably bestow their Grace.

<summary>This page describes the Guru as the essential source of liberation, stating that worldly suffering and the cycle of rebirth only cease when one finds refuge in a true teacher. It emphasizes that pleasing the Guru is the highest spiritual task, as his satisfaction naturally brings the blessings of all major deities and fulfills even the disciple's unspoken desires.</summary>

->When the compassionate Master <term>Guru</term> is satisfied with a disciple's devotion and gives his instruction,<-
->that disciple is released from the bonds of action <term>Karma</term> and becomes worthy of both worldly fulfillment and spiritual liberation. || 23 ||<-

<note>original: "bhukti-muktayo". In this tradition, the path aims for both "Bhukti" (enjoyment/fulfillment in the world) and "Mukti" (final liberation from the cycle of rebirth).</note>

->The disciple must act in a way that ensures the Master remains pleased;<-
->O Queen of the Gods <note>original: "Deveśī"</note>, one should do what is pleasing to him through mind, speech, body, and deeds. || 24 ||<-

->If the Master is satisfied, then wherever that disciple may be,<-
->if the Master declares, "You are free," then the disciple surely attains liberation, O Beloved. || 25 ||<-

->Or perhaps, from His own transcendent and unquestionable state, the Lord Himself<-
->takes the form of a Master to release the soul from its animal-like bonds. || 26 ||<-

<note>The text refers to "Paśu-pāśa," the concept that the individual soul is like a tethered animal (Paśu) bound by the ropes (Pāśa) of ignorance and worldly attachment. Only the Master can cut these bonds.</note>

->A scholar of the four Vedas <term>Chaturvedī</term> is not My favorite if he lacks devotion, but a devotee is dear to Me even if he is an outcast.<-
->One should give to such a person and receive from them, for they are as worthy of worship as I am. || 27 ||<-

<note>original: "Shvapacha" (literally 'dog-cooker'), a term used for those considered at the very bottom or outside of the traditional social hierarchy. The text is making a radical statement that spiritual devotion overrides social status.</note>

->A priest <term>Brahmin</term> endowed with the six traditional virtues is not praised if he lacks devotion;<-
->on the other hand, even a foreigner <term>Mleccha</term> without such virtues is called a true disciple if he possesses devotion. || 28 ||<-

<note>The "six qualities" of a Brahmin traditionally include learning, teaching, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts.</note>

->For one who lacks devotion to the Master, their penance, knowledge, lineage, and religious vows<-
->are all in vain; they are merely external ornaments worn to please the eyes of the world. || 29 ||<-

->An outcast whose sins and evil thoughts are burned away by the fire of devotion to the Master<-
->is to be honored by others; however, even a great scholar is nothing if he is an atheist. || 30 ||<-

<summary>This page concludes that the Master's satisfaction is the sole requirement for liberation, asserting that sincere devotion is far more valuable than high caste status, Vedic scholarship, or external religious rituals.</summary>

### Twelfth Chapter

->What need has one for the four goals of life—virtue <term>Dharma</term>, prosperity <term>Artha</term>, and pleasure <term>Kāma</term>? For the one whose devotion to the Holy Master is forever steady, O Goddess, even liberation <term>Mokṣa</term> is held within the palm of their hand. || 31 ||<-

->“He is the Lord Shiva Himself in the form of the Master, the one who grants both worldly enjoyment and spiritual liberation to me.” For the one who remembers this with devotion, spiritual fulfillment <term>Siddhi</term> is not far away. || 32 ||<-

->O Sovereign of the Clan <note>original: "Kuleśvari," a title for the Goddess as the head of the spiritual lineage</note>! The truths I have spoken shine forth clearly for one who possesses supreme devotion toward the Divine, and possesses that same devotion toward their Master. || 33 ||<-

->O Great Goddess! One should offer the same devotion to their own Master as they would toward the Lord of Preservation <term>Nārāyaṇa</term>, the Great God <term>Mahādeva</term>, their own mother and father, or the King. || 34 ||<-

->One should contemplate the Holy Master and his wife as one's own parents; they should be seen as the divine pairs: Lakshmi and Nārāyaṇa, the Goddess of Speech <note>original: "Vāṇī" or Sarasvatī</note> and the Creator <note>original: "Dhātṛ" or Brahmā</note>, and the Mountain-Born Goddess <note>original: "Girijā" or Parvati</note> and Shiva. || 35 ||<-

->O Beloved! All spiritual perfections <term>Siddhis</term> are obtained through devotion to the Master in a way that cannot be achieved through sacrifices, charity, austerities, pilgrimages, or religious vows. || 36 ||<-

->O Leader of the Clan <note>original: "Kulanāyike"</note>! Just as one’s steady devotion to the Holy Master grows, so too does one's realized wisdom <note>original: "Vijñāna"</note> grow in equal measure. || 37 ||<-

->What use are pilgrimages and the exhausting efforts of religious duties? What use are vows that merely wither the body? O Queen of the Gods <note>original: "Deveśi"</note>! Devotion to a true Master is itself the highest service, performed without pretense or hidden motives. || 38 ||<-

<summary>This page describes devotion to the Guru as the supreme spiritual path, surpassing all external rituals, pilgrimages, and even the traditional four goals of human life. It establishes the Guru and his wife as earthly embodiments of divine couples like Shiva and Parvati, asserting that such devotion is the direct cause of spiritual wisdom.</summary>

# The Ocean of the Kula Tradition
<note>original: "Kulārṇavatantra"</note>

->Whatever reward one seeks through great physical hardship or intense penance <term>Tapas</term> can be easily attained, O Goddess, through service to the Master <note>original: "Guru"</note>. || 39 ||<-

All the fruits anticipated from the austerities involving bodily pains can be easily obtained by a selfless service to the Guru.

->For those who desire both worldly enjoyment <term>Bhoga</term> and spiritual liberation <term>Mokṣa</term>, and who aspire to reach the states of the Creator <term>Brahmā</term>, the Preserver <term>Viṣṇu</term>, and the Lord <term>Īśa</term>, the sacred tradition <term>Śruti</term> declares: Devotion to the Master is the only Path and no other. || 40 ||<-

The sacred texts declare that for those who seek for fulfilments and liberation, who aspire to attain to the divine states of the trinity, devotion to the Guru is the only Path and no other.

->Just as a fire consumes a massive heap of cotton, this devotion burns away in a single moment all inauspicious actions <term>Karmas</term> and even the greatest sins. || 41 ||<-

Like fire consuming a whole heap of cotton, this devotion burns away in a moment all inauspicious actions and great sins.

->Salutations to that Faith which grants all spiritual accomplishments <term>Siddhis</term>. Through such faith, even objects made of clay, wood, or stone yield their full and unfailing rewards. || 42 ||<-

Salutation to that faith in the Guru, the giver of all fulfilments, by which even mud, wood and stone also yield fruit without fail.

->Neither yoga, nor penance, nor any sequence of ritual worship is effective on its own. In this Path of the Clan <term>Kula</term>, which is free from illusion <term>Māyā</term>, devotion alone is supreme. || 43 ||<-

Neither Yoga nor penance nor ritual of worship bear fruit alone; here in this Path of the spiritual lineage, free from the world's illusions, only devotion excels.

->O Goddess, when the entire universe is seen as being filled with the presence of the Master, what sacred chant <term>Mantra</term> could fail to bear fruit in the field of the devoted? || 44 ||<-

When the entire universe is looked upon as pervaded by the Guru, what sacred chant can fail to bear fruit in the life of the devoted?

->**The Master is not to be regarded as a mere mortal:**<-
->One who views the Master as a mere human, the sacred chant as mere letters, and the divine image as a mere stone, goes to a state of suffering <note>original: "Naraka," often translated as hell</note>. || 45 ||<-

*The Guru is not to be regarded as a mere mortal*: To a low state of existence goes he who regards the Guru as a human, the Mantra as mere letters, and the image as stone.

->One should not think of the Master as a mortal. If one does, then success will never be achieved through sacred chants or the worship of deities. || 46 ||<-

The Guru is not to be looked upon as a mortal. Should one do so, then neither the sacred chants nor the worship of a deity would grant him success.

->O Beloved! For those who equate the holy Master with ordinary folk, whether in their thoughts or in their talk, all the merit and good they have done turns into evil. || 47 ||<-

Those who associate the holy Guru with ordinary people either in their memory or in talk find that all the good deeds they have performed turn into spiritual debt.

<summary>This page emphasizes that devotion to the Guru is the most direct path to liberation, surpassing all other religious practices. It specifically warns that viewing the Guru as a common human, or sacred objects as mere physical matter, negates all spiritual progress.</summary>
<keywords>Guru-bhakti, Kula Path, Tapas, Mantra, spiritual success, divinity of the Master, Karma</keywords>

# Twelfth Chapter
<note>original: "dvādaśa ullāsaḥ"</note>

One's parents should be honored with every effort, for they are the cause of one's physical birth. However, the Master <term>Guru</term> <note>literally "one who dispels darkness"</note> should be especially honored, as he is the one who reveals what is righteous and what is unrighteous <term>Dharma</term> and <term>Adharma</term>. || 48 ||

The parents are indeed to be worshipped with all efforts because they are the cause of birth. But the one to be worshipped especially is the Guru who shows what is Dharma and what is not.

Indeed, the Master is the Father; the Master is the Mother; the Master is the Great Lord <term>Maheśvara</term> <note>a title for the supreme deity, Śiva</note> himself. When the Lord <term>Śiva</term> is angry, the Master is the savior; but when the Master himself is angry, there is no one who can save. || 49 ||

Indeed the Guru is the Father, Guru is the Mother, Guru is God Maheśvara himself. When God Śiva is angry the Guru is the saviour; but when the Guru himself is angered there is none to save.

One must act for the benefit of the Master through thought, speech, and physical action <note>original: "manovākkāyakarmabhiḥ"</note>. By acting against his well-being, O Goddess <term>Devi</term>, one is reborn as a worm living in excrement. || 50 ||

By mind, body, speech and action do what is helpful to the Guru. If one does something contrary to his well-being, then, O Devi, he is born as an insect living in excreta.

Those who betray the holy Master regarding their physical service, their wealth, or their very lives, will undoubtedly be reborn as germs, insects, and moths. || 51 ||

Those who betray Guru with body, money and life are indubitably born as germs, insects and flies, etc.

## The Sin of Forsaking the Master and the Sacred Formula
<note>original: "Mantra"</note>

Death comes from abandoning the sacred formula <term>Mantra</term>; poverty comes from abandoning the Master. By abandoning both the Master and the sacred formula, one falls into the <term>Raurava</term> Hell <note>the "Dreadful" hell in Hindu cosmology</note>. || 52 ||

*Sin in forsaking the Guru and Mantra :*

There comes death in forsaking a Mantra, poverty in forsaking the Guru and Raurava Hell in forsaking both Guru and the Mantra.

## Proper Conduct Toward the Master

Maintain your body for the sake of the Master; acquire wealth for the sake of the Master. Even by sacrificing your own life, you should carry out the Master’s work. || 53 ||

*Propriety of behaviours in respect of Guru :*

Bear the body for the sake of Guru; acquire wealth for the sake of Guru; exert yourself for the Guru even by sacrificing your life.

Even harsh words spoken by the Master should be regarded as blessings; even if one is struck by him, it should be remembered as a gesture of grace. || 54 ||

Harsh words spoken by the Guru should be taken as benedictions; even a beating from him should be taken as a gift.

All objects of enjoyment and food should first be offered to the Master. Only then, O Queen of the Kula tradition <term>Kuleśvari</term>, should one enjoy the leftovers, regarding them as a sacred gift. || 55 ||

Whatever objects of enjoyments and food there may be, they should first be offered to Guru, and O Kuleśvari, his leavings should be accepted as gifts.

<summary>This page outlines the supreme status of the Guru, asserting that the Master holds a higher spiritual rank than even parents or the gods, and warns of severe karmic consequences for betrayal or abandonment of the Master.</summary>

### In the Kularnava Tantra

->In the presence of the Master <term>Guru</term>, one should perform no independent austerities, nor fasts, nor religious vows.<-

### Chapter Twelve

->Service <term>Shushrusha</term> <note>original: "śuśrūṣā"; literally the "desire to hear," referring to devoted service</note> is said to be of four kinds: service through one's own self, service through material means, service through honor, and service through a sincere heart.<-
->O Goddess <term>Devi</term>! A disciple should please the Master <term>Guru</term> with a mind dedicated to his service. || 64 ||<-

->One who is dedicated to the service of the Master, the Divine <term>Devata</term>, and the Great Souls <term>Mahatmas</term> <note>highly evolved spiritual beings</note><-
->undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Horse Sacrifice <term>Ashvamedha</term> <note>one of the most significant and merit-heavy rituals of the Vedic tradition</note> with every step they take. || 65 ||<-

->O My Beloved! Service to the Master alone brings about Your grace.<-
->If that service is joined with true devotion <term>Bhakti</term>, it grants the fruits of all desires. || 66 ||<-

->O My Beloved! Through service to the Master, all sins are destroyed and heaps of spiritual merit <term>Punya</term> grow.<-
->Through this service, all undertakings reach success. || 67 ||<-

->Whatever object is dear to one's own soul <term>Atmahita</term>, that very thing should be offered to him.<-
->The merit of one who worships the Master cannot be counted. || 68 ||<-

->Whatever is done for the sake of the Master with devotion and according to one's means,<-
->whether it be a small thing or a great thing, the merit is the same for both the rich and the poor. || 69 ||<-

->A disciple <term>Shishya</term> who gives even his entire wealth to the Master but is devoid of devotion,<-
->attains no fruit; for indeed, devotion is the sole cause of spiritual success. || 70 ||<-

->One should not enjoy any object or wealth for which the Master has a desire.<-
->If there is an absolute necessity to use it, one should only experience it with his permission. || 71 ||<-

<summary>This page outlines the four types of service to the Guru and emphasizes that devotion, rather than the material value of an offering, is the primary requirement for spiritual merit. It equates the act of serving the Guru to the highest Vedic sacrifices, such as the Ashvamedha.</summary>

# In the Kulārṇavatantra

Whoever utilizes even a quantity equal to half a sesame seed <note>original: "tila-ardham"; the sesame seed is used here as a traditional metaphor for the smallest possible unit of measure</note>, or even half of that, from what belongs to the Master, out of greed or delusion, shall be cooked in hell for twenty-one cycles. || 72 ||

One who appropriates even the smallest fraction of what belongs to the Master, unless the Master himself gives it, is born into the animal world <term>Tiryak-yoni</term> <note>literally "oblique womb," referring to a rebirth as an animal, which is considered a regression in spiritual evolution</note> where carrion-eaters devour him, O Beloved. || 73 ||

Those who covet the Master’s belongings and those intent upon enjoying the Master’s wife <note>the Guru's wife is traditionally accorded the same respect as one's own mother</note> are wretches for whom no penance <term>Prayashchitta</term> <note>a ritual or act of atonement to remove the taint of sin</note> exists. || 74 ||

Breaking the Master’s command, the theft of his wealth, and indulgence in behavior disagreeable to him—these are called treachery to the Master. One who commits these is a sinner. || 75 ||

One should not even utilize one's own wealth without first offering it to the Master. One who utilizes it without such an offering becomes like one who has committed Brahmanicide <term>Brahma-ghataka</term> <note>the killing of a priest or a knower of Brahman, considered one of the most heinous "Great Sins" in the Hindu tradition</note>. || 76 ||

He who damages the position of the Master, his lineage <term>Sampradaya</term> <note>the oral and spiritual tradition passed from teacher to student</note>, or his sacred law <term>Dharma</term>, is to be ostracized by other Masters; he deserves punishment, and even death, for he is a destroyer. || 77 ||

Ruin follows from the anger of the Master; sin follows from treachery toward the Master; a foul death follows from criticizing the Master; and great catastrophe follows from the Master's displeasure. || 78 ||

A man may survive having entered the fire, or after drinking poison, or even when caught in the hands of death; but one who has offended the Master does not survive. || 79 ||

# Twelfth Chapter

Wherever the slandering of the Master occurs, O Mother <note>original: "Ambike"; an epithet for the Goddess, addressing her as the Divine Mother</note>, one should cover one's ears and immediately depart from that place so as not to hear it again. Afterwards, one should remember the Master's name; this acts as the spiritual remedy for having heard such speech. || 80 ||

One should not disrespect the Master's friends, companions, or his male and female servants. One must not criticize his traditions <term>Samaya</term> <note>the specific codes of conduct and established customs of a spiritual lineage</note>, whether they are based on the Vedas, the scriptures <term>Shastras</term>, or the sacred traditions <term>Agamas</term>. || 81 ||

The Master’s sacred sandals <term>Sri Paduka</term> are one's true ornaments; the remembrance of the Master’s name is the repetition of sacred prayer <term>Japa</term>; carrying out the Master's command is one's essential duty; and service to the Master is the highest form of worship. || 82 ||

One who desires to enter the Master's residence should possess a peaceful mind and be filled with the highest devotion. Leaving behind one’s vehicle, sandals, umbrella, fly-whisk <term>Chamara</term> <note>a traditional whisk made from a yak's tail, used as a symbol of royalty or divinity</note>, fan, betel nut, collyrium <note>dark eye-salve or kohl</note>, and decorative dress, one should enter slowly. || 83 ||

Upon seeing the Master’s sandals, his seat, his clothing, his vehicle, his umbrella, or his fly-whisk, one should offer a bow; one must never desire these items for one's own personal enjoyment. || 84 ||

Washing one's feet, bathing, massaging the body with oil, brushing one's teeth, urinating, spitting, shaving, sleeping, or engaging in sexual intimacy; || 85 ||

Sitting in the 'hero's pose' <term>Virasana</term> <note>a posture of physical readiness that may imply an air of equality or defiance in this context</note>, speaking harshly, issuing commands, laughing, or weeping; unbinding or loosening the hair, wearing a turban or a jacket, or being naked; || 86 ||

Stretching out the legs, arguing, quarreling, or speaking ill of others, O Beloved; cracking the joints, making music with the limbs <note>such as snapping fingers or slapping the body rhythmically</note>, or clapping and shaking the hands; || 87 ||

Gambling, idle curiosity, wrestling, fighting, dancing, and the like—O Mother! In the presence of the Master, or near Yogis, at great centers of spiritual power <term>Siddhi-pitha</term> <note>sacred sites where spiritual perfection is traditionally attained</note>, in sacred fields, or within hermitages, one should never perform these actions. If one does so out of delusion, they shall incur the curse of the deities. || 88 ||

In the pursuit of spiritual realization, during pilgrimages, and within the sacred hermitages <term>Ashramas</term>, one should take great care to avoid the following actions: washing one's feet, bathing, anointing the body with oil, cleaning one's teeth, urinating, vomiting, shaving, sleeping, engaging in sexual activity, sitting in a conspicuous or arrogant manner, using harsh speech, giving orders, laughter, weeping, loosening the hair, wearing a turban or a heavy cloak, nudity, stretching out the legs, engaging in debate, showing acrimony, casting blame on others, contorting the body, producing musical notes from the body <note>such as snapping fingers or cracking knuckles</note>, striking the hands together, playing dice or gambling, general amusements, bouts of wrestling or similar sports, and dancing. If these actions are performed out of vanity or conceit, they bring about the curse of the Deity.

->One should remain standing in attendance and should not sit down according to one’s own whim in the presence of the Guru. Looking toward his face, one should serve him and perform exactly what he has commanded. || 59 ||<-

->O Beloved <note>original: "Priye"; a term of endearment for the Goddess Parvati, the listener of this teaching</note>! One should not show neglect toward tasks, whether the Guru has explicitly requested them or not. Whatever the Guru speaks, one should accept it upon one’s head <note>a gesture signifying total submission and respect</note> and perform it without hesitation. || 60 ||<-

->Whether for restraint or for blessing <note>original: "nigrahe-anugrahe"; referring to the Guru's power to both discipline and bestow grace</note>, the Guru is the source of all things. Whatever has emerged from the Guru's mouth is said to be the sacred scripture itself. || 61 ||<-

->O Beloved! If one is personally capable of performing the Guru’s work, one should not delegate it to another. Even if one is accompanied by many servants or attendants, a disciple should remain full of devotion in personal service. || 62 ||<-

->Whether walking, standing, sleeping, waking, reciting sacred mantras <term>Japa</term>, or performing fire-offerings <note>original: "juhvat"</note>, one should worship the Master. One should only carry out the Guru’s command, with the inner self dwelling entirely within him. || 63 ||<-

->One should never harbor pride regarding one’s social class <term>Jati</term>, learning, wealth, or other status. A disciple <term>Shishya</term> should always and eternally serve in the presence of the venerable Guru. || 64 ||<-

# Twelfth Illumination

### In the Kularnava Tantra

->One should not engage in speaking, teaching, singing, eating, sleeping, or other such activities without the <term>Guru's</term> <note>spiritual teacher</note> command, nor without first bowing to him. || 103 ||<-

One should not indulge into speaking, reading, singing, eating or sleeping without the Guru's order or without bowing to him.

->Whether one is high-born, or possesses great learning or wealth, upon seeing the Guru from a distance, he should joyfully perform a <term>Dandapranama</term> <note>original: "danda-pranamam"; a full-body prostration where the disciple lies flat on the ground like a fallen staff</note> once and then perform a <term>Pradakshina</term> <note>the ritual of walking around a sacred person or object in a clockwise direction</note> three times. || 108 ||<-

Whether one is endowed with class, learning or wealth, he should, on seeing the Guru from a distance, prostrate himself with joy and then circumambulate around him thrice.

->O My Beloved! Thereafter, according to the hierarchy of the Guru and <term>Parama Guru</term> <note>the Guru's own teacher; the grand-preceptor</note>, one should offer respects three, six, or twelve times. He should observe the proper order of precedence between his Guru and his Guru's teacher when offering salutations. || 109 ||<-

O My Beloved ! Thereafter, according to the order of Guru and Parama Guru, one should pay his obeisance thrice, six times or twelve times. He should then observe due priorities of Guru and the Guru's Guru in offering his respects.

# Twelfth Illumination

->Thereafter, one should bow to the **Guru** <note>spiritual teacher</note> and must never second-guess the **Guru's** command. In the presence of the **Grand-Guru** <note>original: "praguroh"; the teacher's own teacher</note>, the **disciple** <note>original: "shishya"</note> should bow to his own **Guru** mentally. || 110 ||<-

Thereafter, the **disciple** should bow down to his own **Guru** and should not consider the **Guru's** command in this connection (i.e., even if the **Guru** stops the **disciple** from paying his obeisance, he should yet observe the formalities).

->With the mindset that they are the **Guru**, one should bow to everything, from a **God** <note>original: "daivatam"</note> even down to a blade of grass. However, one should not bow to statues made of iron or clay as if they were the **God** itself. || 111 ||<-

One should bow to everything from the **God** to a blade of grass, as to the **Guru**, but he should not bow as to **God** to the idols made of iron or earth.

->One should offer three prostrations to the **Guru** and a single one to elders. Similarly, one should join the palms in reverence to those worthy of worship and offer a verbal greeting to others. || 112 ||<-

One should salute the **Guru** thrice and once to the elders. Then, joining the palms to the honored, he should greet others verbally.

->O **Noble Lady of the Clan** <note>original: "kulanayike"; a title for the Goddess as the primary listener of the Tantra</note>! One should bow to the **Gods**, the **Gurus**, the teachers of the **Lineage** <note>original: "kulacharyan"</note>, those advanced in knowledge, those rich in **asceticism** <note>original: "tapas"</note>, the highly learned, and those who remain firm in their own **duty** <note>original: "dharma" </note>. || 113 ||<-

O **Kulanāyike**! One should bow to the **Gods**, the **Guru**, the Teachers of the **Kula**, the old in Knowledge, the rich in **Tapas**, the highly learned and those who are steadfast in their **Dharma**.

->One should not bow to those who hate women, those cursed by their **Gurus**, heretics, the deceptive, those who perform forbidden acts, the ungrateful, or those who do not follow the **ordained stages of life** <note>original: "anashraminam"; those who have abandoned the traditional four-stage social and spiritual order</note>. || 114 ||<-

One should not bow to the haters of women, those cursed by the **Guru**, the learned heretic, the dunce, the wrong-doer, the ingrate and the transgressor of the ordained stages of life.

->If a **disciple** lives in the same village as the **Guru** but eats without first offering the food to him, that food becomes as impure as filth, and the person is reborn as a pig after death. || 115 ||<-

While staying at the same place, if one eats food without offering to the **Guru**, then that food becomes impure and the partaker himself becomes a pig after death.

->A **disciple** living in the same village should bow to the **Guru** at the three junctions of the day <note>original: "trisandhyam"; the transition periods of dawn, noon, and dusk</note>. A **disciple** living within a **league** <note>original: "krosha"; approximately two miles</note> should bow to the **Guru** every day. || 116 ||<-

*Rules regarding Salutations to the Guru:*
Living in the same place the **disciple** should prostrate before the **Guru** in the three midpoints (i.e. morning, midday and evening). A **disciple** living one **Krośa** (two miles) away should salute the **Guru** daily.

### In the Kularnava Tantra

->A **disciple** living within half a **yojana** <term>yojana: an ancient Indian measure of distance, roughly equivalent to 8 or 9 miles</term> should offer salutations on the five **parva** days <note>auspicious ceremonial days in the lunar calendar, such as the full moon or new moon</note>. For distances ranging from one **yojana** up to twelve, the disciple should salute the holy **Guru** after a corresponding number of days or months, O Beloved! || 117-118 ||<-

A disciple living far away should come to the **Guru** and devotedly salute him after as many months as there are **yojanas** of distance. A disciple who has traveled very far may come for salutation whenever it is possible for him. || 119 ||

->One should never approach a king, a deity, or the **Guru** empty-handed. One should offer fruits, flowers, clothing, and the like, according to one's own capacity. O Goddess! He who does not act thus becomes a **Brahma-Rakshasa** <note>a powerful, malevolent spirit of a deceased person who possessed great knowledge but misapplied it or failed in his duties</note>. || 120 ||<-

The **Guru's consort** <note>original: "Guru-shakti"</note>, the **Guru's** son, and an elder brother are all to be regarded as the **Guru** himself. || 121 ||

->A knower of the **Self** should look after those younger than him as if they were his own sons. O **Mistress of the Gods** <note>original: "Deveshi"</note>! One should offer prostrations to the senior and junior relatives of the **Lineage Teacher** <term>Kulācārya: a high-ranking preceptor within the Kula or Tantric tradition</term> in the same manner as one would to one's own **Guru**. || 122 ||<-

There are four types of elders: the elder in **sacrifice** <note>original: "yaga-jyeshtha"</note>, the elder in **order of initiation** <note>original: "krama-jyeshtha"</note>, the elder in the **lineage** <note>original: "kula-jyeshtha"</note>, and the eldest son of the **Guru**. O Goddess, these are the four distinct elders. || 123 ||

->By greeting the elder in sacrifice and following the eightfold sequence <note>original: "ashtanga"; likely referring here to the prostration where eight points of the body touch the ground</note>, the **Guru** and the **Lineage-Trees** <term>Kula-vrikshas: a metaphor for the respected masters and branches of the spiritual tradition</term> must be venerated according to the prescribed rules. || 124 ||<-

### Twelfth Illumination

Among all relatives who are worthy of worship, such as one's father, mother, and others, one who does not express respect through rising from one’s seat and prostrating is considered at fault. || 125 ||

But when one reveals themselves in the role of the **Teacher** <note>original: "Acharya"</note>, then these very acts of rising and prostrating to biological elders become a fault. <note>In this tradition, the spiritual status of a Master supersedes their previous family role; for a Master to bow to a non-initiate relative would be a violation of the divinity they represent.</note> || 126 ||

One who has attained the status of the **Lord** <term>Pati: a term for a realized soul or the Divine itself</term> and yet offers salutations to a **worldly person** <term>Paśu: literally 'animal' or 'beast,' referring to the uninitiated who are still bound by worldly ties</term> is called a "great animal" and receives the curse of the Gods. || 127 ||

One who has attained the status of a **Guru** through the ritual meditation on the **Holy Sandals** <term>Pādukā: the symbolic sandals of the Guru, representing his power and presence</term> should be regarded as the **Guru** himself, O Beloved! He is to be honored even by his seniors and elders. || 128 ||

Thus I have described to you in brief the characteristics of devotion to the **Holy Sandals**. O **Mistress of the Kula** <term>Kuleśāni: a title for the Goddess as the sovereign of the sacred lineage</term>! What else do you wish to hear? || 129 ||

->Thus ends the Twelfth Illumination,<-
->entitled the "Discourse on the Holy Sandals,"<-
->in the Fifth Section of the Supreme Tradition of the North,<-
->part of the Great Secret, the Gate to Liberation and Creation,<-
->within the illustrious **Kularnava Tantra**,<-
->which consists of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses.<-

# Thirteenth Illumination

---

->**The Holy Goddess said:**<-

->O Lord of the Kula <note>original: "Kuleśa"</note>, Ocean of the Nectar of Compassion! O Lord of Gods <note>original: "Deveśa"</note>, I desire to hear from You the defining characteristics of a Guru and a Disciple <term>Śiṣya: a student or initiate on the spiritual path</term>. || 1 ||<-

->**The Lord said:**<-

->Listen, O Goddess! I shall explain what You have asked of Me. By merely hearing these words, the true spirit of the Guru <note>original: "Guru-bhāva"</note> arises within. || 2 ||<-

One who is born of a corrupt lineage, who is wicked, lacking in virtues, or deformed; one who is already the disciple of another, a hypocrite <term>Pāṣaṇḍa: originally referring to heretics or those who make a false show of piety</term>, an impotent person, or one who is consumed by intellectual pride; || 3 ||

Those with missing or extra limbs, or with malformed bodies; those who are lame, blind, deaf, physically dirty, or afflicted by chronic disease; || 4 ||

One who has been cast out, one who is foul-mouthed, or one who dresses only according to their own whims, My Beloved! One who possesses bad habits in their gestures, gait, speech, or gaze; || 5 ||

One who is consumed by sleep, lethargy, dullness, and laziness, or addicted to vices such as gambling; one who always hides their true self behind walls, pillars, or screens; one who displays inner devotion but is utterly lacking in outward discipline; || 6 ||

One who speaks falsehoods, who is stubborn, or who is a wanderer; one who is a servant <note>implies one who is subservient to worldly masters rather than divine law</note>, a rogue, or lacks purity regarding wealth and women; one who disregards the sacred rules and prohibitions; || 7 ||

One who betrays secrets, O Goddess, or who ruins the work at hand; one who acts like a cat <note>original: "mārjāravadvṛtti"; a traditional idiom for a hypocrite who waits silently to find faults in others or to snatch what they desire</note>, constantly looking for gaps and weaknesses in others; || 8 ||

One who is deceitful, ungrateful, or who harbors hidden agendas; a betrayer of trust, one who is treacherous toward their master, or a doer of sins; || 9 ||

One who causes mistrust, who is full of doubt, or who seeks only the acquisition of supernatural powers <term>Siddhi: psychic or spiritual powers gained through practice</term>; an assassin, a greedy person, one who is easily angered, or a false witness; || 10 ||

One who cheats everyone, O Goddess, and is filled with the pride of being superior to all; one who is untruthful, addicted to cruelty, and speaks excessively of vulgar or worldly matters. || 11 ||

### *Characteristics of Śiṣyas who should be Rejected:*

O Sovereign of the Lineage <note>original: "Kuleśvari"</note>! The Guru shall desist from taking for his disciple one who is of wicked descent; wicked; devoid of good qualities; ugly; a disciple of another; a heretic; impotent; one who fancies himself to be learned; one with a body of less or more or deformed limbs; one who is lame; blind; deaf; dirty; struck with disease; excommunicated; foul of mouth; one who wears any dress he likes; one of ill-formed limbs, movements, gait, speech, and look; one who is sleepy; drowsy; lazy; addicted to vices like gambling; one who is ever hiding himself behind cupboards, walls, or pillars; one who is mean; one who is devoid of external signs of devotion though claiming devotion within; one who is given to exaggeration in speech; dry; exiled; one who is merely instigating others; one who is cunning, impure regarding wealth and wife; one who is given to perform what is prohibited and to omit what is enjoined; or one who is given to divulging <note>The text here ends abruptly, likely referring to divulging the secrets of the lineage</note>.

# Kularnava Tantra

### The Thirteenth Illumination

One who achieves the impossible, a hero endowed with enthusiasm and strength;
Engaged in favorable actions, vigilant, and discerning; (28)

Whose speech is beneficial, truthful, measured, and smiling; free from faults;
Who grasps the meaning of things once spoken; clever and of broad intelligence; (29)

Averse to his own praise and to slandering others; pleasant and kind;
Master of his senses, deeply contented, wise, and a <term>Brahmachārī: a celibate spiritual student or one who practices self-restraint</term>; (30)

Having cast off mental and physical ailments, fickleness, grief, delusion, and doubt.

*Characteristics of acceptable Śiṣyas :*

O <term>Kuleśanī: "Lady of the Kula," an address to the Goddess</term>! The disciple chosen shall be one who is endowed with auspicious features; given to <term>Sādhanā: disciplined spiritual practice</term> that leads to <term>Samādhi: a state of deep meditative absorption</term>; of good qualities and culture; clean of body and apparel; wise; devoted to <term>Dharma: sacred duty and righteousness</term>; pure of mind, steady in observances; of truthful practice; gifted with faith and devotion; diligent; sparsely eating; deep-thoughted; serving without motive; scrutinising; heroic; free from poverty of mind; skilful in all actions; clean; obliging to all; grateful; afraid of sin; approved of the holy and the good; believer in God; liberal; engaged in the good of all creatures. 

He shall be one who has trust and modesty; who is not given to deceive in matters of wealth, body, etc.; achieves the impossible; is brave, enthusiastic and strong; engaged in favourable activities; not intoxicated; able, helpful, truthful, limited and smiling in speech; not given to blaming others; who grasps what is said but once; clever; expansive in intelligence; averse to listen to his own praise and genial to others' criticism of himself; master of his senses; contented with himself; intelligent; celibate; free from worry, disease, fickleness, grief, delusion and doubt.

One eager for meditation on the <term>Guru: the spiritual teacher</term>, for hymns of praise, sacred stories, the worship of deities, and bowing; (31)

Devoted to the Guru and the Deity; a supreme worshipper of the feminine energy <note>original: *kāminī-pūjakaṃ*; in the Kula tradition, this refers to the ritual practice of seeing and honoring the Divine Mother within women</note>;
Always staying near the Guru and causing the Guru’s satisfaction; (32)

Always ready for service with mind, speech, and body;
Obeying the Guru’s commands, O Goddess, and proclaiming the Guru’s fame; (33)

Knowing the Guru’s word as authority; devoted to serving the Guru;
Following the Guru’s mind and acting as an attendant, O <term>Kulanāyikā: the Leader of the Kula lineage</term>; (34)

Devoid of pride regarding his caste, status, or wealth in the presence of the Guru;
Indifferent to the Guru’s property, but longing for his grace; (35)

Fond of the stories of the <term>Kuladharma: the sacred path and tradition of the Kula</term>, of practitioners, of female practitioners <note>original: *yoginī*</note>, and of the Kula community;
Diligent in the Kula worship and not feeling disgust toward the sacred ritual substances <note>original: *kuladravya*; specific ritual items such as wine or meat that are transfigured in Tantric ceremony and must not be viewed with worldly prejudice</note>. (36)

# Kularnava Tantra

Devoted to <term>Japa: the meditative repetition of a mantra</term> and <term>Dhyāna: meditation</term>, desiring the path to <term>Mokṣa: spiritual liberation</term>; fond of the <term>Kula</term> scriptures, O Goddess, and turning away from the scriptures of the <term>Paśu: literally "tethered" or uninitiated souls</term>. Endowed with these and other such characteristics, the Guru should accept the disciple. (37)

### Characteristics of Guru :

He shall be one who is enthusiastic in meditation, praise and speaking of the Guru, worship and prostration to the Deity; well devoted to the Deity Guru; worshipper of the <term>Shakti: the divine feminine creative power</term>; ever in the proximity of the Guru; pleasing the Guru; constantly well engaged in his attendance by mind, speech, and body; carrying out the command of the Guru; spreading the glory of the Guru; knowing the authority of the word of the Guru; occupied in the service of the Guru; following the mind of the Guru; functioning as a servant; free from pride of class, honour, or wealth in the presence of the Guru; not coveting the wealth of the Guru; aspiring for his favours; fond of narration of the <term>Kuladharma: the sacred law of the Kula tradition</term> of <term>Yogīs: male practitioners</term> and <term>Yoginīs: female practitioners</term> and the practitioner of the Kaula Path; engaged in Kula worship and the like; not scared away in disgust at the ingredients <note>This likely refers to the "five substances" (makāras) used in tantric ritual which might shock the uninitiated</note> of Kula worship; engaged in Japa, Dhyāna, etc.; aspiring for the Path of Mokṣa; fond of the Kaula Scriptures; averse to texts of the *paśu*-class. The Guru shall adopt <term>Śiṣyas: disciples</term> who possess these qualities.

The holy Guru, O supreme Goddess, is of pure appearance and captivating; endowed with all auspicious signs and beautiful in every limb. (38)

He knows the essential truth of all the <term>Āgamas: sacred tantric scriptures</term> and the rituals of all Mantras; he charms the world and is as pleasant to behold as a god. (39)

Pleasant-faced, easily approached, and pure, he is the destroyer of delusion and doubt. He understands gestures and appearances; he is wise, brilliant, and expert in reasoning and discernment. (40)

His focus is internal while his gaze is external <note>This describes a specific yogic state where the mind is absorbed in the divine while the eyes remain open to the world</note>; he is all-knowing and understands the nuances of time and place. His commands are fulfilled, he knows the three periods of time <note>Past, present, and future</note>, and is capable of both restraint and grace. (41)

He is the piercer of ignorance, the awakener, peaceful, and devoted to compassion for all living beings. He has mastered the movement of his senses and is capable of conquering the <term>Ṣaḍvarga: the "six enemies" of the soul—lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy</term>. (42)

He is foremost, very profound, and knows the distinction between the worthy and the unworthy. He is equal to <term>Shiva</term> and <term>Vishnu</term>, and he censures the wicked and the dull-witted. (43)

Stainless, eternally satisfied, independent, and possessing the power of Mantras. He is affectionate toward good devotees, steadfast, compassionate, and his speech is full of smiles. (44)

Dear to his devotees, always generous, deep, and a practitioner among the disciplined. He is eager to worship his own chosen Deity, his Guru, elders, and women <note>In the Kaula tradition, women are revered as living embodiments of the Goddess (Shakti)</note>. (45)

# Kularnava Tantra

->Chapter Thirteen<-

### Characteristics of Guru :

O <term>Parameśāni: Supreme Goddess</term>! The Guru himself is one who wears clean apparel; he is charming, endowed with all auspicious features, and perfect in limb. He knows the truth of all <term>Āgamas: sacred scriptures</term> and the practical application of all <term>Mantras</term>. He is a person who bewitches the world with his presence, appearing as sweet-looking as a God, with a happy countenance, yet remains easy to approach and pure.

He is one who dissipates all delusion and doubt in his followers; he understands the subtle meaning of gestures and is wise enough to weigh the pros and cons of any situation. His attention is directed within even while his gaze is turned outward. He knows all; he understands the importance of place and time; and within his command lies <term>Siddhi: spiritual fulfillment or supernatural power</term>. He possesses knowledge of the past, present, and future, and is capable of both restraint and the granting of boons.

Capable of piercing the hearts of others with spiritual insight, he is an instructor who is quiet and compassionate to all living creatures. He has total control over his senses and has conquered the "six enemies": desire, anger, greed, delusion, jealousy, and pride. He is a foremost leader, highly solemn, and knows how to distinguish between a fit student and one who is unready. He is equal-minded toward <term>Śiva</term> and <term>Viṣṇu</term> <note>This indicates a non-sectarian approach, seeing the divine as one despite different names</note>. He is good, stainless, ever content, and independent, yet he condemns the doctrines of those who remain unawakened.

Endowed with the power of <term>Mantra</term>, he is a lover of faithful devotees, steadfast and merciful. He always speaks with a preliminary smile and is dear to those who follow him. Ever-generous and a superb practitioner, he is enthusiastic in the worship of his chosen Deity, his own Guru, the elders, and the <term>Śakti: the divine feminine power</term>.

He is devoted to the three types of blameless ritual: the <term>Nitya: daily obligatory rites</term>, the <term>Naimittika: occasional rites for specific times</term>, and the <term>Kāmya: voluntary rites performed for specific desires</term> (46). He is devoid of anger, hate, fear, pain, ostentation, and egoism. He is deeply engaged in the practice of his <term>Vidyā: sacred science or knowledge</term>, acquiring <term>Dharma: righteousness</term> and other spiritual goals (47). Content with whatever comes to him by chance, he distinguishes between good and bad. He is unattached to women, wealth, bad company, or vice; he lives with a feeling of oneness with all beings, free from dualities, and constant in the observance of his vows (48).

He is not greedy, but wise and discerning; he never sells <term>Mantras</term>, <term>Yantras: mystical ritual diagrams</term>, or <term>Tantras</term> for the sake of wealth or worldly status (49). He is unattached, free from mental wavering, established in the final truth of the scriptures, and profoundly righteous. Treating praise and blame as equal, he remains silent, independent, and free from all affliction. O Dear One, the Holy Guru is said to be endowed with these and other such auspicious characteristics (50).

# Kularnava Tantra

->Chapter Thirteen<-

### Characteristics of Guru:

...vance; not over-eager; without self-desire and partiality; able; not selling <term>Mantra: a sacred utterance or sound-syllable</term>, <term>Yantra: a geometric diagram used in meditation</term> and <term>Tantra: the system of ritual and philosophy</term> for the sake of money or learning; un-attached, without doubts, with decided views, supremely conforming to <term>Dharma: the path of righteousness and cosmic order</term>, equal in praise and criticism, silent, without preference, free from disease. O My Beloved! These are the characteristics of a Guru.

->He who is Śiva, all-pervading, subtle, beyond the reach of the mind, without parts, and undying;<-
->He who is shaped like the sky, unborn and infinite—how can such a one be worshipped, my dear?<-
->Therefore, Śiva himself takes refuge in the form of the Guru.<-
->When worshipped with devotion, O Goddess, he bestows both worldly enjoyment and final liberation.<-

### *Though Formless yet the Gurus-form of Śiva:*

O My Beloved! Śiva is really all-pervading, subtle, above the mind, without features, imperishable, of the form of ether, eternal, infinite; how can such a one be worshipped? That is why, out of compassion for his creatures, Śiva takes the form of the Guru and when so worshipped in devotion, O Devi, grants liberation and fulfilment.

->I am Śiva; I have no physical form, O Devi, and am not visible to the human eye.<-
->Therefore, He protects the disciples who follow Dharma in the form of the Holy Guru.<-
->Enclosed in human skin, the Supreme Śiva himself<-
->wanders the earth in secret for the sake of bestowing grace upon good disciples.<-
->For the protection of true devotees, though he is formless, he takes on a form;<-
->Śiva, the ocean of mercy, acts in this world just like an ordinary person.<-
->Hiding his forehead-eye, his crescent moon, and two of his arms,<-
->I remain on the surface of the earth in the form of the Guru.<-

Śiva has no binding form, Śiva is not perceivable by the human eye; therefore, He protects the disciple conforming to Dharma in the form of the Guru. The Guru is none other than the supreme Śiva enclosed in human skin; he walks the earth concealed, for bestowing grace on the good disciples. Though formless, Śiva, the store of compassion, takes form for the protection of the good devotees and acts in the world as though he were a householder <note>The Sanskrit 'samsariva' suggests one who participates in the world of births and deaths</note>. He conceals his eye on the forehead, his crescent of moon and two of his hands and functions in the form of the Guru on the earth,

->The Holy Guru is described, my dear, as Śiva without the three eyes,<-
->as Viṣṇu without the four arms, and as<-
->Brahmā without the four faces.<-
->In this world, the Holy Guru is seen as a mere human by those of sinful deeds;<-
->He is seen as Śiva himself, O Bhavāni, by those of virtuous deeds.<-

<summary>This page explains that because the ultimate deity Śiva is formless and infinite, he manifests in human form as a Guru to guide and protect disciples. It emphasizes that while a Guru appears human to the ignorant, he is actually a divine incarnation to the spiritually realized.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Thirteenth Illumination of the Kularnava Tantra. Following the previous page’s description of the Guru as the physical manifestation of the formless Shiva, this section deepens the theological identity between the Teacher, the Divine, and the sacred Mantra.</meta>

# Kularnava Tantra

## Thirteenth Illumination

Those of poor fortune do not see the Supreme Teacher, the ultimate reality, even when he stands right before their eyes; they are like the blind who cannot see the sun once it has risen. <note>Verse 59</note>

The Teacher is truly <term>Sadashiva: the eternal, auspicious form of the Divine</term> himself; of this there is no doubt. If the Teacher were not Shiva himself, who else could grant both worldly fulfillment and spiritual liberation? <note>Verse 60</note>

O Parvati, there is no difference between the Lord Sadashiva and the Holy Teacher. One who creates a distinction between them is a transgressor. <note>Verse 61</note>

Assuming the form of the Guide, he cuts away the endless bonds that tether the <term>pashu: the "animal" or individual soul bound by ignorance</term>. Because he leads the soul to the supreme state, he is called the Guru <note>literally "the dispeller of darkness"</note>. <note>Verse 62</note>

As the source of all grace and a treasury of compassion, the Lord <note>original: Īśvara</note> takes the form of the Teacher to liberate these bound souls through <term>diksha: sacred initiation</term>. <note>Verse 63</note>

->*Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śivatva of Śrī Guru:*<-

The Guru is none other than **Shiva** without His three eyes, **Vishnu** without His four arms, and **Brahma** without His four faces. To one who is burdened with sinful <term>Karma: the law of cause and effect</term>, the Guru appears to be merely human; but to one whose Karma is auspicious and full of merit, the Guru appears as Shiva. The less fortunate do not recognize the Guru, the embodiment of the supreme Truth, even when face to face with him, like the blind before the risen sun. Verily, the Guru is none else but Sadashiva; that is the truth; there is no doubt about it. Shiva himself is the Guru; otherwise, who is it that gives fulfillment and liberation? There is no difference between God Sadashiva and the Guru; it is sinful to make a distinction. He is the Guru because, taking the form of the Preceptor, he cuts asunder all the bonds of the bound soul and leads it to the supreme status. Store of compassion, the Lord, being the fount of all Grace, takes the form of the Guru and releases the "animal" by his Initiation.

Just as the words for "vessel," "pitcher," and "jar" <note>original: "ghata, kalasha, kumbha"</note> all refer to the same object, so too are the Deity, the <term>Mantra: the divine sound-vibration</term>, and the Teacher said to be one and the same. <note>Verse 64</note>

As is the Deity, so is the Mantra; as is the Mantra, so is the Teacher. The fruit of the worship of the Deity, Mantra, and Guru is the same. <note>Verse 65</note>

"Taking the form of Shiva, O Parvati, I accept the worship; assuming the form of the Guru, I sunder the bonds of worldly birth." <note>Verse 66</note>

->*No difference between the Deity, Mantra and Guru:*<-

Just as vessel, pitcher, jar all designate the same thing, similarly **Devata** <note>Deity</note>, **Mantra**, and **Guru**—all designate the same subject. The Deity in truth is the same as the Mantra; the Mantra in truth is the same as the Guru. The fruit of the worship of the Deity, Mantra, and Guru is the same. "Taking the form of Shiva, O Parvati! I accept the worship; assuming the form of the Guru I sunder the bonds of birth."

<summary>This page establishes the absolute ontological identity between the Guru, the high deities (Shiva, Vishnu, Brahma), and the sacred Mantra, explaining that the Guru is the compassionate human form Shiva assumes to initiate and liberate bound souls.</summary>
<keywords>Guru-tattva, Sadashiva, liberation, initiation, Diksha, Pashu, Mantra-Devata-Guru unity, spiritual vision</keywords>

# Kularnava Tantra

->The one who brings about the realization: "I am the knower of the essence of all established truths <note>original: "Siddhanta-sara"</note>, I am the seed of all, I am undivided, and my heart is ever joyful"—he is called the Guru.<- <note>Verse 67</note>

->**Characteristics of a Superior Guru:**<-

He who makes his disciple know: "I am the knower of the essence of all philosophy, I am the core/seed <note>original: "bija"</note>, who is inseparable from <term>Brahman: the ultimate reality or absolute consciousness</term> and who is ever-pleased in heart"—he is the Guru.

->He who transcends the <term>Ashramas: the four stages of life</term> and the <term>Varnas: the social classes</term>, dwelling always within the Self; he for whom the Supreme Light itself is both his stage of life and his social order—that yogi is declared to be the Guru, O Beloved.<- <note>Verse 68</note>

->O My Beloved! He who understands according to the sacred tradition the Six Paths <note>original: "Adhvan"</note>, the Six Centers <note>original: "Cakras"</note>, and the determination of the Sixteen Supports <note>original: "Adhara"</note>, he is declared to be the Guru.<- <note>Verse 69</note>

<note>The Six Paths refer to the organization of sacred sound and cosmos: Letters, Mantras, Words, Instruments, Principles, and Worlds. The Six Centers are the energy hubs of the subtle body: Base, Sacral, Solar Plexus, Heart, Throat, and Brow. The Sixteen Supports are specific focal points for meditation ranging from the base of the spine to the crown of the head and beyond.</note>

->The one whose gaze is steady even without a physical object to see, whose mind is steady without a point of support, and whose <term>Prana: the vital breath or life-force</term> is steady without effort—he is the Guru, O Beloved.<- <note>Verse 70</note>

->That which generates pure consciousness and gives rise to supreme bliss—he who has realized that Truth, O <term>Kulanayike: Mistress of the Kula tradition</term>, is the Guru.<- <note>Verse 71</note>

->He who knows the past and the future, the <term>Tantras: the sacred texts of ritual and philosophy</term> and the <term>Mantras: the sacred chants</term>, who knows the paths of the Goddess <note>original: "Shakta"</note> and the Lord Shiva <note>original: "Shambhava"</note>, and the sixfold Piercing <note>original: "Vedha"</note>—he is truly the Guru who pierces through ignorance.<- <note>Verse 72</note>

<note>The Piercing (Vedha) is a specialized form of initiation where the Guru’s power enters the disciple. It is categorized into three types: individual, energetic, and divine, each further divided into external and internal methods.</note>

**Technical Vocabulary:**
<term>Guru: a spiritual weight or teacher who dispels darkness</term>, <term>Ashrama: the four life stages—student, householder, retiree, and renunciant</term>, <term>Varna: the traditional social orders</term>, <term>Adhvan: the "paths" of cosmic manifestation</term>, <term>Cakra: the "wheels" or energy centers of the subtle body</term>, <term>Adhara: the sixteen "supports" for internal concentration</term>, <term>Prana: the breath or life-current</term>, <term>Kulanayike: an address to the Goddess as the leader of the Kula lineage</term>, <term>Tantra: the ritual and philosophical systems of this tradition</term>, <term>Mantra: divine sound-forms</term>, <term>Shakta: pertaining to the power of the Goddess</term>, <term>Shambhu: pertaining to the grace of Shiva</term>, <term>Vedha: the "piercing" or transmission of spiritual energy</term>, <term>Brahman: the all-pervading Absolute</term>.

**Guru:** A spiritual teacher or "dispeller of darkness."
**Sisya:** A dedicated student or disciple.
**Samsara:** The cycle of worldly existence, often described as an ocean of suffering.
**Moksha:** The state of ultimate liberation and freedom.
**Jnana:** Spiritual knowledge or direct realization of truth.
**Devi:** The Goddess, to whom these teachings are often addressed in the form of a dialogue with Shiva.

<summary>This page describes the characteristics of a true Guru, contrasting those who merely teach rules with the rare master who can grant instant liberation and spiritual joy. It emphasizes that a genuine Guru acts like the Sun, providing universal illumination rather than the limited light of a household lamp.</summary>

# Chapter Thirteen

->Even one who is devoid of all external marks of a teacher is considered a Guru if they are a Knower of Truth. Therefore, in this world, only the Knower of Truth is liberated and is also the one who liberates others. [Verse 121]<-

### *Knower of Truth alone is the Real Guru:*

One who knows the Truth is the Guru even though they may lack all traditional physical or social features. The knower of Truth <note>original: "Tattva-vid"</note> alone is the Liberated and also the Liberator.

->O Great Goddess <note>original: "Maheshani"</note>, the knower of Truth can awaken even a bound soul <term>Paśu: literally "cattle," referring to an uninitiated person bound by worldly delusions</term>. But for one who is devoid of Truth, how is it possible to receive the knowledge of the Supreme Self? [Verse 122]<-

The knower of Truth makes even the <term>Paśu</term> understand the Truth. But one who is devoid of knowledge, how is it possible for them to receive the Truth of the Self?

->Those who are instructed by the Knowers of Truth become Knowers of Truth themselves, without a doubt. O Goddess <term>Devi</term>! Those who are instructed by the bound souls <term>Paśus</term> are themselves considered bound souls. [Verse 123]<-

Those who are instructed by the Knowers of Truth become undoubtedly knowers of Truth themselves. O <term>Devi</term>! Those who are instructed by the <term>Paśus</term> are verily <term>Paśus</term>.

->O Goddess, only one who has been "pierced" <note>referring to a spiritual awakening or initiation that "pierces" the veil of ignorance</note> can pierce others; one who is not pierced cannot be the piercer. Only the liberated can liberate the bound; how indeed can the unliberated be the liberator? [Verse 124]<-

It is only one who is pierced himself can pierce others; one who is not pierced can hardly be the piercer. Only the liberated can liberate; how indeed can the unliberated be the liberator?

->Only the wise can uplift the foolish; how indeed can the foolish uplift the foolish? A boat can ferry a stone across the water, but can one stone ferry another stone? [Verse 125]<-

Only the proficient in knowledge can uplift the foolish; how indeed can the foolish uplift the foolish? Only the boat can ferry the stone across; surely a stone cannot ferry a stone.

->By obtaining a Guru who is devoid of Truth and is instead engrossed in the affairs of the world, a person obtains no fruit either in this life or the next, O Beloved. [Verse 126]<-

By getting a <term>Guru</term> engrossed only in the affairs of the world and not knowing the Truth one obtains no fruit either here or in the other world.

->In the traditions of Shiva <term>Shaivas</term>, three types of Gurus are spoken of; in the traditions of Vishnu <term>Vaishnavas</term>, there are five. In the ancient scriptures <term>Vedas</term> and technical treatises <term>Shastras</term>, there are hundreds, but in the Divine Lineage <term>Kula</term>, there is only one Guru. [Verse 127]<-

### *Kinds of Guru:*

Three are the <term>Gurus</term> among <term>Śaivas</term>; five among the <term>Vaiṣṇavas</term>; hundreds in the <term>Vedas</term> and <term>Śāstras</term>; but in the <term>Kula</term> <note>original: "Kulanvaye," referring to the specific tantric tradition or "family" of the Kularnava</note> there is only one <term>Guru</term>.

<summary>This page argues that internal spiritual realization (knowing the Tattva) is the only valid qualification for a Guru, as an unliberated teacher cannot liberate a student any more than a stone can help another stone float. It concludes by contrasting the many types of teachers found in other traditions with the singular, essential Guru of the Kula path.</summary>

# In the Kularnava Tantra

->The impeller, the indicator, the explainer, the shower, the teacher, and the illuminator—these six are known as Gurus. [Verse 128]<-

Gurus are said to be of six kinds: 
1. *Impeller* <note>original: "Preraka"; one who encourages the initial interest in the spiritual path</note>
2. *Indicator* <note>original: "Sūcaka"; one who points towards the path or specific practices</note>
3. *Explainer* <note>original: "Vācaka"; one who explains the scriptures and doctrines</note>
4. *Shower* <note>original: "Darśaka"; one who demonstrates the path through their own example</note>
5. *Teacher* <note>original: "Śikṣaka"; one who instructs in the actual methods of discipline</note>
6. *Illuminator* <note>original: "Bodhaka"; the one who awakens the direct experience of reality</note>

->These five are the effects; the illuminator is the cause. The Guru who performs the full initiation—his sandals alone are to be worshiped, O Great Goddess, even if there are many others. There is no doubt about it. [Verse 129]<-

Of these, the first five are, as it were, the effects of the last, the Illuminator <note>original: "Bodhaka"</note>, acting as the primary Cause. In spite of having many Gurus for different purposes, only the Guru who gives the full Initiation <note>original: "Purnabhiseka"</note>—his <term>Pādukā: literally "sandals," referring to the Guru's feet or the spiritual power transmitted through them</term>, O Great Goddess <note>original: "Maheshani"</note>, is to be venerated. There is no doubt about it.

->Having obtained a holy Guru endowed with the right qualities, who removes all doubts and grants knowledge, one should not seek another Guru. [Verse 130]<-

Having once obtained a Guru who is endowed with the necessary features, who cuts asunder all doubts and gives knowledge excellently, one should not resort to another.

->If one has found a Guru who is ignorant and always causes doubt, there is no fault in going to another Guru. [Verse 131]<-

But if one has a Guru who does not possess the knowledge and always creates doubt, there is no blemish attached to resorting to another Guru.

->Just as a bee greedy for honey goes from flower to flower, so the disciple eager for knowledge goes from Guru to Guru. [Verse 132]<-

Like the bee greedy for honey going from flower to flower, the disciple eager for knowledge goes from Guru to Guru <note>this passage famously permits a seeker to seek higher wisdom from multiple teachers if the current one is insufficient</note>.

->Thus I have told you briefly the characteristics of the Guru and the disciple. O Queen of the Kula, what else do you wish to hear? [Verse 133]<-

Thus I have described to You in brief the characteristics of the Guru and the Disciples <note>original: "Shishyas"</note>. Now, O Queen of the Kula <note>original: "Kuleshani"</note>, what else do You want to hear?

->Thus in the holy Kularnava, the Gate to Nirvana and Liberation, the Great Secret, the highest of all traditions, the work of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, the thirteenth chapter titled "Characteristics of Guru and Disciple" in the fifth section of the Upper Tradition.<-

# Chapter Fourteen

->The Auspicious Goddess said:<-

->O Lord of the Family! I desire to hear about the testing of the teacher and the disciple. O Lord, tell me the sequence of instruction and the different kinds of tests. [Verse 1]<-

<note>The "Lord of the Family" (original: "Kuleśa") refers to Shiva as the head of the Kula, the spiritual community or lineage of the Tantric path.</note>

->The Lord spoke:<-

->Listen, O Goddess! I shall explain what you have asked of me. By merely hearing this, purification of the mind and heart occurs. [Verse 2]<-

->Without initiation, there can be no liberation; so it is said in the teachings of Shiva. And that initiation cannot occur without a master; such is the traditional lineage of masters. [Verse 3]<-

***No Liberation without Initiation and No Initiation without a Master:***

It has been laid down by Lord Shiva that there can be no <term>Liberation: Mokṣa, the release from the cycle of birth and death</term> without <term>Initiation: Dīkṣā, the formal ritual of spiritual awakening</term>, and this initiation cannot exist without a <term>Master: Ācārya, a teacher who establishes the rules of conduct</term>. This forms the traditional lineage of the masters.

->Therefore, after grasping the established doctrine through the traditional lineage and other means—for without an instructor, the sacred chants become fruitless. [Verse 4]<-

Therefore, after knowing the principles through the <term>Tradition: Sampradāya</term> and similar means, one should secure a teacher capable of giving internal instruction; otherwise, the <term>Sacred Chants: Mantras</term> would become ineffective.

->The gods praise only that teacher who promotes the traditional lineage, who is an expert in the sacred chants and scriptures, and who observes the traditional code of conduct. [Verse 5]<-

The <term>Devatās: the shining ones or divine beings</term> provide protection only to those teachers who are promoters of the lineage, who are well-versed in the sacred chants and <term>Āgamas: traditional scriptures</term>, and who strictly follow the <term>Samayācāra: the internal code of ethics and conduct of the lineage</term>.

<summary>This page introduces the fourteenth chapter, emphasizing that spiritual liberation is impossible without a formal initiation (Diksha) performed by a qualified teacher (Acharya) within a recognized lineage.</summary>
