# IN THE KULARNAVA TANTRA

->One should perform ritual actions only after knowing the goal, the practitioner, the specific act, the writing instrument, and the five ritual materials.<-
->One must also understand the proper location, the sacred diagram, and the correct measurements before attempting the work. (21)<-

Only after knowing the <term>Sādhya|The objective or person targeted by the ritual</term>, the <term>Sādhaka|The spiritual practitioner</term>, the <term>Karma|The specific ritual action</term>, the <term>Lekhanī|The ritual stylus or pen</term>, and the <term>Dravya|The physical materials</term>—these being the five essential elements—and also the place, the <term>Yantra|Sacred geometric diagram</term>, and the <term>Pramāṇa|Correct proportions or measurements</term>, should one engage in the ritual.

->Understand the origin, the mental impression, the color, the form, the consecration, and the arrangement.<-
->Only after knowing the dimensions of the fire-pit and the ritual materials should one perform the fire sacrifice. (22)<-

After knowing the <note>original: Utpatti</note> Origin, the <note>original: Vāsanā</note> Mental Impression, the <note>original: Varṇa</note> Color or Syllable, the <note>original: Mūrti</note> Form, the <note>original: Saṁskāra</note> Consecration, the <note>original: Saṁsthāna</note> Arrangement, the <term>Kuṇḍa|The specially shaped pit used for sacred fire</term>, and the quantity of the materials for the <term>Homa|The act of making offerings into a consecrated fire</term>, should one perform the sacrifice.

->Observe the glow of the fire, the color of the smoke, the sound, the scent, and the shape of the flames.<-
->By knowing these auspicious movements and signs, one should determine whether the result will be favorable or unfavorable. (23)<-

After knowing the color of the fire and smoke, the <note>original: Dhvani</note> Sound, the <note>original: Gandha</note> Scent, the <note>original: Śikhā</note> Flame, the various forms, and the auspicious actions, one should infer the positive or negative outcomes of the rite.

->Research the essence of the mantra and the signs of divine possession in the body.<-
->Knowing the distinctions in the pronunciation of the mantra, one should then accomplish the ritual acts. (24)<-

Based on a deep investigation into the <term>Mantra-tattva|The essential principle or science behind a sacred sound</term>, one should observe the symptoms of <term>Dehāveśa|The infusion of divine energy or a state of 'being possessed' by the mantra's power</term> and related signs. Only after mastering the specific nuances of how the Mantra is pronounced should the practitioner enter into the <term>Sādhanā|Disciplined spiritual practice</term>.

->Understand the sacred circle, the purification of the ritual jar and materials, and the eight scents.<-
->Knowing the process of initiation and the giving of the secret name, one should perform the initiation. (25)<-

After knowing the <term>Maṇḍala|The sacred circle or diagram</term>, the <term>Kalaśa|The ritual water pot representing the deity</term>, the <note>original: Dravya-śuddhi</note> purification of materials, the <term>Gandhāṣṭaka|A consecrated mixture of eight fragrant substances</term>, the <term>Dīkṣā|The formal initiation from teacher to student</term>, and the <note>original: Nāmakaraṇa</note> bestowing of a spiritual name, one should perform the ritual of initiation.

->Know the daily, occasional, and optional rites, the rules, and the mental contemplations.<-
->Knowing the method of worship and the diagrams to be meditated upon, one should perform the rituals. (26)<-

After knowing the <term>Nitya|Daily obligatory duties</term>, the <term>Naimittika|Occasional rites triggered by specific events</term>, and the <term>Kāmya|Optional rituals performed for a specific desired result</term>, as well as the <note>original: Niyamas</note> rules of conduct, the internal visualizations <note>original: Bhāvanās</note> of the Names, the method of worship, and the diagrams to be used in meditation, should the practitioner perform his spiritual work.

->Know the method for entering the house of worship and the characteristics of a traditional practitioner.<-
->Knowing the purification of the traditional ritual materials, one should perform the worship. (27)<-

After knowing the correct method for entering the shrine or place of worship, the characteristics of a practitioner of the <term>Kula|The 'Family' or tradition of Tantric practice</term>, and the method for purifying the <note>original: Kula-dravyas</note> traditional ritual substances, should one begin the worship.

### CHAPTER SIXTEEN

->Internal worship, external worship, the method of establishing the sacred vessel and the offering water,<-
->And the five handfuls of flowers—O Goddess, one should know these before performing ritual actions. (28)<-

One must understand <term>Antaryāga|Internal worship or meditation within the heart</term>, <term>Bahiryāga|External ritual worship with physical objects</term>, the method of establishing the <term>Ghaṭa|Sacred clay pot or vessel representing the deity</term> and the <term>Arghya-pātra|Vessel for the water used in welcoming a deity</term>, and also the method of the five <term>Puṣpāñjalis|Handfuls of flowers offered with devotion</term>. These should be mastered before starting the <term>Sādhanā|Systematic spiritual practice</term>.

->The ritual cup and its base, the nectar and the meat, the mystical divisions, the hand gestures, and the union of paths;<-
->The offerings to the guardian spirits—O Goddess, one should know these before performing ritual actions. (29)<-

One should perform the rituals only after knowing the <term>Pātra|Ritual cup</term>, its <term>Ādhāra|Base or stand</term>, the <term>Ali|Consecrated wine, often called nectar</term> (also known as <note>original: Madya</note>), the <term>Piśit|Meat offering</term> (also known as <note>original: Māṁsa</note>), the <term>Kalā|Mystical aspects or divisions of time and energy</term>, the <term>Mudrā|Sacred hand gestures or ritual snacks</term>, the <note>original: Adhva-melana</note> union of the ritual paths, and the method of offering oblations to <term>Baṭuka|The youthful guardian aspect of Shiva</term> and other protector spirits.

->The distinction between the Absolute and the Manifest, the signs of the spiritual partner,<-
->The auspicious marks, the purification and worship of the woman,<-
->And the sacred time of union—knowing these, one should accept a spiritual partner. (30)<-

After knowing the <note>original: Kula-akula</note> movements of the Absolute and the Manifest, the distinctions of the <term>Śakti|The female spiritual partner who embodies the Goddess</term>, the auspicious signs, the method of purifying a woman for ritual, the method of worship, and also the sacred timing of <note>original: Sambhoga</note> ritual union, should one adopt the Shakti.

->The varieties of drinking, the measure of the joy of the results, the signs of one’s state,<-
->The acceptance of the three principles—knowing these, one should drink the nectar of the Kula path. (31)<-

One should drink the <note>original: Kula-sudhā</note> sacred nectar only after knowing the distinctions of the ritual drinks, their spiritual fruits, the correct measures, the specific situations, the signs of <term>Ullāsa|The progressive stages of spiritual intoxication or joy</term>, and the method of accepting the three <term>Tattvas|Essential principles or elements</term>.

->Entering the circle, the bowing, the staying, and the departure, O Beloved!<-
->Knowing the behavior and movements of the Yoginis, one becomes a Kaulika. (32)<-

O My Beloved! After knowing the method of entering into the <term>Cakra|The sacred circle of initiates</term>, the formalities of salutations, and the etiquette of the circle—meaning the norms of behavior within it, how to stay, and how to depart—and understanding the actions of the <term>Yoginīs|Semi-divine female spirits or highly realized female practitioners</term>, does one truly become a <term>Kaulika|A follower of the Kula path</term>.

->The time of the exhilaration of union, the offering of the Kula lamp,<-
->And the reading of the hymns of peace—knowing these, one becomes a Master of the Kula. (33)<-

The timing for the joy of <note>original: Rati</note> union, the submission of the <note>original: Kuladīpaka</note> ritual lamp, and the method of reciting the pacificatory praises—after knowing all these, one becomes a <term>Kuladeśika|A teacher or guru of the Kula tradition</term>.

->The blessing of the ritual couple, the worship of the sixty-four and the maiden,<-
->And the worship on special dates—knowing these, one should perform the ritual actions. (34)<-

The <note>original: Anugrahas</note> blessings of the <note>original: Mithuna</note> ritual couple, the <note>original: Aṣṭāṣṭa-pūjana</note> worship of the sixty-four (eight times eight) deities, the worship of the <note>original: Puṣpiṇī Kumārī</note> maiden, and the various kinds of worship performed on special lunar days—all these must be known before beginning the practice.

->One must know the distinctions of the sacred traditions, the secret signs, the ritual contraction of flowers, the three lineages of teachers, and the specific spiritual tradition before performing ritual actions. (35)<-

A practitioner should only begin their <term>Sādhanā|Systematic spiritual practice</term> after mastering several advanced concepts: the <term>Āmnāyas|The various regional or elemental "buckets" of Tantric tradition</term>, the <term>Saṁketa|Secret codes or symbols used between initiates</term>, the <term>Puṣpa-saṁkoca|A specific ritual technique involving the "contraction" or offering of flowers</term>, the <term>Gurutraya|The three-fold lineage of Gurus (the individual Guru, their Guru, and the Supreme Guru)</term>, and the particular <note>original: Sampradāya</note> Sect or tradition to which they belong.

->O Goddess, one should know the sacred Vedic knowledge, the Kula conduct, the various types of mantras, the lineage of the sacred sandals, and the three sacred lines of descent before performing ritual actions. (36)<-

Before starting the practice, one must understand <term>Śrauta-vidyā|Knowledge derived from the Vedas</term>, the <term>Kulācāra|The specific code of conduct for the Kula path</term>, the variations in mantras (<note>original: Manu-bheda</note>), the <term>Pādukā|Literally "sandals," referring to the spiritual power and lineage of the Guru</term>, and the <term>Caraṇa-tritaya|The three "feet" or lineages of the tradition</term>.

->After knowing the sequence of Kula worship for those of greater, equal, or lesser status, and knowing the perfected gestures and icon worship, one should engage in the practice. (37)<-

One must understand the <term>Kaulika|Relating to the Kula or family of practitioners</term> order of worship, specifically how to treat those with more or less experience/initiation than oneself. Additionally, one must master the <term>Siddha-mudrā|Perfected ritual hand gestures</term> and the worship of <term>Arcā|Sacred images or icons</term>.

->After knowing the rites for the Guru's fire, the sacraments for the deceased, the final obsequies, the offerings to the directions, and the ritual of the Lamp of Liberation, one should perform ritual actions. (38)<-

The practitioner is expected to know the rites for the <term>Kulāgni|The sacred fire of the Kula lineage</term>, the <term>Preta Saṁskāra|Sacraments for the newly departed</term>, the <term>Antyeṣṭhi|Final funeral rites</term>, the <term>Digbali|Offerings made to the guardians of the cardinal directions</term>, and the <term>Mokṣadīpa|The "Lamp of Liberation" ritual</term>.

->These are some of the special matters that have been described, O Queen of the Kula. However, the procedural order for all mantras follows a universal method. (39)<-

O <note>original: Kulanāyikā</note> Leader of the Kula! While these are specific requirements, there is a general, universal method that applies to the practice of all mantras.

->**The Sex-differentiation of the Mantras:**<-

->The Mantras of male deities are masculine, and those of "Vidyas" are feminine, my dear.<-
->Masculine mantras end in the sounds "Hum" or "Phat"; they awaken when the life-breath moves through the right nostril.<-
->Feminine mantras (Vidyas) end in the sound "Svaha," my dear; they awaken when the life-breath moves through the left nostril.<-
->Those ending in the sound "Namah" are considered neuter; they are active when the life-breath moves through both nostrils. When the breath flows through both channels, all mantras reach a state of awakening. (40-41)<-

In Tantra, mantras are not just words but energetic beings with "gender." Masculine <term>Mantras|Usually associated with male aspects of the divine</term> are linked to the <term>Piṅgalā|The solar energy channel on the right side of the body</term>. Feminine <term>Vidyās|Knowledge-mantras associated with Goddesses</term> are linked to the <term>Iḍā|The lunar energy channel on the left side of the body</term>. Neuter mantras, ending in "Namah" (I bow), are linked to the balanced state of the <term>Prāṇa|Life-breath or vital energy</term> flowing through the central channel.

<header>SIXTEENTH CHAPTER 265</header>

Gentle mantras are used in rituals of peace. They are mostly composed of moon-like, "nectar-essence" letters. They end with the word <term>Svāhā|An exclamation used when offering oblations to the gods</term> and are generally associated with the element of space, while fiery mantras are used in cruel or aggressive acts. (42)

The syllable <term>Phaṭ|A "weapon" syllable used to shatter obstacles</term> is used for prosperity; <term>Vaṣaṭ|An exclamation used to direct power</term> for subjugation; <term>Huṁ Phaṭ|A fierce combination of sounds</term> for the act of killing. <term>Namaḥ|An expression of surrender or bowing</term> is prescribed for immobilization, and <term>Svāhā</term> is used for both peaceful and fortifying rituals. (43)

### *Difference of Mantras on the basis of the Desired ends :*

Gentle (<note>original: Saumya</note>) Mantras are used in the pacificatory rituals. The letters of such Mantras are, so to say, full of the essence of nectar (<note>original: Amṛta-tattva</note>), and at the end of these Mantras comes **Svāhā**. In cruel rituals, the Fiery (<note>original: Āgneya</note>) Mantras are used. In rituals for prosperity, **Phaṭ** Mantras are used; in captivating rituals, **Vaṣaṭ** Mantras; in rituals for inflicting death on the enemy, **Huṁ Phaṭ** Mantras; in immobilization rituals, **Namaḥ** Mantras; and in pacificatory rituals, the **Svāhā** Mantras are used.

For fire-offerings and water-libations, use **Svāhā**; for the ritual placement of mantras on the body and for general worship, use **Namaḥ**. The practitioner should join these to the end of the mantra as required by the circumstances during the period of meditative recitation. (44)

In fire-offerings (<note>original: Homa</note>) and water-libations (<note>original: Tarpaṇa</note>), **Svāhā** should be used, and in the ritual charging of the body (<note>original: Nyāsa</note>) and worship (<note>original: Pūjana</note>), **Namaḥ** should be used at the end of a Mantra as required by the circumstances during the period of recitation (<note>original: Japa</note>).

For peaceful rituals, use silver or copper; for subjugation rituals, use birch-bark. Gold leaves may be used for all types of rituals. For cruel rituals, a shroud from a corpse is prescribed. (45)

Silver and copper plates have been prescribed in the pacificatory rituals. In captivating rituals, one should use birch-bark (<note>original: Bhūrja-patra</note>), while gold leaves can be used in all types of rituals. For cruel rituals, a shroud (<note>original: Preta-karpaṭa</note>) is prescribed.

The "three-fragrances" are prescribed for peaceful rituals, and the "five-fragrances" for subjugation. For all purposes, use the "eight-fragrances," but for cruel rituals, use the "eight-poisons." (46)

Three fragrances (<note>original: Tri-gandhā</note>) in pacificatory rituals, five fragrances (<note>original: pañca-gandha</note>) in captivating rituals, eight fragrances (<note>original: Aṣṭagandha</note>) in all types of rituals, and eight poisons (<note>original: Aṣṭa-viṣas</note>) in cruel rituals are prescribed.

For peaceful rituals, the pen should be made of Durva grass; for subjugation and similar acts, a peacock's tail-feather. Gold may be used for all purposes, but for cruel rituals, it must be a crow's tail-feather. (47)

One should use a pen of <term>Dūrvā|A sacred grass, Panicum dactylon</term> in pacificatory rituals, of a peacock's tail-feather in captivating rituals, of gold in all types of rituals, and of a crow's tail-feather in cruel rituals.

A peaceful ritual should be performed in one's own home; a subjugation ritual in the temple of the Goddess Candika. All types of rituals may be done in the temple of a deity, but a cruel ritual must be done in a cremation ground. (48)

It is prescribed to perform pacificatory rituals in one's own house, captivating rituals in the temple of the goddess <term>Caṇḍikā|A fierce form of the Divine Mother</term>, all types of rituals in the temple of a Deity, and the cruel rituals in a cremation ground.

->Having learned these signs and others from the mouth of the <term>Guru|A spiritual teacher and initiator</term>, O Beloved, the practitioner of mantras should perform all rituals to attain their respective fruits. (49)<-

Knowing all these characteristics from the mouth of a Guru, O My Beloved, one should perform the respective rituals for the attainment of their fruits.

### *Meditations for various rituals:*

->In the <term>Mūlādhāra|The root energy center located at the base of the spine</term>, one should contemplate the <term>Prāsāda-bīja|The "palace" seed-syllable (Hauṁ), representing the seat of the deity</term>, which shines like the rising sun. In the crown of the head, one should contemplate the <term>Parā-bīja|The supreme seed-syllable (Sauḥ), representing the Goddess</term>, which has the brilliance of ten thousand moons. (50)<-
->Filled with the bliss born from the contact between these two, one perceives a continuous form stretching from the root center to the <term>Brahmarandhra|The 'aperture of the Creator' at the top of the head</term>. (51)<-
->One should constantly imagine themselves being drenched from head to foot by the sprinkling of this supreme nectar-essence (<note>original: Parāmṛta-rasa</note>); such a person becomes ageless and immortal. (52)<-
->By meditating in this way, O <term>Kuleśāni|Lady of the Kula lineage; a title for the Goddess</term>, one should accomplish all rituals. O Goddess, success comes swiftly; of this, there is no need for further consideration. (53)<-

*Meditations for various rituals :*

Contemplating in the root center the "palace" seed-syllable, luminous as the young Sun, and in the head the supreme seed-syllable of the brilliance of millions of Moons, one who experiences the exhilaration of the Bliss originating out of the mutual contact of these two, and thus feels completely drenched from head to feet by the supreme nectar-essence, continuously flowing from the root center to the aperture of the crown, becomes immortal and remains perpetually young. O Lady of the Kula ! contemplating thus one who performs <term>Sādhanā|Disciplined spiritual practice</term> of all the rituals, soon obtains the fructification of all his desires—there is no doubt about it.

### *Pure Meditation and its Fruits:*

->I shall now speak of the different types of meditation that grant all success, O Beloved, through which one obtains what is desired even without <term>Pūjā|Ritual worship</term> or <term>Homa|Fire sacrifice</term>, etc. (54)<-

*Pure (<note>original: Sāttvika</note>) Meditation and its Fruits :*

O My Beloved ! I shall now tell the distinctions of all–fructifying meditation from which one can get the desired fruits even without ritual worship and fire sacrifice, etc.

->In a beautiful place, O Goddess, the practitioner with a steady mind, sitting in the <term>Bhadrāsana|The "auspicious" yoga posture</term>, should meditate after first saluting the spiritual teacher. (55)<-
->Within the circle of the full moon located in the head, one finds the sacred supreme "palace" seed-syllables joined with the sixteen vowels. (56)<-
->O Beloved, this is as white as pure crystal, camphor, the jasmine flower, or the moon; the body becomes flooded with the nectar produced from that very lunar orb. (57)<-

It emphasizes that these meditations are so powerful they can replace external worship like fire sacrifices.</summary>

*Tāmasa Dhyāna and its Fruit:*
<note>Tāmasa Dhyāna refers to "dark" or "heavy" meditation. In this context, it often relates to rituals that deal with the material world, protection, or the removal of heavy karmic obstacles.</note>

"Constructing a Triangle, a hexagon, an octagon and a Bhūpura, one should, in its centre, write the Mūla Mantra along with the name of the Sādhya (name of a thing or person desired)."

"Bone, blood, veins, fibers, earth, flesh, blood-water, skin, cloth, stone, tortoise-shell, coconut-fruit, or a skull <note>These materials are used to represent the physical elements of the body or are used as the material for the ritual vessel itself in specific Tāmasa rites</note>. One should worship the Deity of the Jar, who is joined with the life-force of the mantra." (85-86)

"Worship the solar goddess Savitri, the secondary limbs, and the Mother-goddesses accompanied by the <term>Bhairavas|Fierce, protective forms of Shiva</term>. In the intermediate directions, O Beloved, one should worship the Teacher, the Lord of Obstacles <note>Ganesha</note>, Durga, and the Lord of the Field. Having worshiped them in the jars according to the rules, the most excellent knower of mantras should sprinkle the beloved disciple to pacify all sins." (87-88)

Sacred materials include the Sacred Fig (*Ficus religiosa*), the White Fig (*Ficus infectoria*), the Chaff-flower (*Achyranthes aspera*), white lotus and other white substances, fruits, edibles, rice boiled in milk with sugar, the <term>Three Sweets|Madhura-traya</term> <note>A traditional ritual mixture of sugar, honey, and clarified butter</note>, or rice and sesame seeds mixed in <term>wine|Surā</term>.

All ailments—including hysteria, epilepsy, <term>consumption|Yaksma</term> <note>historically identified with pulmonary tuberculosis</note>, and various other troubles—are undoubtedly driven away by this ritual immediately. O My Beloved! Through this practice, one obtains all forms of peace, spiritual knowledge, and learning.

Whether residing in a sacred pilgrimage site or a profane place, or even dwelling within the waters, one who knows the <term>Para-prasada Mantra|the supreme mantra of the inner temple</term> is surely liberated; of this there is no doubt. (117)

<note>The Para-prasada Mantra refers to the "Hamsa" or breath-mantra, considered the highest path to liberation.</note>

O Parvati! One should first understand the directions, the <term>Pithas|sacred seats of power</term>, the holy fields, the <term>Mudras|ritual hand gestures</term>, as well as the specific trees, creepers, and <term>Mathas|monasteries</term>. One must also know the <term>Bhairavas|fierce manifestations of Shiva</term> and the Goddesses belonging to the <term>Urdhvamnaya|the upper or celestial lineage of Tantric tradition</term>. (118)

->*Methods of causing enmity, aversion and death:*<-

Using <term>Nimb|the Neem tree</term> <note>original: Azadirachta Indica</note>, <term>Karaskara|the poisonous strychnine tree</term>, <term>Unmatta|the thorn apple plant</term> <note>original: Pterospermum acerifolium; however, in most Tantric contexts, Unmatta refers to the hallucinogenic Datura</note>, various thorny plants, the tooth of a priest, bones, and other inauspicious materials; or using black ritual pellets, specific fuels, leaves, and fruits—all these combined with soot from the kitchen, embers from a funeral pyre, and a collyrium made of <term>Trikatu|the "three bitters"</term> <note>original: a mixture of black pepper, long pepper, and dried ginger</note> and funeral ash. (119-120)

These should be thoroughly soaked in the juice of the <term>Unmatta</term> plant and ground into a paste. Taking this mixture along with the dust from the footprints of the <term>Sadhya|the target of the ritual</term> and ashes from a cremation ground, one should fashion an effigy of the target. (121)

This likeness of the target should be made from the wood of a tree associated with the person’s birth star. After performing the rite to "infuse life" into the image, the practitioner should hang it over the sacrificial pit. (122)

The practitioner, with a darkened mind, a fierce gaze, and filled with wrath, should then bury that image beneath the sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rules. (123)

In a fire kindled with wood from poisonous trees and seven types of wood from a funeral pyre, the one most skilled in <term>Mantras|sacred sound formulas</term> should offer those aforementioned materials into the flames. (124)

By doing so, one will undoubtedly achieve the effects of <term>Vidveshana|causing enmity</term>, <term>Ucchatana|expulsion or causing someone to flee</term>, and <term>Marana|death</term>.

This model <note>likely referring to an effigy or ritual diagram</note> should be buried under the firepit. It is as brilliant as the fire of the final cosmic dissolution. (129)

->*Method of destroying those causing injury:*<-

Surrounded in reverse order by the ten "pervading" letters, the practitioner himself—becoming like the fire of time and appearing terrifying to all beings—should face the South. With an extremely fierce gaze and a face darkened by soot, filled with the exuberance of youth, he should perform one thousand and eight <term>Japas|meditative repetitions</term> of the mantra group called <term>Para-prasada</term>. (130-131)

### Sixteenth Chapter
**277**

One should contemplate all injurious beings, those who cause strife and exhaustion, [132] those who harbor groundless hatred, the cruel ones, and those who obstruct worship; evil spirits, secondary planetary spirits, goblins, ghosts, nature spirits <note>original: "Yakṣas"</note>, demonic beings <note>original: "Rākṣasas"</note>, [133] and all other such wicked creatures who always cause supreme suffering. One should imagine them falling into the middle of that fire and being thrice-burned. In an instant, they go to their destruction, just like moths in a flame. [134]

In whose head one contemplates the <term>Bīja|a "seed-syllable" or sacred sound representing the essence of a particular power or deity</term>, that person meets with death. O Queen of the Gods <note>original: "Deveśi"</note>! Through this meditation, one may even destroy Time and Death itself <note>original: "Kāla"</note>. [135]

O Beloved! Thus I have told you briefly the rules regarding <term>Kamya-karma|rituals performed to achieve specific worldly or spiritual desires, often involving specialized or magical objectives</term>. O Queen of the Kula lineage <note>original: "Kuleśānī"</note>! What more do you wish to hear? [136]

->Thus, in the glorious **Kularnava Tantra**,<-
->the gateway to **Nirvana** <note>ultimate liberation or "extinction" of the ego</note> and liberation, the Great Mystery,<-
->the most excellent of all scriptures, consisting of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses,<-
->in the fifth section of the **Urdhvamnaya Tantra** <note>the "Upper Tradition" or highest lineage of teaching</note>,<-
->is the Sixteenth Chapter, named:<-
->**The Rules for Rituals for Desired Objectives.**<-

# Seventeenth Chapter

->The Resplendent Goddess said:<-

O Lord of the Kula! <note>original: "Kuleśa," referring to the head of the spiritual lineage or family</note> I desire to hear about the spiritual significance <note>original: "vasana," meaning the underlying impression or contemplation</note> of the Guru's name and other details. O Supreme Lord! Tell me the essential truth regarding the ritual substances <note>original: "kula-dravyas," the specialized offerings used in Tantric worship</note> of the Kula tradition. [1]

->The Lord said:<-

Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim to You that which You have asked of me. By the mere hearing of this, the wisdom of the Kula tradition <note>the path of the "family" or totality of spiritual forces</note> is made manifest. [2]

**A Prayer to the Divine Teacher**

Salutations to You, O Lord, O Divine One! You are the Auspicious <note>original: "Shiva"</note> appearing in the form of the Teacher <note>original: "Guru"</note>. You have accepted many different physical forms for the purpose of the manifestation and perfect fulfillment of the descent of sacred knowledge. [3]

You are the embodiment of the All-Pervading One <note>original: "Narayana"</note> and the Supreme Soul. You are the Sun that pierces the darkness of all ignorance with the light of knowledge, O Master of the Perfected Ones <note>original: "Siddhanatha"</note>! [4]

You are all-knowing, Your form is fashioned out of mercy, and You are the very soul of the Auspicious. You are the one who grants well-being to Your devoted followers in this world and the world to come. [5]

I offer my salutations to You in front, at Your sides, at Your back, above, and below. You who exist eternally as **Truth and Pure Consciousness** <note>original: "Sat-Cit"</note>, please grant that I may always remain Your servant. [6]

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter (Saptadaśa Ullāsaḥ) of the Kularnava Tantra. It provides the esoteric etymologies for the titles of spiritual teachers—Guru, Ācārya, and Ārādhya—explaining how their names reflect their divine functions and internal realizations.</meta>

# Seventeenth Chapter

### The Definition of a Teacher

The syllable *Gu* signifies darkness; the syllable *ru* signifies the one who restrains it. Because he restrains the darkness of ignorance, he is called the *Guru*. [7]
<note>This is a classic etymology in Indian traditions, where the teacher is literally the "dispeller of darkness."</note>

->**Contemplation of the Names of the Guru and Others**<-

***Guru:***
The letter *Ga* is said to be the giver of fulfillment <note>original: "siddhida"</note>; the letter *Ra* <note>original: "repha," the technical term for the 'r' sound</note> burns away sin; the letter *U* is said to be the Preserver <note>original: "Vishnu"</note>. The Supreme Teacher is the very soul of these three combined. [8]

The letter *Ga* signifies the wealth of knowledge; the letter *Ra* is the illuminator of that knowledge; the letter *U* signifies identity with the Auspicious <note>original: "Shiva"</note>. He who contains these qualities within himself is called the *Guru*. [9]

Because he brings understanding to those who are bound and blinded to the Truth of the Self and the secret sacred traditions <note>original: "guhyāgama," the hidden tantric scriptures</note>, and because he takes the form of the gods such as the Roarer <note>original: "Rudra," a fierce and transformative form of Shiva</note>, he is called the *Guru*. [10]

***Ācārya (The Preceptor):***
He conducts himself <note>original: "ācarate"</note> according to the Norms of Truth, establishes his disciples in those same standards of conduct <note>original: "ācāra"</note>, and gathers together <note>original: "ācinoti"</note> the various meanings of the sacred scriptures <note>original: "shastras"</note>; therefore, he is called the *Ācārya*. [11]

He who personally teaches all that comes to him, whether moving or unmoving <note>original: "carācara," meaning all of creation</note>, and who has achieved perfection in the yogic path of self-restraint <note>original: "yama"</note> and other disciplines, is called the *Ācārya*. [12]

***Ārādhya (The Adorable One):***
Because he grants the consciousness of the Self <note>original: "ātmabhāva"</note>, because he has rejected all likes and dislikes <note>original: "rāgadveṣa"</note>, and because his mind is centered solely in meditation <note>original: "dhyāna"</note>, he is called the *Ārādhya*. [13]

<vocab>
**Guru**: Spiritual teacher / dispeller of darkness.
**Ācārya**: Preceptor or spiritual guide who leads by example.
**Ārādhya**: An adorable or worshipful teacher.
**Guhya**: Secret or hidden.
**Ācarate**: To practice or conduct oneself.
**Ācinoti**: To collect or assemble knowledge.
**Ācāra**: Conduct, custom, or established rule.
**Carācara**: The world of moving and unmoving beings.
**Yama**: The first limb of Yoga, involving moral restraints.
**Ātmabhāva**: The state or feeling of the Self.
**Rāgadveṣa**: Attachment and aversion (likes and dislikes).
**Dhyāna**: Meditation.
**Viṣṇu**: The Pervader / Preserver of the universe.
**Śiva**: The Auspicious One.
**Rudra**: The Howler / a fierce form of the Divine.
**Śāstra**: Sacred scripture or systematic treatise.
</vocab>

# In the Kularnava Tantra

->Because he assumes the form of the deity to bestow grace upon his disciples,<-
->and because he is the very embodiment of compassion, he is called the Guide, O Beloved. [14]<-

**The Guide** <note>original: "Deśika"</note>: O My Beloved! Because he wears the form of the deity <note>original: "devatā"</note>, because he bestows grace on the disciples, and because he is the embodiment of compassion <note>original: "karuṇā"</note>, he is called the Guide.

->Because his inner peace blossoms from contemplating the meaning of the Supreme Truth,<-
->and because he is free from false knowledge, he is called the Master, O Beloved. [15]<-

**The Master** <note>original: "Svāmī"</note>: Because he exudes his inner <note>original: "svānta"</note> peace and deliberates on the supreme truth, and because he is devoid of false understandings <note>original: "mithyājñānas"</note>, he is called the Master.

->Because he is distant from mental defects and rejects dry intellectual arguments,<-
->because he sees himself even in creatures like dogs, and because he is delightful, he is the Great Lord. [16]<-

**The Great Lord** <note>original: "Maheśvara"</note>: Because he is devoid of the blemishes of the mind <note>original: "manodoṣa"</note>, such as ego and desire; because he rejects dry logic and circular arguments <note>original: "hetuvāda"</note>, because of his likeness to—or equanimity toward—all creatures including dogs <note>original: "śvādi"; this implies the teacher sees the same divine spark in all life, high or low</note>, and because he is pleasing <note>original: "ramya"</note>, he is called the Great Lord.

->Because he gives the knowledge of liberation and divine splendor, and awakens the soul to the Eternal Absolute,<-
->and because he pierces the veil of ignorance, he is called the Auspicious Lord, O Beloved. [17]<-

**The Auspicious Lord** <note>original: "Śrīnātha"</note>: Because he imparts the knowledge of prosperity <note>original: "śrī"</note> and liberation, because he instructs on the Eternal Sound of the Absolute <note>original: "Nāda Brahman"</note> and the Self, and because he is the one who cuts through the concealment <note>original: "sthagita"</note> of Ignorance, he is, O My Beloved, called the Auspicious Lord.

->Because he exists within the Sacred Tradition without conflict regarding space or time,<-
->and because he has mastered the world and all living beings, he is called the Divine. [18]<-

**The Divine** <note>original: "Deva"</note>: Because he transcends the limits of space and time <note>original: "deśa-kāla"</note> while following the Sacred Tradition <note>original: "Kulāgama"</note>, and because he has acquired mastery <note>original: "vaśīkṛta"</note> over the world and the individual soul <note>original: "jīva"</note>, he is called the Divine.

->Because he pacifies the bonds of worldly life, and bears the crescent moon on his head,<-
->and because of his protection and charm, he is called the Venerable One. [19]<-

**The Venerable One** <note>original: "Bhaṭṭāraka"</note>: Because he removes the bonds of worldly existence <note>original: "bhava"</note>, because he bears the moon of the form of the letter 'ṭa' <note>original: "ṭaṅkāra-indu"; 'ṭa' is traditionally associated with a circular or crescent shape in tantric iconography</note> upon his head, because he protects <note>original: "rakṣaṇa"</note> and is charming <note>original: "kamanīya"</note>, he is called the Venerable One.

->Because he contemplates the hidden meanings of the well-guarded scriptures and the end of knowledge,<-
->and because he grants both worldly enjoyment and spiritual liberation, he is called the Sovereign. [20]<-

**The Sovereign** <note>original: "Prabhu"</note>: Because he deliberates upon the knowledge of the mystic intent of the end of knowledge <note>original: "Vedānta"</note> and the Sacred Traditions <note>original: "Āgamas"</note> which are well-guarded <note>original: "pragupta"</note>, and because he grants both enjoyment <note>original: "bhukti"</note> and liberation <note>original: "mukti"</note>, he is called the Sovereign.

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter of the Kularnava Tantra, which provides esoteric etymologies for the various titles of a realized spiritual teacher. Having previously defined the Guide (Desika) and the Master (Svami), the text now explains the meanings behind terms like Yogi, Ascetic, and the Kaulika practitioner.</meta>

# Chapter Seventeen

->Through the contemplation of the womb-gesture, and by the throbbing glory of sacred sound,<-
->he is adorable to the host of the gods; thus, O Beloved, he is called a Yogi. [21]<-

**The Yogi**: O My Beloved! Because he vibrates with the majesty of the sacred mantra through the practice of the womb-gesture <note>original: "yoni-mudrā"; a ritual hand position or internal practice representing the source of creation</note>, and because he is worthy of worship by the assembly of divine beings <note>original: "gīrvāṇa gaṇa"</note>, he is called a **Yogi**.

->By renouncing the misery of attachment, and by dwelling in any stage of life,<-
->by binding himself to the Self in solitude, he is known as the Self-Controlled. [22]<-

**The Self-Controlled** <note>original: "Saṃyamī"</note>: Because he rejects the suffering caused by worldly attachment <note>original: "saṅga-duḥkha"</note>, because he is indifferent to whichever stage of life <note>original: "āśrama"; referring to the four traditional stages: student, householder, forest-dweller, or monk</note> he may find himself in, and because he fastens his mind to the inner Self in private contemplation, he is called **Saṃyamī**.

->By leading his vision toward the true nature of reality, and by avoiding all slander,<-
->by accepting all auspicious works, he is known as the Ascetic. [23]<-

**The Ascetic** <note>original: "Tapasvī"</note>: Because he focuses his mind upon the true nature of Reality <note>original: "tattva"</note>, because he shuns all forms of gossip or censure <note>original: "parivāda"</note>, and because he embraces <note>original: "svīkāra"</note> only those actions that are spiritually beneficial, he is called **Tapasvī**.

->Because he is eternal and excellent, having shaken off the bonds of the world,<-
->and because he has realized "You are That," he is called the Liberated. [24]<-

**The Liberated** <note>original: "Avadhūta"</note>: Because he is immutable <note>original: "akṣara"</note> and supreme, because he has shaken off <note>original: "dhūta"</note> the chains of worldly existence, and because he has realized the ultimate truth of the great saying "You are That" <note>original: "Tat Tvam Asi"; the realization that the individual soul and the Divine are one</note>, he is called **Avadhūta**.

->Free from passion, pride, suffering, anger, envy, and delusion,<-
->and far removed from restlessness and inertia, he is called the Hero. [25]<-

**The Hero** <note>original: "Vīra"; the Sanskrit verse also suggests "Dhīra," the steadfast</note>: Because he is free from passion <note>original: "rāga"</note>, intoxication, affliction, anger, jealousy, and delusion, and because he is far beyond the qualities of restlessness <note>original: "rajas"</note> and dullness or inertia <note>original: "tamas"</note>, he is called **Vīra**.

->The Family is known as the lineage born of Power and the Absolute.<-
->He who knows that liberation comes from this Family is called a Kaulika. [26]<-

**The Kaulika**: The "Family" <note>original: "Kula"</note> is defined as the group or totality born of the union between Divine Power <note>original: "Śakti"</note> and the Absolute <note>original: "Śiva"</note>. One who possesses the knowledge that true liberation comes from this spiritual Family is called a **Kaulika**.

->The "Beyond" is the Absolute, and the "Family" is the Divine Power.<-
->Those expert in the contemplation of both are the Kaulikas, O Beloved. [27]<-

**Kula** is the Divine Power <note>original: "Śakti"</note>, while the **Beyond** <note>original: "Akula"</note> is the Absolute <note>original: "Śiva"</note>. O My Beloved, those who are proficient in the constant meditation on the union of both the manifest Power and the unmanifest Absolute are the **Kaulikas**.

<summary>This page defines various titles for an advanced spiritual practitioner—such as Yogi, Avadhuta, and Kaulika—using esoteric etymologies that link their character traits to the realization of non-dual consciousness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter of the Kularnava Tantra, continuing the series of esoteric etymologies for spiritual titles. # In the Kularnava Tantra

->Because he gathers the essence, and because he sets forth on the path of righteousness,<-
->and because he restrains the assembly of the senses, he is called a Practitioner. [28]<-

**The Practitioner** <note>original: "Sādhaka"</note>: Because he gathers the essence <note>original: "sāra"</note>, because he treads the path of righteous duty <note>original: "dharma"</note>, and because he controls the entire collection of his active senses <note>original: "karaṇagrāma"</note>, he is called a **Sādhaka**.

->Through adoration with supreme devotion, by mind, speech, body, and action,<-
->he crosses over all miseries; therefore, he is called a Devotee. [29]<-

**The Devotee** <note>original: "Bhakta"</note>: Because of his adoration <note>original: "bhajanāt"</note> performed with supreme devotion through his mind, speech, body, and actions <note>original: "kāyakarmabhiḥ"</note>, he crosses over <note>original: "tarati"</note> all worldly miseries; thus, he is spoken of as a **Bhakta**.

->He who, having offered his body, wealth, and life-breaths to the true Teacher,<-
->learns Yoga from that Teacher, is called a Disciple. [30]<-

**The Disciple** <note>original: "Śiṣya"</note>: One who dedicates his physical body, his wealth, and his very life-forces <note>original: "prāṇas"</note> to the holy Guru, and learns <note>original: "śikṣate"</note> the science of union <note>original: "yoga"</note> from the Teacher, is called a **Śiṣya**.

->Through the contemplation of the womb-gesture, and by serving the feet of the Mountain-Born Goddess,<-
->and from the glory of dissolving all worldly attributes, she is called a Female Yogi. [31]<-

**The Female Yogi** <note>original: "Yoginī"</note>: Because she practices the womb-gesture <note>original: "yoni-mudrā"; a ritual hand position or internal practice representing the source of creation</note>, serves at the feet of *Girijā* <note>the "Mountain-Born," a name for the Divine Mother Parvati</note>, and because of the splendor of her total immersion into the Absolute without any limiting conditions <note>original: "nirlīnopādhi"</note>, she is called a **Yoginī**.

->Because she is the cause of joy for a billion great divine female spirits,<-
->and because she grants swift liberation, she is called Power. [32]<-

**The Power** <note>original: "Śakti"</note>: Because she is dear to a hundred <note>original: "śata"</note> crores <note>a crore is ten million, thus a billion total</note> of the great divine *Yoginī* deities, and because she bestows rapid liberation <note>original: "tīvramukti"</note>, she is called **Śakti**.

->Because it protects, because it severs misfortune, and increases what is desired,<-
->it is known as the Footwear; this is My reality, O Beloved! [33]<-

**The Sacred Footwear** <note>original: "Pādukā"</note>: Because it provides protection <note>original: "pālanāt"</note> from the blows of misfortune, and causes the fulfillment of one's desires <note>original: "kāmitārtha"</note> to grow, it is known as the **Pādukā**, O My Beloved! This is My very essence. <note>In Tantra, the "Pādukā" often refers to the feet or sandals of the Guru, representing the transmission of grace.</note>

->By the destruction of sins committed in thousands of previous lives,<-
->and through the revelation of the Supreme Deity, it is called Recitation. [34]<-

**The Recitation** <note>original: "Japa"</note>: Because it destroys the sins accumulated over thousands of previous births <note>original: "janmāntara"</note>, and because it luminously reveals the Supreme Deity <note>original: "paradeva-prakāśāt"</note>, it is called **Japa**.

# Chapter Seventeen

->Because, little by little, it brings supreme joy to the mind,<-
->and because it ferries the singer across, O Goddess, it is called a Hymn. [35]<-

**The Hymn** <note>original: "Stotra"</note>: Because it brings delight to the mind bit by bit <note>original: "stokastokena"</note>, and because it carries <note>original: "santāraṇāt"</note> the person who offers praise <note>original: "stotṛ"</note> safely across the ocean of worldly existence, it is called a **Stotra**.

->Restraining the affliction of the senses by the power of the mind,<-
->contemplation of the chosen deity within the heart is called Meditation. [36]<-

**Meditation** <note>original: "Dhyāna"</note>: Controlling the pain and agitation of the senses through the mind, the steady contemplation by the inner being of one's chosen deity <note>original: "iṣṭa-devatā"</note> is called **Dhyāna**.

->Because of the unfolding of one’s life-purpose and because of protection, O Parvati,<-
->and because it takes the form of both man and woman, it is called the Way. [37]<-

**The Way** <note>original: "Caraṇa"</note>: Because it leads to the flowering <note>original: "vikāśāt"</note> of a successful life <note>original: "caritārtha"</note>, provides protection, and encompasses the nature of both the masculine and feminine <note>original: "nara-nārī-svarūpāt"</note>, it is known, O Beloved, as **Caraṇa**. <note>The term 'Caraṇa' can refer to the divine feet of the Guru or the Goddess, as well as the specific school or lineage of practice.</note>

->Because it reveals the meaning of all scriptures and defines the holy Law,<-
->and because it is the valid standard of all philosophies, it is called the Veda. [38]<-

**Sacred Knowledge** <note>original: "Veda"</note>: Because it determines the ultimate purpose of all communicated scriptures <note>original: "vedita-akhila-śāstrārtha"</note> and the nature of the holy Law <note>original: "dharma"</note>, and because it serves as the authoritative standard for all philosophical systems <note>original: "darśanas"</note>, it is called the **Veda**.

->By describing merit and sin and warding off demons and evils,<-
->and by generating ninefold devotion, it is called the Ancient Lore. [39]<-

**Ancient Lore** <note>original: "Purāṇa"</note>: Because it recounts the nature of merit and sin <note>original: "puṇyapāpa"</note>, protects against demonic forces <note>original: "rākṣasas"</note>, and inspires the nine forms of devotion <note>original: "navabhakti"</note>, it is called a **Purāṇa**. <note>Ninefold devotion refers to a classical list of practices: hearing, chanting, remembering, serving the feet, worshiping, bowing, servitude, friendship, and self-surrender.</note>

->Because it provides constant instruction to those living in the social orders,<-
->and saves them from all sins, it is called Scripture. [40]<-

**Scripture** <note>original: "Śāstra"</note>: Because it constantly provides guidance and commands <note>original: "śāsanāt"</note> for those living within the rules of social classes <note>original: "varṇa"</note> and stages of life <note>original: "āśrama"</note>, and because it rescues <note>original: "tāraṇāt"</note> the soul from all sins, it is called **Śāstra**.

->Because it defines Law and Lawlessness for those devoted to remembrance,<-
->and because it uproots the darkness of ignorance, O Goddess, it is called Tradition. [41]<-

**Tradition** <note>original: "Smṛti"</note>: Because it defines the nature of righteous duty <note>original: "dharma"</note> and unrighteousness <note>original: "adharma"</note> for those established in single-minded remembrance <note>original: "smaraṇa"</note>, and because it tears out the darkness <note>original: "timira"</note> of spiritual ignorance, it is called **Smṛti**.

# In the Kularnava Tantra

->Because it narrates the approved dharma and other duties,<-
->shatters the darkness of ignorance, and removes all miseries,<-
->it is remembered as History. [42]<-

**History** <note>original: "Itihāsa"</note>: Because it narrates of approved <note>original: "iṣṭa"</note> dharma <term>Dharma: the righteous path or duty</term> and other merits, breaks the darkness <note>original: "timira"</note> of ignorance, and removes <note>original: "haraṇāt"</note> all miseries, it is called **Itihāsa**.

->Because it narrates the course of conduct and the cause of attaining the divine goal,<-
->and because it speaks of the truth of the Great Soul, O Beloved, it is called the Revealed Tradition. [43]<-

**The Revealed Tradition** <note>original: "Āgama"</note>: Because it narrates the course of conduct <note>original: "ācāra"</note> with a view to arrive at the godly goal <note>original: "divyagati"</note>, and because it speaks of the truth of the Great Soul <note>original: "mahātma"</note>, it is, O My Beloved, called **Āgama**.

->Because he is adorable by the hosts of Shakinis,<-
->carries one across the ocean of worldly existence,<-
->and is in the presence of the Supreme Primal Power, he is called a Shakta. [44]<-

**The Shakta** <note>original: "Śākta"</note>: Because he is adorable by the hosts of **Shakinis** <note>Shakinis are a class of female spirits or yoginis who serve the Goddess</note>, because he carries the seeker across <note>original: "tāraṇā"</note> the ocean of life, and because of the presence of the Supreme, Primal Power <note>original: "Parā-ādi-Śakti"</note>, he is called **Śākta**.

->Because it sets aside the usual stages of life starting with youth,<-
->destroys birth and dissolution, and because of its connection to the endless Family,<-
->it is known as the Path of Totality. [45]<-

**The Path of Totality** <note>original: "Kaula"</note>: Because it sets aside the usual stages of life beginning with youth <note>original: "kaumāra"</note>, destroys birth and death or dissolution <note>original: "layā"</note>, and because it is related to the **Kula** <note>original: "aśeṣa-kula"</note> without end, it is called **Kaula**. <note>In this tradition, "Kula" refers to the spiritual lineage or the totality of the divine manifest as the cosmic family.</note>

->Because it severs the bonds, O Goddess, and delights the Supreme Light,<-
->and because it is meditated upon by ascetics, it is called the Lineage. [46]<-

**The Lineage** <note>original: "Pāramparya"</note>: Because it severs the bonds <note>original: "pāśa"</note> <note>These "bonds" are the fetters of ego, desire, and ignorance that bind the soul.</note>, because it delights <note>original: "rañjanāt"</note> the supreme Light <note>original: "paratejasaḥ"</note>, and because it is meditated upon by ascetics <note>original: "yatibhiḥ"</note>, it is called **Pāramparya**.

->Because it is the essence of worldly life, and yields both light and joy,<-
->and because it brings fame and good fortune, it is called the Tradition. [47]<-

**The Tradition** <note>original: "Sampradāya"</note>: Because it is the essence of life in the world <note>original: "saṃsāra"</note>, because it yields light and joy <note>original: "prakāśānanda-dānataḥ"</note>, and because it brings fame <note>original: "yaśas"</note> and good fortune, it is called **Sampradāya**.

->Because it is the premier of all paths, and increases the joy of the mind,<-
->and because it is the cause of dharma in the form of sacrifice, it is called the Sacred Lore. [48]<-

**The Sacred Lore** <note>original: "Āmnāya"</note>: Because it is the premier <note>original: "āditvāt"</note> among all paths, because it sets into movement a joy in the mind <note>original: "manollāsa"</note>, and because it is the cause of dharma in the form of sacrifice <note>original: "yajña"</note>, it is called **Āmnāya**.

# Chapter Seventeen

->Because he has heard many great mantras, instruments, scriptures, and deities,<-
->and because he remains unbroken in what he has heard, he is called One of the Sacred Hearing. [49]<-

**One of the Sacred Hearing** <note>original: "Śrauta"</note>: Because he has heard <note>original: "śruta"</note> several **Great Mantras** <term>Mahāmantra: a supreme sacred sound or chant</term>, **Yantras** <term>Yantra: a geometric diagram used for meditation and ritual</term>, **Tantras** <term>Tantra: a manual of ritual and spiritual discipline</term>, and **Deities** <note>original: "Devatā"</note>, and because his very being lives without interruption in what he has so heard, he is called **Śrauta**.

->Because it embodies the truth of the sacred tradition and explains the four-fold aim with skill,<-
->and because it calms attraction and aversion, it is celebrated as Conduct. [50]<-

**Conduct** <note>original: "Ācāra"</note>: Because it embodies the truth found in the **Sacred Traditions** <note>original: "Āmnāya"</note>, because it defines the truth with extraordinary skill <note>original: "cāturyārtha-nirūpaṇāt"</note>, and because it stills the waves of **attraction and aversion** <note>original: "rāgadveṣa"</note>, it is called **Ācāra**.

->Because it grants a divine state of being and washes away all sin,<-
->and because it releases one from the bonds of worldly existence, it is called Initiation. [51]<-

**Initiation** <note>original: "Dīkṣā"</note>: Because it bestows the **divine state of being** <note>original: "divyabhāva"</note>, washes away <note>original: "kṣālanāt"</note> sins, and liberates the seeker from the chains of worldly existence, it is called **Dīkṣā**.

->Because it removes the sense of 'I,' destroys fear, and involves sacred sprinkling,<-
->and because it produces trembling and bliss, it is remembered as Consecration. [52]<-

**Consecration** <note>original: "Abhiṣeka"</note>: Because it strips away the **ego or sense of 'I'** <note>original: "ahaṃbhāva"</note>, churns away all **fear** <note>original: "bhīti"</note>, involves the **sprinkling of holy water** <note>original: "secana"</note>, and triggers spiritual **trembling** <note>original: "kampa"</note> and supreme **bliss** <note>original: "ānanda"</note>, it is known as **Abhiṣeka**.

->Because it is intense and supreme, pleasing to the deity,<-
->and because it arises from the descent of power, it is remembered as Instruction. [53]<-

**Instruction** <note>original: "Upadeśa"</note>: Because it is **intense** <note>original: "ulvaṇa"</note>, **supreme** <note>original: "parā"</note>, and dear to the **deity** <note>original: "devatā"</note>, and because it is made possible by the **descent of spiritual power** <term>Śakti-pāta: the transmission of spiritual energy from guru to disciple</term>, it is called **Upadeśa**.

->Through meditation on the form of truth of the God of immeasurable light,<-
->it protects from every fear; therefore, it is called a Mantra. [54]<-

**Sacred Chant** <note>original: "Mantra"</note>: By **meditation** <note>original: "manana"</note> on the luminous Deity who is the very form of Truth, it **saves or protects** <note>original: "trāyate"</note> the practitioner from all fear; for this reason, it is called **Mantra**.

->O Pārvatī! Because it takes form in the bodies of the devoted and grants boons,<-
->and because it stills the three kinds of distress, it is celebrated as the Deity. [55]<-

**The Deity** <note>original: "Devatā"</note>: O **Pārvatī** <note>The Goddess to whom this scripture is revealed</note>! Because the divine presence takes its stand within the **body** <note>original: "deha"</note> of the devotee, grants **boons** <note>original: "varadānāt"</note>, and calms the **three types of suffering** <term>Tāpatraya: the threefold miseries—those caused by oneself, by other beings, and by natural or divine forces</term>, it is called **Devatā**.

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter of the Kulārṇava Tantra. He provides "mystical linguistics" (nirukta) to explain why sacred tools like the rosary, the pot, and the ritual seat are named as they are, linking their phonetic roots to their spiritual functions.</meta>

# In the Kulārṇava Tantra

->Because it places wealth acquired by right means upon the limbs,<-
->And because it provides all-around protection, O Goddess, it is called Nyāsa. [56]<-

**Nyāsa** <term>Nyāsa: the ritual practice of "placing" or "touching" various parts of the body while reciting mantras to imbue the physical self with divine energy</term>: Because it involves the placing <note>original: *viniveśanāt*</note> of treasures or energies acquired through righteous means <note>original: *nyāyopārjita*</note> onto the limbs, and because it acts as a total protector <note>original: *sarvarakṣākarāt*</note>, it is known as **Nyāsa**.

->Because they grant joy to the gods and melt their hearts,<-
->Therefore, O Queen of the Kula, they are known as Mudrās and must be shown. [57]<-

**Mudrā** <term>Mudrā: symbolic hand gestures or seals used in yoga and ritual to seal energy and communicate with the divine</term>: O **Kuleśvarī** <note>original: "Queen of the Kula," a title for the Goddess</note>! Because these gestures give pleasure <note>original: *mudam*</note> to the gods and cause their hearts to melt with compassion <note>original: *drāva*</note>, they are celebrated as **Mudrās**.

->Because it yields endless fruit and destroys all sin,<-
->And because it brings gain through the alphabet of the Mother, it is the Rosary. [58]<-

**Akṣamālikā** <term>Akṣamālikā: a ritual rosary or garland of beads, where each bead often corresponds to a letter of the Sanskrit alphabet</term>: Because it bears fruit that is endless <note>original: *ananta*</note>, completely burns away <note>original: *kṣapita*</note> all impurities, and brings about spiritual gain through the power of the "Mother" letters <note>original: *mātṛkā*, referring to the sacred phonemes of the alphabet</note>, it is called **Akṣamālikā**.

->Because the Dakini who occupies it is auspicious,<-
->Because it is the abode of the Yoginis, and because of its beauty, it is called a Mandala. [59]<-

**Maṇḍala** <term>Maṇḍala: a sacred geometric diagram representing the palace of a deity or the structure of the universe</term>: Because the **Dākinī** <note>a type of female semi-divine spirit</note> residing within is auspicious <note>original: *maṅgalatvāt*</note>, because it is the meeting place of the hosts of **Yoginīs** <note>female practitioners or goddesses</note>, and because of its inherent grace and beauty <note>original: *lalitatvāt*</note>, O Goddess, it is known as a **Maṇḍala**.

->Because it takes the form of the lotus-seat and destroys lower states,<-
->And because it pacifies boundless sin, it is celebrated as the Pitcher. [60]<-

**Kalaśa** <term>Kalaśa: a consecrated water pot or pitcher used in rituals to represent the deity or the womb of creation</term>: Because it resembles the form of a lotus-seat <note>original: *kamalāsana*</note>, because it destroys the lower or "heavy" elements of existence <note>original: *laghu-tattva*</note>, and because it stills or pacifies <note>original: *śamita*</note> immeasurable sins, it is called a **Kalaśa**.

->Because it protects always from the Lord of Death and all fears,<-
->Therefore, O Queen of the Kula, it is spoken of as a Yantra. [61]<-

**Yantra** <term>Yantra: a "machine" or mystical diagram used as an instrument of worship, protection, and meditation</term>: Because it constantly saves or protects <note>original: *trāyate*</note> the practitioner from all fears, including those caused by **Yama** <note>the God of Death</note> and elemental spirits, it is called a **Yantra**, O Kuleśvarī.

->Because it grants self-attainment and wards off all disease,<-
->And because it gives the nine perfections, it is called a Seat, O Beloved. [62]<-

**Āsana** <term>Āsana: a ritual seat, rug, or physical posture that provides a stable foundation for spiritual practice</term>: O My Beloved! Because it provides the attainment of the Self <note>original: *ātmasiddhi*</note>, prevents all diseases <note>original: *sarvaroga*</note>, and bestows the **Nine Perfections** <note>original: *navasiddhi*; these are supernatural powers or spiritual accomplishments</note>, it is called **Āsana**.

### Seventeenth Chapter

->Because it quells the net of illusion and defines the path of liberation,<-
->And because it removes the eight-fold sorrows, it is known as Wine. [63]<-
->Because it takes the form of the Great Gift and is the sole cause of the ground of Union,<-
->And because it generates My own State, O Goddess, it is known as Wine. [64]<-

**Wine** <term>Madya: literally "intoxicant"; in this context, it refers to the ritual nectar that induces a state of divine intoxication or expanded consciousness</term>: Because it destroys the entire web of **illusion** <note>original: *māyā*</note>, reveals the way to **liberation** <note>original: *moksha*</note>, and separates the seeker from the **eight afflictions** <note>original: *aṣṭa-duḥkha*; traditionally these are: hatred, shame, fear, doubt, reproach, lineage pride, cultural ego, and status</note>, it is called *Madya*. Furthermore, because it signifies the **Great Gift** <note>original: *mahādāna*</note>, because the sacred ground of **sacrifice** <note>original: *yāga*</note> is the *only* place that requires its use, and because it produces the **state of Shiva** <note>original: *Mad-bhāva*, literally "My state"</note>, it is called *Madya*.

->Because it is served by the pure-minded and grants sovereignty, O Beloved,<-
->And because it bestows the very form of the gods, it is celebrated as Liquor. [65]<-

**Liquor** <term>Surā: wine or spirits; the name is etymologically linked here to the "Suras" (gods)</term>: O My Beloved! Because it is partaken of by those with **pure minds** <note>original: *sumanasaḥ*</note>, because it grants the **sovereign kingdom** <note>original: *rājya*</note> of one’s desires, and because it bestows the **form of a god** <note>original: *surākāra*</note>, it is called *Surā*.

->Because its nature is like the moon and it removes the fear of death,<-
->And because it causes the Truth to shine forth, it is called Nectar, O Beloved. [66]<-

**Nectar** <term>Amṛta: the "deathless" nectar of immortality; in yogic practice, it is the divine fluid that flows from the crown chakra during deep meditation</term>: O My Beloved! Because it possesses the nature of the **nectar-rayed moon** <note>original: *amṛtāṃśu*</note>, because it wards off the **fear of death** <note>original: *mṛtyu*</note>, and because it is the catalyst for the **revelation of Truth** <note>original: *tattva-prakāśa*</note>, it is called *Amṛta*.

->Because the universe itself is its form and it is the support for the phases of creation,<-
->And because it protects the fallen, O Goddess, it is called the Vessel. [67]<-

**The Vessel** <term>Pātra: the ritual cup or bowl; symbolically, it refers to a "worthy vessel" or student capable of holding divine knowledge</term>: Because the entire universe is the very **substance to be consumed** <note>original: *pānāṅga*</note>, because it serves as the foundation for the **triads and quartets** <note>original: *tri-catuṣka*; referring to various cosmic groupings, such as the three states of consciousness or the four stages of speech</note> of creation, and because it **protects** <note>original: *trāṇa*</note> those who have fallen, it is called *Pātra*.

->Because it is the form of fire and is dear to the Creator-God,<-
->And because it guards what is placed within it, the wise know it as the Base. [68]<-

**The Base** <term>Ādhāra: the ritual stand or support for the vessel; also refers to the "root support" or Mūlādhāra chakra</term>: Because it has the nature of **Fire** <note>original: *āśuśukṣaṇi*</note>, because it is beloved by the **Creator Lord** <note>original: *dhātṛ-deva*</note>, and because it **guards** <note>original: *rakṣaṇa*</note> that which is placed upon it, the wise call it *Ādhāra*.

->Because it generates auspiciousness and bestows the bliss of consciousness,<-
->And because it is dear to all the gods, O Goddess, it is called Meat. [69]<-

**Meat** <term>Māṃsa: ritual flesh; symbolically represents the "flesh" of worldly attachment being offered into the fire of wisdom</term>: Because it produces **auspiciousness** <note>original: *māṅgalya*</note>, because it grants the **bliss of consciousness** <note>original: *saṃvid-ānanda*</note>, and because it is **dear to all the gods** <note>original: *sarva-deva-priya*</note>, it is called *Māṃsa*.

<summary>This page provides the esoteric etymologies for the ritual elements of the Tantric feast, including wine, nectar, meat, and their vessels. Each element is reinterpreted not as a mundane object, but as a symbolic tool for destroying illusion and achieving the state of Shiva.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter of the Kulārṇava Tantra. Having previously defined the spiritual essence of ritual wine and liquor through esoteric etymology (nirukta), Lord Shiva now proceeds to explain the hidden meanings behind the various offerings and acts of worship, such as scent, flowers, and unbroken grains.</meta>

### In the Kulārṇava Tantra

->Because it quells the consequences of previous births and prevents the cycle of birth and death,<-
->And because it yields complete results, O Beloved, it is called Worship. [70]<-

**Worship** <term>Pūjā: the act of honoring a deity; here the author derives the word from the roots *pū* (to complete/purify) and *ja* (birth/death)</term>: O My Beloved! Because it destroys the legacy of **previous births** <note>original: *pūrvajanma*</note>, because it prevents the cycle of **birth and death** <note>original: *janmamṛtyu*</note>, and because it yields the full fruit of spiritual practice, it is called *Pūjā*.

->Because it grants desired fruits and supports the four-fold goals of life,<-
->And because it delights all the gods, it is celebrated as Honoring. [71]<-

**Honoring** <term>Arcana: formal ritual adoration</term>: Because it yields the **desired fruit** <note>original: *abhīṣṭaphala*</note>, holds the rewards of the **four goals of human life** <note>original: *caturvarga*; these are Dharma (duty), Artha (prosperity), Kama (desire), and Moksha (liberation)</note>, and **delights** <note>original: *nandanāt*</note> all the gods, it is called *Arcana*.

->Because it generates nine-fold bliss for the God who is Truth,<-
->And who is surrounded by His retinue, it is celebrated as Satiation. [72]<-

**Satiation** <term>Tarpaṇa: the act of pleasing or "satiating" a deity through liquid offerings</term>: Because it gives **nine-fold delight** <note>original: *navānanda*; likely referring to the nine forms of bliss or the nine aesthetic flavors (rasas)</note> to the God, who is the very essence of **Truth** <note>original: *tattva*</note>, and who is surrounded by His **retinue** <note>original: *parivāra*</note>, it is called *Tarpaṇa*.

->Because it destroys the afflictions of deep and boundless misfortune,<-
->And because it bestows the knowledge of righteousness, it is known as Scent. [73]<-

**Scent** <term>Gandha: typically refers to sandalwood paste or other aromatic substances offered to the deity</term>: Because it destroys the **deep and boundless** <note>original: *gambhīra-apāra*</note> affliction of misfortune, and because it provides the knowledge of **righteousness** <note>original: *dharma*</note>, it is called *Gandha*.

->Because it gives birth to all that is based on smell and shows the path to salvation,<-
->And because it subdues burnt grief, it is called Fragrance. [74]<-

**Fragrance** <term>Āmoda: a strong, pervasive perfume; etymologically linked here to "joy"</term>: Because it causes the birth of all that is based on **Smell** <note>original: *āghrāṇana*; referring to the elemental principle or *tattva* of earth</note>, shows the **path of salvation** <note>original: *mokṣamārga*</note>, and subjugates **cursed grief** <note>original: *dagdhaduḥkha*; literally "burnt sorrow"</note>, it is called *Āmoda*.

->Because they yield food, O Mistress of the Kula, and exhaust all sins,<-
->And because they create identity with the Divine, O Goddess, they are celebrated as Unbroken Grains. [75]<-

**Unbroken Grains** <term>Akṣata: raw, whole rice grains; the word literally means "unbroken" or "undecayed"</term>: Because they yield **food** <note>original: *anna*</note>, **completely eliminate** <note>original: *kṣapita*</note> all sin, and make the seeker **identified** <note>original: *tādātmya*</note> with the Supreme Truth, they are called *Akṣata*.

->Because it increases merit and removes the heap of sins,<-
->And because it yields much wealth, it is known as a Flower. [76]<-

**Flower** <term>Puṣpa: the standard floral offering</term>: Because it increases **merit** <note>original: *puṇya*</note>, removes the **heap of sin** <note>original: *pāpa*</note>, and yields **abundant wealth** <note>original: *puṣkalārtha*</note>, it is called *Puṣpa*.

<summary>This page provides the esoteric etymologies for standard ritual offerings, shifting the focus from physical substances (flowers, grain, scent) to their spiritual functions in destroying sin and granting liberation. It defines key Tantric terms like Pūjā, Arcana, and Akṣata through a symbolic lens.</summary>
<keywords>Pūjā, Arcana, Tarpaṇa, Gandha, Āmoda, Akṣata, Puṣpa, Caturvarga, Dharma, Moksha, Kulārṇava Tantra</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter of the Kulārṇava Tantra, where Lord Shiva explains the esoteric etymology of ritual objects. Following the previous definitions of "Worship," "Honoring," and "Satiation," this section defines the inner spiritual significance of incense, lamps, food offerings, and sacrificial gifts.</meta>

### Chapter Seventeen

->Because it drives away the stench of the great faults completely,<-
->And because it generates supreme bliss, it is known as Incense. [77]<-

**Incense** <term>Dhūpa: fragrant smoke offered to a deity</term>: Because it completely drives away <note>original: *dhūta*</note> the foul smell of spiritual blemishes and because it yields **supreme bliss** <note>original: *paramānanda*</note>, it is called *dhūpa*.

->Because it discards the ego and the deep darkness of long-standing ignorance,<-
->And because it illuminates the Supreme Truth, it is known as the Lamp. [78]<-

**Lamp** <term>Dīpa: a ritual light source, usually a wick in oil or ghee</term>: Because it dispels **extending** <note>original: *dīrgha*</note> ignorance, the heavy darkness of the soul, and the sense of ego, and because it brings to light the **Supreme Truth** <note>original: *paratattva*</note>, it is called *dīpa*.

->Because it stills the darkness of delusion and prevents the distress of decay,<-
->Because it grants a celestial form and reveals the Supreme Truth,<-
->The "Lamp of Liberation" is famous as the only means for the path to freedom. [79]<-

**Lamp of Liberation** <term>Mokṣa-dīpa: the spiritual light that leads to salvation</term>: Because it eliminates the darkness of **delusion** <note>original: *moha*</note>, prevents the **distress of decay** <note>original: *kṣayārti*</note>, bestows a **celestial form** <note>original: *divyarūpa*</note>, and lights up the highest reality, it is celebrated as the lamp of *Mokṣa*, the singular tool for achieving liberation.

->O Mistress of the Kula, the four types of substances endowed with the six tastes,<-
->Bring satisfaction when they are offered; thus, it is called the Food Offering. [80]<-

**Food Offering** <term>Naivedya: an offering of food; in Tantra, this often includes four categories: that which is chewed, sucked, licked, or drunk</term>: O **Mistress of the Kula** <note>original: *Kuleśāni*; a title for the Goddess</note>! Because this substance of four kinds, possessing the **six tastes** <note>original: *ṣaḍrasa*; sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent</note>, provides satisfaction through the act of **being offered** <note>original: *nivedanāt*</note>, it is called the great *naivedya*.

->Because it is the cause of joy for many different kinds of living beings,<-
->And because it destroys the sin that is stuck to one, it is called the Sacrificial Offering. [81]<-

**Sacrificial Offering** <term>Bali: a portion of food or a gift offered to spirits, animals, or the elements</term>: Because it is dear to a **wide variety** <note>original: *bahu-prakāra*</note> of living creatures and because it wipes away the sin that has **stuck** <note>original: *lipta*</note> to the practitioner, it is called *bali*.

->O Beloved, the purification of the three essentials occurs by your service alone;<-
->Because it is the cause for revealing the Truth, it is called the Three Essentials. [82]<-

**The Three Essentials** <term>Tattvatraya: the three-fold fundamental principles, often identified in this tradition as the Self, the Knowledge, and the Divine (Atma, Vidya, and Shiva)</term>: O My Beloved! By the mere act of serving you, the three elements are purified; because it serves as the means to reveal the **Truth** <note>original: *tattva*</note> of this **triad** <note>original: *traya*</note>, it is called *tattvatraya*.

<summary>This page provides esoteric definitions (nirukta) for ritual offerings—incense, lamps, food, and sacrifice—explaining how each physical act corresponds to a profound internal spiritual transformation or purification.</summary>
<keywords>incense, ritual lamp, liberation, food offering, sacrifice, three principles, Kuleśāni, esoteric etymology, Tantric ritual</keywords>
