<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter of the Kulārṇava Tantra, where Lord Shiva explains the esoteric meanings of ritual actions to Goddess Parvati. Having previously defined incense and lamps, he now proceeds to define the spiritual significance of the ritual sip (caluka), the consecrated offering (prasāda), ritual drinking (pāna), and the stages of worship (upāsti, puraścaraṇa, upahāra, and udvāsana).</meta>

### In the Kulārṇava Tantra

->Because it attains the fruit of the fourfold goals of life,<-
->Because it snatches away the bonds of ignorance,<-
->And because it is the root of auspicious virtue, it is called *caluka*. [83]<-

**Ritual Sip** <term>Caluka: a small amount of water or liquid taken in the palm</term>: O My Beloved! Because it secures the fruits of the **four goals of life** <note>original: *caturvarga* - virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation</note>, because it **plunders** <note>original: *luṇṭhita*</note> the grip of **ignorance** <note>original: *ajñāna*</note>, and because it is the foundation of **auspicious virtue** <note>original: *kalyāṇadharma*</note>, it is known as *caluka*.

->Because it generates the bliss of spiritual light,<-
->Because it grants the state of perfect harmony,<-
->And because of the vision of the Supreme Truth, it is called *prasāda*. [84]<-

**Grace or Consecrated Offering** <term>Prasāda: literally "clarity" or "favor"; food or items offered to a deity</term>: Because it produces **bliss** <note>original: *ānanda*</note> in the form of **spiritual light** <note>original: *prakāśa*</note>, because it bestows **harmony** <note>original: *sāmarasya* - the essential oneness of the soul and the divine</note>, and because it enables the **vision** <note>original: *darśana*</note> of the **Supreme Truth** <note>original: *paratattva*</note>, it is called *prasāda*.

->Because it severs the bonds, O Goddess, and prevents hell,<-
->Because it is purifying, O Supreme Mistress, it is called *pāna*. [85]<-

**Ritual Drinking** <term>Pāna: the act of drinking a consecrated liquid</term>: O Supreme Mistress! Because it cuts through the **bonds** <note>original: *pāśa* - the spiritual nooses that tie the soul to worldly existence</note>, prevents the experience of **hell** <note>original: *naraka*</note>, and because of its **purifying nature** <note>original: *pāvanāt*</note>, it is called *pāna*.

->By deed, by mind, and by speech, in all states and at all times,<-
->Service performed nearby according to the rules is called *upāsti*. [86]<-

**Worshipful Service** <term>Upāsti: the act of "sitting near" or devout service</term>: Consistent service performed in close proximity to the divine as prescribed by tradition—carried out through one's actions, thoughts, and words in every state of being—is called *upāsti*.

->Because it pleases the chosen Deity through five-limbed adoration,<-
->And because it walks in front of the devotee, it is *puraścaraṇa*, O Beloved. [87]<-

**Preparatory Rite** <term>Puraścaraṇa: a preliminary ritual to empower a mantra</term>: Because it brings joy to the **chosen Deity** <note>original: *iṣṭadevatā*</note> through five-part worship, and because it **walks in front** <note>original: *puraḥ carati*</note> of the devotee to lead them to success, it is called *puraścaraṇa*.

->The ritual acts beginning with "the invitation" and so on,<-
->Performed according to the rules in twelve or sixteen steps, are known as *upahāra*. [88]<-

**Ritual Offering** <term>Upahāra: a formal gift or presentation to the deity</term>: The proper performance of rituals starting with the **invitation** <note>original: *āvāhana*</note> and continuing through twelve or sixteen specific **services** <note>original: *upacāra*</note> is remembered as *upahāra*.

->Having worshipped the Deity with their attendants using sixteen services,<-
->Sending the Deity back to their own place is called *udvāsana*, O Beloved. [89]<-

**The Ritual Conclusion** <term>Udvāsana: the formal dismissal or "re-seating" of the deity</term>: O My Beloved! After fully worshipping the Deity along with their **surrounding powers** <note>original: *sāvṛtti* or *āvaraṇa-devatā*</note> using the sixteen standard offerings, the act of **sending them back to their own place** <note>original: *svasthānapreṣaṇam* - often back into the worshipper's own heart</note> is called *udvāsana*.

<summary>This page provides the esoteric etymological definitions for various ritual components, framing them as tools for spiritual liberation and union with the divine. It covers the symbolic meanings of ritual sipping, offerings, drinking, and the sequence of formal worship from invitation to dismissal.</summary>
<keywords>Caluka, Prasāda, Pāna, Upāsti, Puraścaraṇa, Upahāra, Udvāsana, Kularnava Tantra, four goals of life, spiritual bonds, ritual services</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the seventeenth chapter of the Kulārṇava Tantra, where Lord Shiva defines the ritual actions and offerings used in the worship of the Divine. Having just finished the definitions of the ritual sip and the consecrated offering, he now explains the specific mudras (gestures) and substances used to invite and honor the deity.</meta>

### Chapter Seventeen

->Calling the deity for the purpose of worship is known as Invocation.<-
->Placing the deity upon the seat, O Lady of the Kula, is Installation. [60]<-

**Invocation** <term>Āvāhana: the act of calling or inviting a deity to manifest</term>: O Mistress of the Kula <note>original: *Kulanāyike* — a title for the Goddess as the head of the tantric lineage</note>! The act of calling the Deity to attend the worship is called *Āvāhana*.

**Installation** <term>Sthāpana: the act of fixing or grounding the divine presence</term>: Placing the Deity upon a suitable and prepared seat is known as *Sthāpana*.

->The state of being positioned face-to-face is called Bringing Near.<-
->Preventing any movement elsewhere is called Restraining. [61]<-

**Presence** <term>Sannidhāpana: bringing the deity into close proximity</term>: Establishing a mutual face-to-face presence between the worshiper and the worshiped is called *Sannidhāpana*.

**Restraint** <term>Sannirodhana: confining the presence to the ritual space</term>: Ensuring the divine presence remains fixed and does not depart to any other place is called *Sannirodhana*.

->The ritual placement of the six limbs on the body of the deity is Integration.<-
->The act of covering is declared to be Veiling. [62]<-

**Integration** <term>Sakalīkṛti: "making whole"; the ritual of making the deity's form complete</term>: Performing the **Six-Limb Placement** <note>original: *Şaḍaṅga Nyāsa* — a ritual where specific mantras are assigned to parts of the body (heart, head, etc.)</note> upon the form of the Deity is called *Sakalīkṛti*.

**Veiling** <term>Avaguṇṭhana: a protective or secretive covering gesture</term>: The act of ritually covering or screening the deity is called *Avaguṇṭhana*.

->Showing the Cow Gesture is Nectarizing, O Beloved.<-
->The folded palms with the words "Forgive me" is Divinizing, O Beloved.<-
->One should speak a welcome and an inquiry of welfare before the deity. [63]<-

**Nectarizing** <term>Amṛtīkaraṇa: the act of turning the offering into "Amrita" or divine nectar</term>: O My Beloved! Displaying the **Cow Gesture** <note>original: *Dhenu Mudrā* — a hand gesture where the fingers are interlaced to resemble the udders of a cow, symbolizing the flowing of divine milk/nectar</note> is known as *Amṛtīkaraṇa*.

**Divinizing** <term>Paramīkaraṇa: "making supreme"; the final sanctification</term>: Showing the **Folded Palms Gesture** <note>original: *Añjali*</note> after saying "Forgive me" <note>original: *Kṣamasva*</note> is, O My Beloved, called *Paramīkaraṇa*.

**Welcome** <term>Svāgata: a formal greeting</term>: Asking the Deity about their well-being and comfort is called *Svāgata*.

->Water for the feet is said to contain millet, durva grass, lotus, and blue pea.<-
->Water for sipping is said to contain jasmine, cloves, and kakkola berries. [64]<-

**Water for the Feet** <term>Pādya: the first hospitable offering of water to wash the feet of a guest</term>: This offering consists of **Millet** <note>original: *Śyāmāka* - Panicum frumentaceum</note>, **Bermuda Grass** <note>original: *Dūrvā* - Panicum dactylon</note>, **Lotus** <note>original: *Abja*</note>, and **Blue Pea** <note>original: *Viṣṇukrāntā* - Clitoria ternatea</note>.

**Water for Sipping** <term>Ācamanīya: water offered to the deity to rinse the mouth</term>: This contains **Cloves** <note>original: *Lavaṅga*</note>, **Spanish Jasmine** <note>original: *Jāti* - Jasminum grandiflorum</note>, and **Kakkola** <note>an aromatic berry, often Piper cubeba</note>.

->Because it pacifies all sins, and increases wealth and children,<-
->And because it yields priceless fruits, it is called the Offering. [65]<-

**Ritual Offering** <term>Arghya: a respectful offering of water, usually to the head or hands</term>: It is called *Arghya* because it destroys all transgressions, increases one's wealth and lineage, and bestows rewards that are beyond price.

<meta>This page continues the definitions of ritual offerings from Chapter Seventeen of the Kulārṇava Tantra. While the previous page focused on the preliminary gestures of invocation and installation, this section defines the material offerings—the liquids, scents, and grains—presented to the deity, and concludes with instructions on the sanctity of the scripture itself.</meta>

### In the Kulārṇava Tantra

->White mustard, unbroken rice, the tip of Kusha grass, and sesame seeds;<-
->Barley, fragrant paste, fruit, and flowers are declared to be the eight-fold offering. [66]<-

**Eight-fold Offering** <term>Aṣṭāṅga-arghya: a formal libation consisting of eight sacred substances</term>: 1. White mustard <note>original: *Siddhārtha*</note>, 2. Unbroken grains of rice <note>original: *Akṣata*</note>, 3. The tip of the sacred grass <note>original: *Kuśāgra* — botanical name *Poa cynosuroides*</note>, 4. Sesame <note>original: *Tila*</note>, 5. Barley <note>original: *Yava*</note>, 6. Fragrant sandalwood paste <note>original: *Gandha*</note>, 7. Fruits <note>original: *Phala*</note>, and 8. Flowers <note>original: *Puṣpa*</note>. Together, these constitute the **Aṣṭāṅga-arghya**.

->The mixture of honey, clarified butter, and curd is called the Honey-Mixture, O Mistress of the Kula.<-
->Washing the body with fragrant waters [67]<-
->along with moon-white sandalwood, musk, and black aloe-wood is described as the Bath.<-

**Honey-Mixture** <term>Madhuparka: a traditional offering of hospitality for a guest or deity</term>: 1. Honey <note>original: *Madhu*</note>, 2. Clarified butter <note>original: *Ājya* or Ghee</note>, and 3. Curd or yogurt <note>original: *Dahī*</note>. These three, O Mistress of the Kula, constitute the **Madhuparka**.

**Ritual Bath** <term>Snāna: the ceremonial purification of the deity's image</term>: Washing the body with water perfumed with sandalwood, musk <note>original: *Kastūrī*</note>, and aloe-wood <note>original: *Agaru* or *Aquilaria Agallocha*</note> is called **Snāna**.

->The eight-limbed prostration is declared to be the Salutation, my Beloved. [68]<-
->All this world, including the moving and the unmoving, is called the Field.<-
->He by whom that Field is protected is called the Guardian of the Field. [69]<-

**Salutation** <term>Vandana: the act of bowing or showing reverence</term>: O My Beloved! The **Eight-limbed Salutation** <note>original: *Aṣṭāṅga-praṇipāta* — a prostration where the forehead, chest, hands, knees, and feet touch the ground</note> is **Vandana**.

**The Field** <term>Kṣetra: the "field" of existence or a sacred site</term>: The entire world is called **Kṣetra**.

**Guardian of the Field** <term>Kṣetrapāla: a protective deity who watches over a specific territory or spiritual boundary</term>: The Supreme Guard of the **Field** is called **Kṣetrapāla**.

->Thus I have told you briefly the inner meaning of the names of the Guru and others.<-
->O Supreme Goddess, one who knows this in summary is a true Worshiper. [100]<-

O Supreme Goddess <note>original: *Maheśāni*</note>! Thus I have disclosed to You in brief the contemplation of the names of the Guru and the related concepts. One who knows these is a **Kaulika** <note>an initiate of the Kula tradition</note>.

->This is the secret of all secrets, O Great Goddess.<-
->The Upper Tradition has been described in brief and not in detail. [101]<-

O Great Goddess <note>original: *Maheśvari*</note>! This **Upper Tradition** <term>Ūrdhvāmnāya: the highest and most esoteric of the five or six "currents" of Tantric revelation</term>, which is the secret of all secrets, has been described only in brief.

->This scripture, the Ocean of the Kula, resides in the hearts of the Yoginis.<-
->It is disclosed by Me today, but it must be kept secret with great effort. [102]<-

This **Kulārṇava Scripture** <note>original: *Kulārṇava Śāstra* — literally "The Ocean of the Kula"</note> is situated in the hearts of the **Yoginis** <note>female spirits or highly realized practitioners</note>. I have disclosed it today, but it should be kept a secret with all effort.

->O Supreme Goddess, one should not place the book in the house of a beast-like man.<-
->One should not give it into the hands of a beast-like man, nor read it in his presence.<-
->One should not read it while intoxicated, nor should the book ever be placed upon the ground. [103]<-

**Prohibition of keeping the book in the house of a beast-like person** <term>Paśu: literally "animal"; refers to an uninitiated person who lives by instinct without spiritual awareness</term>:

O Supreme Goddess! One should not leave the manuscript in the house of a **Paśu**...

It concludes with strict warnings against sharing the sacred text with uninitiated individuals (Paśus) or treating the physical book with disrespect.</summary>

# Page 263
### Seventeenth Chapter 263

The <term>Paśu</term> <note>literally "beast" or "animal," referring here to the uninitiated or those bound by worldly conventions who lack spiritual insight</note>. It should not be given into the hands of a <term>Paśu</term> or read before a <term>Paśu</term>. The chapter on the Divine Nectar <note>original: *Āsavollāsa*</note> should not be read [publicly] and the book must not be dropped on the ground.

->One should always worship the book with devotion and receive its knowledge from the mouth of a <term>Guru</term> <note>spiritual teacher</note>.<-
->It should never be disclosed to a son who is unfit, nor ever to a disciple who has not been initiated. [104]<-
->If one reveals it out of affection, greed, or fear, they will surely meet their destruction in a short time.<-

**Daily worship of the Book:**

It should always be worshipped with devotion and its knowledge obtained from the mouth of a Guru. It should not be given to an incompetent son or an uninitiated disciple. One who discloses it out of greed, love or fear soon meets his destruction.

->O Goddess! Whatever wisdom exists, all of that has been briefly declared by Me,<-
->for the benefit of the <term>Sādhakas</term> <note>spiritual practitioners</note> who desire the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and final liberation. [105]<-

O Devi! I have described all what explicitly needs to be known for the benefit of the Sādhakas desirous of the fruits of enjoyment <note>original: *Bhukti*</note> and liberation <note>original: *Mukti*</note>.

->The one who reads the greatness of the Upper Tradition in the presence of the <term>Śrī Cakra</term>,<-
->or who listens to it with supreme devotion, O Goddess, that person is a true <term>Kaulika</term>. [106]<-
->The merits gained from vows, ritual baths, penance, pilgrimages,<-
->sacrifices, and the worship of various deities— [107]<-
->he obtains those fruits multiplied ten-million fold; of this there is no doubt.<-
->He shall dwell in Your very presence; there is no need for further deliberation on this. [108]<-

**Fruit of reading or hearing the glory of the Upper Tradition:**

One who reads or hears the Glory of the Upper Tradition <note>original: *Ūrdhvāmnāya*</note> near the <term>Śrī Cakra</term> <note>the supreme yantra or sacred geometric diagram of the Goddess</note>, is a real <term>Kaulika</term> <note>a follower of the Kula path</note>. Whatever meritorious fruits are obtained from observances, bathing in the <term>Tīrthas</term> <note>sacred river crossings or pilgrimage sites</note>, pilgrimage, sacrifice and worship of a Deity, are all obtained a billion times more from the aforesaid Glory and the Kaulika undoubtedly resides in Your proximity.

->Thus ends the Seventeenth Chapter in the glorious *Kulārṇava Tantra*,<-
->which is the gateway to Nirvana and Liberation, the Great Secret,<-
->the best among all the sacred traditions, a work of one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses,<-
->contained within the Fifth Section, titled the Tantra of the Upper Tradition. [17]<-
->**THE BOOK IS COMPLETED.**<-

<summary>This concluding page of the Kulārṇava Tantra emphasizes the strict secrecy required of the practitioner and the immense spiritual merit gained from studying the "Upper Tradition" (Ūrdhvāmnāya). It ends with a formal colophon identifying the text as a supreme authority on the path to liberation.</summary>
